INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel,
Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorised by the Committee to present its
Report, do hereby present this Twenty Ninth Report on Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism.
2. The subject Public Grievance Redressal Mechanism was identified by the Committee as a
part of consideration of the subject “Administrative Reforms”.
3. In view of the importance of the subject, the Committee visited Goa, Mumbai, Bangalore,
Bhubaneshwar, Chennai, Hyderabad, Kochi, Port Blair, Kolkata, Jaipur, Ahmedabad and Bhopal and
held discussions with various authorities, organisations, individuals on “Public Grievances
Redressal Mechanism” in Public Sector Enterprises/Undertakings/Trusts and leading Banks.
4. The Committee held discussions on the subject with the Heads of 24 banks and 40 PSUs
to collect information related to the subject and to acquaint latter with the mechanisms available
for redressal of grievances.
5. The Secretary, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions made a detailed
presentation on the subject on 14th December 2005. The Committee also heard the Secretaries and
senior officers of the Six Ministries of the Government of India viz. Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare, Ministry of Mines, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Ministry of
Information and Broadcasting and Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.
6. While considering the subject, the Committee took note of the following documents/
information placed before it:—
(i) Background notes on the subject furnished by the Government;
(ii) Guidelines for Grievance Redressal Mechanism in Government of India;
(iii) Replies received from the Government to the questionnaire prepared by the Secretariat;
(iv) Submissions by the banks/PSUs on the subject; and
(v) Replies received from banks/PSUs to the questionnaire prepared by the Secretariat.
7. The Committee considered and adopted the Report on 21st October, 2008.
8. For the facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
DR. E.M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN

Public Grievances, Law and Justice.

1
REPORT
In 2004 the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public
Grievances, Law and Justice, after its bifurcation from Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Home Affairs, continued to examine the subject ‘Administrative Reforms’. The
Committee then chose to examine and report on the ‘Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism’ as
a part of Administrative Reforms.
CITIZEN’S CHARTER AND PGRM
The Committee feels that Citizen’s Charter of the Ministries/Departments/Organizations/
PSUs/Banks/Institutions etc. invariably provide for a strong inbuilt mechanism to redress the
grievances being faced by its stakeholders. In that backdrop, it was felt necessary to examine
Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism’ (PGRM) vis a vis the Citizen’s Charter.
2. The future of an organisation depends on how successfully it can usher the culture of
customer orientation in all aspects of its functioning. Well-defined and formatted consumer policy
statements need to be developed. The United Nations Guidelines for Consumer Protection adopted
by the UN General Assembly on April 9, 1985 gives a fairly well-defined and formatted consumer
policy statement at the international level. The Guidelines call upon Member Governments to
develop, maintain and strengthen a strong consumer policy, and provide for enhanced protection
of consumers by enunciating various steps and measures. In 1995, the Guidelines were reviewed,
and some issues, which needed further elaboration and expansion, were espoused by consumer
organisations. Among the issues are: access to basic needs, appropriate regulatory policies,
sustainable consumption, etc. Some countries such as Japan and Sweden have adopted Consumer
Policy Statements, and the concept of Citizen’s Charter has gained wide acceptance in many
countries, particularly in the UK.
3. The Government of India also firmly believes in the need for a total change of it’s image
and orientation as the citizens have become increasingly aware of their rights and civic
responsibilities. The challenge, therefore, for the administration is not merely to respond to
increased demands of the citizens but also to anticipate the same. The task becomes further
challenging due to the rapidly escalating expectations of the citizens. It was against this backdrop
that from 1996 onwards a consensus emerged in the Government on effective and responsive
administration culminating in the Chief Ministers’ Conference convened by the Prime Minister of
India on May 24, 1997. One of the major decisions of the Conference was to formulate and
operationalise Citizen’s Charters at the Centre and in the States in sectors which dealt with a large
public interface such as Railways, Telecom, Post, Public Distribution Systems, Hospitals, Revenue,
Electricity, Petroleum, Banks, etc.
4. A good Citizen’s Charter should have the following components:
• Vision and Mission Statement of the Organisation.
• Details of Business Transacted by the Organisation.
• Details or Citizens’ or ‘Clients’.
• Statement of Services Including Standards, Quality, Time-Frame, etc., Provided to
each Citizen/Client Group separately and how/where to get the services.
• Details of Grievance Redress Mechanism and how to access it.

2
• Expectations from the ‘Citizens’ or ‘Clients’.
• Additional Commitments such as Compensation in the Event of failure of Service
Delivery.
• A Road Map to Formulate the Citizen’s Charter in an Organisation Formulation of
Citizen’s Charter is a crucial step and needs to be done very meticulously. A broad
framework for formulation would include the following:
• Identification of all stakeholders in the Organisation.
• Setting up of a Core Group in the Organisation — consisting of representatives
from all Stakeholders which inter alia  may include Top Management, Middle
Management, cutting edge level staff representatives, strategic partners,
customers/clients, etc.
• Overseeing by the Core Group the formulation of the Citizen’s Charter,
approving it and monitoring its implementation thereafter.
• Setting up of a Task Force in the Organisation to formulate the Citizen’s Charter.
• Consultation with all the stakeholders.
• Formulation of the Draft Citizen’s Charter.
• Pilot run of the Citizen’s Charter.
• Approval of the Charter with necessary modifications by the Core Group and
the head of the Organisation and implementation.
• Review and evaluation.
5. Prompt and Effective Redress of Grievances: This calls for the following:
(a) All grievances should be necessarily acknowledged, with an interim reply within 3 days
of receipt and redressed within 3 months of receipt in the Organisation. The same time
limit should apply even if co-ordination with subsidiary offices or another Department/
Organisation is involved. In such instances special efforts, to be suo moto disclosed
when reports are called, should be made.
(b) No grievance is to be rejected without having been independently examined. At a
minimum, this means that an officer superior, to the one who delayed taking the original
decision or took the original decision that is cause for grievance, should actually examine
the case as well as the reply, intended to be sent to the grievance holder.
(c) Make the ‘Director of Grievances’ effective through the following inter-related steps:—
(i) Secretaries/Organisational Heads ensuring that Director of Grievances are fully
‘empowered’ in accordance with instructions to perform their role.
(ii) All grievance representations received in the Department/Organisation, either by
mail, fax, e-mail to be invariably routed through Director of Grievances before
they go to concerned sections/divisions. At this stage, Office of the Director of
Grievances shall go through the representations and come to a prima-facie view
regarding the gravity of the matter involved and decide whether it shall monitor
the case or allow down-the-line functionaries to independently deal with it.
Directors of Grievances should monitor and follow up at least 3 to 5
per cent of grievances received to enable them to assess the efficacy of
grievance redress mechanism.

3
(iii) Fix responsibility in each case of delay, default and dereliction of duty, identified
by Director of Grievances, and take appropriate action against concerned
personnel. In addition, consider feasibility of prescribing specific penalty clauses
for such failures.
6. The Committee is of the firm opinion that citizens charters specify standards of
services and time limits that the public can reasonably expect from the organization. It also
contains the details of grievances redressal mechanism and how it can be accessed. It,
therefore, provides for an independent mechanism with the involvement of citizens and
consumer groups. The Committee notes that in most of the Government organizations, the
Charters are in the initial or middle stage of formulation and implementation. These need
to be expedited and put in place on priority. Further, in most cases, Citizens Charters are
not formulated through a consultative process. The Committee therefore, recommends that
there is a need for citizens and staff to be consulted at every stage of formulation of the
Charter and there is a need for orientation of staff about the salient features and goals of
the Charter.
7. The Committee also recommends that the Charters so formulated by each of the
Ministries/Department/State Governments/UTs should be widely publicized through print/
electronic media and displayed at conspicuous places in the organization or establishment.
8. The Committee is of the view that charter should be precise and as far as possible
simple and spoken language should be used.

4
CHAPTER-I
GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL — CONCEPTUAL FRAME WORK
1. The word ‘grievance’ can be defined as ‘a complaint or resentment, against an unjust or
unfair act’ and the system to settle that grievance can be termed as ‘public grievance redressal
mechanism’ (PGRM).
1.1 Grievance Redress Mechanism is part and parcel of the machinery of any administration.
No administration can claim to be accountable, responsive and user-friendly unless it establishes an
efficient and effective grievance redressal mechanism. In fact, the grievance redress mechanism of
an organization is the gauge meter to measure its efficiency and effectiveness as it provides
important feedback on the working of the administration.
1.2. Nowadays, the empowered and enlightened citizenry is far more demanding services in
convenient and comfortable channels. And the Government, therefore, has to develop, evolve and
enable itself to meet the evolving demands of the society. A citizen-friendly Government should give
high priority to redressal of public grievances since the Government being a service provider, it is
bound to meet people’s needs and aspirations. Effective and timely redressal of public grievances
is a hall mark of responsive and responsible governance. This has become more important after
enactment of Right to Information law. The society today is impatient with the old system of
governance that is not coming up to its expectations. To them, a Government employee is
perceived as insensitive, aloof, corrupt and overall the administrative system as autocratic, opaque
and with no work culture. This requires a paradigm shift in governance to a system where the
citizen is in the centre and he is consulted at various stages of formulatim and implementation of
public policy. To achieve this objective, our country needs a public service, which is capable,
innovative and forward looking. The traditional role of civil service which was of administrator,
service provider and controller of development activities has to make way for the new roles of
facilitator and regulator so as to create best environment and conditions in the country for building
a nation of excellence.
1.3 Nation adopted consumer protection legislation — the Consumer Protection Act, in 1986.
Its National Consumer Policy statement takes into account inter alia two rights of consumers i.e.,
‘basic needs and a healthy environment. The right to basic goods facilities and services guarantees
dignified living. It includes adequate food, clothing, health care, drinking water and sanitation,
shelter, education, energy and transportation. Healthy environment entails the right to a physical
environment that enhances the quality of life. It includes protection against environmental damage
and acknowledges the need to protect and improve the environment for future generations as well.
One of the significant objectives of the National Consumer Policy is to make it mandatory that
consumer impact assessment is required in every area of governance where consumer interests are
affected.
1.4 From 1996 onwards a consensus emerged in the Government on effective and responsive
administration culminating in the Chief Ministers’ Conference in May, 1997. One of the major
decisions of the Conference was to formulate and operationalise Citizens’ Charters at the Centre
and in the States in sectors which dealt with a large public interface such as railways, telecom,
post, public distribution systems, hospitals, revenue, electricity and petroleum among others.
4

5
1.5 The efforts at the Centre were coordinated under the direction of the Cabinet Secretariat
by the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievance (DAR&PG), in consultation
with the Department of Consumer Affairs. The DAR&PG also simultaneously formulated guidelines
for structuring a model charter as also lists of do’s and don’ts to guide Government organisations.
1.6 Every Ministry/Department was asked to form a Task Force which would, apart from
senior officers, have representatives from among its employees and users and, if desired, from the
Department of AR&PG, for identifying areas of public interface and formulating a Users’ Charter
on it. The Charter would carry the objective, the specific commitments for improved services and
grievances redressal machinery of the Organisation. It would be open to public scrutiny and would
also clarify the obligations on the part of the user, if any. The Charter would of necessity and
operationalised after due orientation of staff and given due publicity.
1.7 All Ministries/Departments were asked to make information pertaining to their organisation
available to their users, so far as it was not classified. Separately all classified information were
reviewed to see whether its classification was justified or not. Applications and grievances are also
received at these counters which are being progressively computerised with connectivity to officers
handling the cases so as to obtain regular update on static information as well as status reports
on individual applications.
1.8 A sound complaint handling system should ideally be accessible, simple, quick, fair, and
respect confidentiality. Also, it should be responsive, effective, accountable and be able to provide
feedback to management for systematic reform. It is clear that implementation of these directives
by the service providers on a sustained basis would go a long way in creating confidence in the
users.
1.9 In most of the offices, there is an established method/system to give information to the
general public but something somewhere is lacking. This causes difficulty to the people who cannot
easily gather information regarding the fate of their representations. To reduce this difficulty the
Government had issued detailed instructions for organizing facilitation centre in most of the offices
having direct interaction with the public. But by efflux of time, most of these centres have become
ineffective.
1.10 Model offices on the lines of the above concept are being set up in States/Union territories.
It is proposed that six model offices (five at District Headquarters and one at State Headquarters)
will be set up with the assistance of Central Government primarily through provision of hardware,
software and training from the National Informatics Centre. The States and UTs that have started
moving in this direction are Goa, Assam, Haryana, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, Lakshdweep, Madhya
Pradesh, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Himachal Pradesh, Maharashtra, Chandigarh, Kerala,
Orissa, Bihar and Andhra Pradesh.
1.11 In August 1998, a Standing Committee of Secretaries for Public Grievances Redressal was
constituted. The Committee was to consider proposals for systematic reforms and grievances
redressal brought out by the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances. Besides,
the Committee was also to consider the proposals in respect of all Departments of the Central
Government with Public interface. In addition, the Committee was to communicate with those
Ministries/Departments which have substantial interface with the public and whose grievances
redressal machinery needed to be strengthened.
1.12 To begin with, the Committee has identified 28 Ministries/Departments with a large public
interface for a detailed review. Since September 1999, the Committee has been meeting on a
monthly basis to conduct the review. It has so far reviewed 23 Ministries/Departments, prominent
among them being Ministries of Railways, External Affairs, Home Affairs, Finance, Defence,
Petroleum and Natural Gas, Surface Transport, Tourism, Information and Broadcasting,

6
Environment and Forests, Urban Development, Civil Aviation and the Departments of
Telecommunications, Posts and Company Affairs.
1.13 After reviewing the Grievances Mechanism of 26 Ministries/Departments the Committee has
in its directives called for promptness and courtesy in dealing with the cases. Also names of the
Grievance Officers of the Ministries/Departments be published in the Newspapers by the DAVP
every month. Publicity through the print media and Doordarshan about the grievance redress
mechanism was also called for.

7
CHAPTER-II
STRUCTURE OF GRIEVANCE REDRESS MACHINERY AT APEX LEVEL
2. The grievances of public are received on, various issues in the Government of India. There
are primarily three designated nodal agencies in the Central Government handling these grievances.
These agencies are:—
• PMO
• Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, Ministry of Personnel,
Public Grievances and Pensions
• Directorate of Public Grievances, Cabinet Secretariat
The Public Grievances Wing of the PMO
2.1 A large number of petitions received are given the name of public grievances though their
nature varies from case to case which are duly segregated and forwarded to the concerned
Ministries/Departments for further necessary action. A few cases, which deserve closer attention,
are pursued by the PMO, once again with the concerned Ministry/Department. The Public Wing
is placed in the charge of an Officer on Special Duty and the handling of grievances is
computerised.
Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances
2.2 Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal agency in respect
of policy initiatives on public grievances redress mechanism and citizen-centric initiatives. The role
of Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances consists primarily to undertake
such citizen-centric initiatives in the fields of administration reforms and public grievances in the
Government so as to enable the Government machinery to deliver quality public services to the
citizen in a hassle-free manner and eliminate the causes of grievance.
2.3 The Department is the driving engine of reforms in administration and governance. The
Department proposes to introduce and lead Change to establish a public service of quality,
efficiency, integrity and effectiveness and modernize the public service. It is the nodal agency in
Government for facilitating administrative improvements and reengineering of processes across the
Government. Citizen’s Charter initiative, Public Grievance Policy, Quality Management in
Government, e-Governance, Review of Administrative Laws etc. Documentation and Dissemination
of Best Practices, Organisation and Methods, Information and Facilitation Counters, Civil Services
Reforms are some of the areas under the ambit of Department of Administrative Reforms and
Public Grievances.
2.4 The grievances received by the Department are forwarded to the concerned Ministries/
Departments/State Governments/UTs, who are dealing with the substantive function linked with the
grievance for redress under intimation to the complainant. The Department ‘takes up’ about 1000
grievances every year depending upon the seriousness of the grievance and follows them regularly
till their final disposal. This enables the Department to evaluate the effectiveness of the grievance
redress machinery of the concerned Government agency. On the basis of the grievances received,
7

8
the Department identifies the problem areas in Government which are complaint-prone. These
problem areas are then subjected to studies and remedial measures are suggested to the
Department/Organisation concerned.
Directorate of Public Grievances (DPG), Cabinet Secretariat
2.5 Based on the review of the public grievances redress machinery in Government of India
carried out in 1987, the Directorate of Public Grievances was set up in the Cabinet Secretariat with
effect from 1st April, 1988. This Directorate was set up initially to look into individual complaints
pertaining to four Central Government Departments, which were more prone to public complaints.
Subsequently, more Departments having larger public interface were added to its purview and
presently this Directorate is handling grievances pertaining to 16 Central Government Organisations.
2.6 The Directorate was envisaged as an appellate body investigating grievances selectively and
particularly those where the complainant had failed to get redress at the hands of internal
machinery and the hierarchical authorities. Unlike the Department of AR&PG, Directorate of Public
Grievances has been empowered to call for the files and officers for discussion to see that
grievance handling has been done in a fair, objective and just manner. Wherever the Directorate is
satisfied that the grievance has not been dealt in such a manner, it makes suitable recommendations
for consideration and adoption by the concerned Ministry/Department, which are required to be
implemented within a period of one month.
Guidelines to All Central Government Ministries/Departments/Organisations on Public
Grievance Redress Mechanism
2.7 The Public Grievance Redress Mechanism functions in Government of India on a
decentralized basis. The Central Government Ministries/Departments, their attached and subordinate
offices and the autonomous bodies dealing with substantive functions as per Allocations of Business
Rules, 1961 have their respective grievance redress machinery. An officer of the level of Joint
Secretary is required to be designated as Director of Grievances of the Ministry/Department/
Organisation. The role and functions of Directors of Grievances are given in Department of
Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances O.M.no.l/PLCY/PG-88(7) dated 01.03.1988. This
inter alia empowers the Directors of Grievances to call for files/reports and take decisions or
review decisions already taken, in consultation with Secretary/HOD even in those areas, which do
not fall within his/her domain/charge.
2.8 The functioning of Public Grievances Redress Machineries in various Ministries/
Departments/Organisations is regularly reviewed by a Standing Committee of Secretaries under the
Chairmanship of Cabinet Secretary with Additional Secretary Department of Administrative Reforms
and Public Grievances as member-secretary.
2.9 With a view to ensure prompt and effective redress to the grievances, a number of
instructions have been issued by Department of AR&PG from time to time which, inter alia
include:—
(1) Observe every Wednesday as a meeting less day in the Central Secretariat Offices
when all the officers above a specified level should be available at their desks from
1000 hrs. to 1300 hrs. to attend to public grievances. Field level offices having contact
with the public have also to declare one day in the week as a meetingless day.
(2) Designate a Joint Secretary level officer as Director of Grievances including in
autonomous bodies and public sector undertakings.
(3) Deal with every grievance in a fair, objective and just manner and issue self speaking
reply for every grievance rejected.

9
(4) Analyse public grievances received to help identification of the problem areas in which
modifications of policies and procedures could be undertaken with a view to making
the delivery of services easier and more expeditious.
(5) Issue booklets/pamphlets about the schemes/services available to the public indicating
the procedure and manner in which these can be availed and the right authority to be
contacted for service as also the grievance redress authority.
(6) Pick up grievances appearing in newspaper columns, which relate to them and take
remedial action on them in a time bound manner. Issue rejoinders to newspapers after
investigation in cases, which are found to be baseless and/or damaging to the image
of the Organisation.
(7) Strengthen the machinery for redress of public grievance through strictly observing
meetingless day, displaying name designation, room number, telephone number etc. of
Director of Grievances at the reception and other convenient places, placing locked
complaint box at reception.
(8) Set up Staff Grievance Redress Machinery and designate a Staff Grievance Officer.
(9) Include the public grievances work and receipt/disposal statistics relating to redress of
public grievances in the Annual Action Plan and Annual Administrative Report of the
Ministries/Departments.
(10) Fix time limits for disposal of work relating to public grievances and staff grievances
and strictly adhere to them.
(11) Acknowledge each grievance petition within three days of receipt, indicating the name,
designation and telephone number of the official who is processing the case. The time
frame in which a reply will be sent should also be indicated.
(12) Constitute Lok Adalats/Staff Adalats, if not already constituted, and hold them every
quarter for quicker disposal of public as well as staff grievances and pensioners’
grievances.
(13) Constitute a Social Audit Panel or such other machinery, if not already constituted, for
examining areas of public interface with a view to recommending essential changes in
procedures to make the organization more people-friendly.
(14) Establish a single window system at points of public contact, wherever possible to
facilitate disposal of applications.
(15) Indicating telephone/fax number of the officer whose signature over a communication
regarding the decision/reply is to issue to the petitioner.
(16) Monitoring of grievances in organisations under Ministries/Departments on a monthly
basis.
(17) Publicising the grievances redress mechanism through the print and electronic media.
(18) Review of receipt and disposal of grievances by Secretaries of Ministries/Departments
in the weekly meetings taken by them.
(19) Quarterly Progress Reports regarding the receipt and disposal of grievances in the
Ministry/Department and Organisation under it.
(20) Grievances received and disposed of in the Ministry/Department and Organisations
under it should be monitored by the Joint Secretary/Director (PG) every month.

10
(21) Each Ministry/Department should prepare a consolidated directory of officers holding
public/staff grievances responsibility in the Ministry/Department and Organizations
under it.
(22) Should give wide publicity of Director (PG) through Citizens’ Charters, Broadcast of
audio-visual capsules, sports, websites; etc.
(23) Focus attention on analysis of public grievances to identify grievance prone areas and
implement systemic changes to reduce grievances.
(24) Brochures/Pamphlets prepared by various Ministries/Departments and their subordinate/
attached/autonomous agencies may be kept at accessible contact points including the
railway stations, bus stands etc.
(25) Citizens’ level of satisfaction should be measured on a regular basis.
(26) In order to make the grievance redress mechanism more effective, the following steps
need to be taken:
• Careful analysis of grievances.
• Decision on grievances to be taken at a fairly senior level.
• Forwarding the grievances to the Departments concerned for prompt redress.
• Reply to complainant reforming details of authorities setting grievances.
• Obtaining reply/report from the Departments concerned.
• A reasoned reply to the complainant, if a grievance cannot be settled.
(27) Place Citizen’s Charters of Ministry/Department and Organisations under them on the
website.
Types of Public Grievances
2.10 Majority of grievances received in Department of Administrative Reforms and Public
Grievances and Directorate of Public Grievances related to inordinate delay in taking decisions,
extending from several months to several years and refusal/inability to make speaking replies/
disclose basic information to the petitioners to enable them to examine whether their cases have
been correctly decided. Had the concerned organizations expeditiously and appropriately dealt with
the grievances in the first instance, the complainants would not have approached Department of
Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances/Directorate of Public Grievances.
Systemic Problem Areas
2.11 There are rules, regulations, instructions which are archaic and aimed at shifting the work
towards citizens. Slackness in administration, low morale of the services, inherent inertia, absence
of incentives, lack of proper authority and accountability are the delay-breeders and the delay is
the major factor that generates the grievances. These factors need to be tackled properly through
systematic changes. Prevention is better than cure. On these lines, the best method to redress a
grievance is not to allow the grievance to arise at the first instance. Even the redress of a
grievance, that arose on account of delay, is also delayed in many instances.
2.12 Many a times Departments/Organisations are found to avoid taking appropriate decisions by
resorting to rejection without application of mind, not taking appropriate interest in functioning of
subsidiary offices/linked autonomous organizations, and emphasize on disposal and not on the

11
quality disposal. Decisions taken earlier are reiterated without subjecting the cases of independent
examination. There is inertia to review decisions taken by down-the-line functionaries. In many
cases Departments/Organisations justify the delay and continue with their inability to take decisions
by putting the onus on another agency or on the petitioner. Many a times, the actual cause of
grievance lay in internal inefficiency of the system and failure to identify simple systemic solutions.
It is also observed that the time norms set by Departments for providing services were not being
adhered to in many cases.
2.13 There is no doubt that grievances continue to arise because of a high systemic tolerance
for delay, poor work quality and non-accountability in every day performance of functions. Failure
to review archaic, redundant and incongruous rules, policies and procedures and to initiate simple,
workable systemic changes is another cause for grievance generation. However, Departments and
Organisations, which work with policies and procedures on a day-to-day basis, do not appear to
have developed the ability to continually look ‘within’ and identify deficiencies. All these factors
have ensured that grievances, once arisen, many a time do not get resolved in ‘normal’ course and
need intervention at the highest administrative level.
2.14 Slackness in efficient functioning of ‘Directors of Grievances’ is identified as one of the
prime cause for continuing delay in redress of grievances. Poor work quality, non-accountability
in everyday performance of functions and failure to systemically review policies/procedures and
suggest systemic changes are other important causes. In most Ministries, Departments and
Organisations, the mechanism of Director of Grievances is not functioning as per the mandate
prescribed.
Focus Areas
2.15 In this context, it is the need of the time that the Government should review its pledge of
providing hassle-free public services to the citizens by focusing on systemic changes to minimize
the grievances in Government domain. In order to achieve this objective in a focused manner, it
is necessary to evolve a multi-pronged strategy to be implemented in a time-bound and effective
manner. Keeping in view the various factors involved in grievance redress issue, following areas
need focused attention:
2.16 Performance Review — Foreseeing areas of dissatisfaction:
(a) To review processes, functions etc. in the organization and to cast them pro-actively in a
manner that would foresee areas of dissatisfaction, identify activities where transparency, equity,
prudence and propriety are compromised, interventions that can help achieve better outcomes,
improve satisfaction of internal and external stakeholders.
(b) An annual review of laws, rules, regulations, instructions and procedures be carried out
with a view to simplify the procedure making the administration more transparent, accountable and
citizen-friendly. Information Technology should be employed in re-engineering of governmental
processes in order to improve efficiency and effectiveness and ensuring transparency and accountability.
Identification of grievance prone areas and analysis
(a) Identify areas susceptible to corruption and/or grievance generation and conduct work audit
of such areas. In addition, consider external/social audit in areas of very high public interface, with
the aim of identifying wrong doers and improving processes and systems. Involve NGOs in the
exercise.
(b) Analyse the nature and causes of grievances with the aim of identifying systemic
deficiencies in laws, rules, regulations, policies, instructions, work practices and procedures, and

12
effecting systemic changes to remove/correct these deficiencies. The Directors of Grievances be
the nodal officers for such purpose. The analysis should be conducted in the month of April every
year and studies of identified grievance prone areas be undertaken. Recommendations made in the
studies should be implemented by December of that year so as to bring systemic changes and
remove the causes of grievances.
(c) Fix responsibility in each and every case of delay, default or dereliction in performance of
every day duties on failure to deliver services, and take disciplinary action to avoid recurrence. This
will send a clear signal that in the event of failure to perform duties or deal appropriately with
grievances within the time frame norms prescribed, a real possibility of having responsibility fixed on
one’s shoulder exists. Consider the feasibility of prescribing specific penalty clauses in such cases.
2.17 Citizen’s Charter Formulation and effective implementation of Citizen’s Charters, which
should, inter-alia, include disclosure of time norms for providing various services to the citizens/
clients and details of all levels of grievance redress machinery that may be approached.
Information and Facilitation Counters (lFC)
2.18 To ensure effective and responsive administration and speedy and easy access of
information to the public of the services and activities of the Government, the Government of India
has set up Information and Facilitation Counters (IFCs) in 36 Ministries and 2 Departments of the
Central Government to administer and serious to the citizens.
2.19 Functions of the Facilitation Centre:
1. The most important function of the Centre is to respond to enquiries. If the enquiring
person physically visits the Centre, the details shall be obtained in a prescribed format.
2. The enquiry shall be serially numbered in the computer and a slip containing the number
and subject will be supplied to the visitor. On his subsequent visits to enquire regarding the same
matter the visitor shall bring this slip for reference.
3. Once enquiry is numbered in the computer it shall be closed only when the issue is finally
decided and closed by the concerned Administrative Department.
4. Wherever a matter is not to be processed in that office, the visitor shall be politely told so
and the appropriate officer to be contacted has to be intimated to him.
5. Till the fully computerized information system is introduced the Officer in charge of the
Centre shall gather information from the respective sections either over phone or through the
officers posted in the Centre and pursuing the concerned file. The entire office shall be liable to
show their files to the designated officer except where it relates to a vigilance case, purchases or
any other classified information.
6. The Facilitation Centre need not render itself a file processing section parallel to the one
that is having the subject as their allotted work. What really is intended is to inform the visitor
regarding the stage of action on an issue and to follow it up till disposal.
7. The Nodal Officer of the concerned Department shall be responsible to function as the
Contact Point  for this purpose.
2.20 Handling of Enquiries
1. When a serial number is allotted to a paper the officer in charge of the Counter shall gather
the information from the nodal officer of the respective section at the earliest and pass it on to
the visitor.

13
2. In case the matter enquired into has to be located and verified, the enquiries received till
a cut off time on every working day shall be replied to across the counter in the afternoon. In
any case, every visitor should be told as to when he could come back to the counter to get the
required information or contact over phone.
3. All the departments/sections are bound to supply information to the officer in charge of the
Centre. In complicated matters the file also may be made available to the Officer in charge for
perusal. Nodal officer of the respective departments will be personally responsible to furnish
information to the Centre.
4. When the issue enquired about is kept pending for want of additional information from the
petitioner, the fact may be intimated to the visitor.
5. The enquiry shall be limited to issues affecting the person, group of people etc. general
matters like the financial position of the State, Law and Order, Taxation etc. shall not be entertained
as enquiries.
6. When the enquiry is made by MLA/MP the instructions relating to the interaction with them
have to be kept in mind and observed.
7. The Facilitation Centre shall not add any paper or document to the file, which is given to
them for perusal. In the same way, they shall not hand over the file to any other officer and only
return it to the giver.
8. Non supply of relevant information by any section or officer shall be brought to the
immediate notice of the Secretary or the Additional Secretary by the incharge of the Department
of Administrative Reforms. Such lapses that affect the credibility of the machinery of Government
would be viewed seriously.
9. The Facilitation Centre is only to facilitate the providing of information in response to
enquiries to the visitors. The Sections and officers charged with the processing of papers should
ensure that instructions relating to processing of papers are observed properly and any assurance
given through the counters are also accomplished.
2.21 Miscellaneous
1. Enquiries recorded at one window shall be followed up till the staff of the same window
finally disposes of the matter.
2. The list of enquiries shall also be drawn up department wise and supplied to the Secretary
in charge of the subject. While holding the monthly staff conference of the department, the
Secretary shall review the pendency with reference to the list also.
3. Whenever possible the persons who make an enquiry during the office hours may be
provided with information over phone also.
4. The communication and gathering of information by the Centre Staff from the office need
not be in writing. It may be either conversation over phone or in person.
5. The establishment of the Facilitation Centre does not take away the responsibility of the
higher officers to entertain visitors on important issues.
Publications of different departments i.e. functioning, projects, information etc. should be
made available in this Centre for wide circulation.

14
Review and Monitoring of Grievance Redress Mechanism
2.22 Ensure meaningful review of the performance of grievance redress machinery of the
Ministry/Organisation as well as that of attached/subordinate organization by Secretary/Head of the
Department on a monthly basis. Review should also cover action against defaulters.
Role of Regulators, Ombudsman and Like Bodies
2.23 An explosive issue today in context of public grievance redress is the pace and phasing of
the movement towards open markets after the gradual abandonment of centralized planning model.
The Government is today withdrawing from various service sectors traditionally monopolized by it
and private enterprise is moving in. This may lead to a scenario where the Government monopolies
are replaced by even more vicious private monopolies or cartels in the absence of adequate
regulation, enforcement and recourse to grievance redress.
2.24 This has significant implications for the role of Government. The Government can not just
abandon the interests of citizens to be taken care of by the market forces in areas of service
delivery covered by the private sector. In the open market scenario, it is often the major
stakeholders and players, which define the cost, quality and mechanism etc. of service delivery.
2.25 The Government therefore needs to put in place appropriate mechanisms in the regulatory
authorities, ombudsmen and like bodies in such sectors so that the concerns of individual citizens
are also accorded equal importance and weightage and are appropriately and effectively addressed.
They should safeguard the interests of the common citizens and ensure that the grievances of the
citizens are attended to promptly and effectively.
Steps Taken by the Department to make the common people aware about the PGR
Mechanism
2.26 The Department has taken the following steps to make the common people aware about the
PGR Mechanism existing in the Government to take advantage of the existing fora:
(a) Advertisement on PGR mechanism existing in the Central Government Ministries/
Departments is issued every year in various newspapers throughout the Country indicating the
names of Directors of Grievances in the Ministries/Departments of Government of India and their
addresses, telephone numbers, e-mail etc. Similar advertisement is also issued every year indicating
the names and address, telephone number etc. of Nodal Officers of Citizens’ Charters of various
Central Ministries/Departments/Organisations;
(b) Director General, Doordarshan (Prasar Bharti) had been requested to give wide publicity to
make the people aware about the existence of PGR mechanism in Government of India.
Doordarshan has accordingly issued instructions to all the Doordarshan Kendras to give wide
publicity. Similar request had also been made to Director General, All India Radio (Prasar Bharti);
and
(c) The Department undertakes studies of Public Grievances Redress Mechanism available in
States/UT Administrations and initiatives taken towards implementation of Citizens’ Charters. The
studies involve examination of the mechanism upto Taluka level. The Department makes
recommendations/observations for proactive and citizen-friendly administration.

CHAPTER-III
PGRM IN COMMITTEE’S EARLIER REPORTS
As stated in above, consequent upon expansion of the Department Related Parliamentary
Standing Committees, the Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice came into
existence on 20th July, 2004 following bifurcation of the Department Related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Home Affairs. It is also pertinent to mention that the all important issue
of public grievances redressal mechanism had engaged the attention of the earlier Committee i.e.
Committee on Home Affairs and it had recommended time and again about strengthening the
grievances redressal mechanism. The Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice
also in its 1st, 5th, 14th and 19th Report on the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Personnel,
Public Grievances and Pensions recommended for improving and strengthening the mechanism. The
recommendations of the Committee are reproduced below:—
1st Report The Ministry should keep close vigil over monitoring of grievance redressal in
every Ministry/Department as the essence of good governance is defeated in the
absence of efficient and timely redressal of grievance.
5th Report The Committee recommends that every Ministry/Department in the Union
Government should have a dynamic PGR mechanism in place with special focus
on the information delivery system. People friendly interface of the Government
is the need of the day. The Committee is of the opinion that in this direction
local languages should be used extensively to disseminate information amongst
public.
14th Report The Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure to install PGRAMS
software in all Ministries/Departments/Organisations so that the grievances of the
public are redressed quickly and efficiently and public grievance redress officers
should be appointed and notified in all the Departments and Ministries. The
Committee further desires that the Ministry should ensure that follow-up action
is taken by the officers promptly and effectively.
The Committee recommends that the review of the Public Grievances Redress
in the Grievances Mechanism remaining Ministries/Departments should be
completed expeditiously and that Ministry should ensure that the other Ministries/
Departments submit their compliance reports well in time.
The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that the local languages
should be used extensively to disseminate information regarding Public
Grievances Redressal Mechanism amongst the public in line with the various
recommendations of the Commission on Linguistic Minorities of Government of
India.
19th Report The Committee recommends that the Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism
should be envisaged in a statutory form on the line of the Right to Information
Act, 2005 which would make it mandatory on all Departments/Ministries/
Organisations to pursue the grievances till their logical end.
15

16
25th Report The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should make a
study as to the nature of cases pending in Courts simple because of non-
application of in built Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism and make the
erring office accountable and punished. This will reduce the cases in Courts due
to non-application of mind and soul into the dispute.
The Committee is of the view that public service delivery system is inefficient
unless it caters to the needs and issues of the common man. In order to assuage
the concerns of the people regarding the efficiency of the public services, it is
pertinent that their grievances are redressed promptly.
The Committee strongly feels that enacting a statute for PGRM will go a long
way in ensuring participatory governance and the Ministry should seriously
examine this issue and the Committee be apprised of the outcome therefrom.
3.1 The Committee has very often been termed as the ‘Public Grievance’ Committee and it is
in this regard that the Committee receives a large number of public grievance cases. It has, also,
in genuine cases having policy ramifications, forwarded the grievances to the DAR&PG for
redress. It has been the experience of the Committee that, through proper monitoring, grievances
can be addressed and disposed of within a reasonable time.
3.2 The Committee has, therefore, taken up for examination and study, the existing mechanism
of public grievances redress in the organizational set-ups having a large public interface to assess
the effectiveness and impact of the mechanism in the working of the organization vis-a-vis its
relations with the public.
Committee’s Deliberations
3.3 As the Committee receives number of representations from the citizens as well as the
employees of different organizations, banks, PSUs, individuals and Government Departments on the
issue of Grievance Redressal System giving an impression to the Committee that the guidelines
issued from time to time by the Ministry were not being addressed to by the Government
Departments and PSUs/Banks etc. due to which individuals suffer and very often curse the
Government. The Committee, in this background, decided to examine mechanism’s compliance in
the public sector banks, public sector undertakings, statutory bodies, Government Departments and
also make on the spot study of the Banks/PSUs etc.
3.4 In order to have a proper background on the subject, a letter in this regard was written
to the Secretary, Ministry of Personnel, PG and Pensions on 28th November, 2005 to furnish the
background note on the rules and guidelines followed in the grievance handling system, procedure
and mechanism of monitoring the implementation thereof in Ministries/Departments/Offices/Public
Sector Enterprises etc. wherever these are applicable.
3.5 The Committee then decided to hear the representatives of Department of Administrative
Reforms and Public Grievances (DAR&PG) along with the representatives of Department of
Consumer Affairs and Director General, Bureau of Indian Standards on the subject on
14th December, 2005. In their presentation, the representatives had apprised the Committee that
Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism exists in all Central Government Offices and Public Sector
Undertakings. They had further stated that the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public
Grievances was the nodal agency, under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions
which receives public grievance cases and that they make every effort to redress each and every
grievance meticulously. They also stated that the DAR&PG has its own website, where a
grievance could be lodged online and the status could be seen by simply putting the specific

17
number allotted to a particular grievance. The Secretary had also apprised the Committee about the
Citizen Charter and Benchmark Excellence Scheme of UK and USA.
3.6 While considering the Subject, the Committee also decided to invite views/suggestions from
various individuals/organisations/stakeholders on the subject. A press communique was accordingly
issued on 30th December, 2006 which was published in the major English and Hindi dailies and
vernacular newspapers all over the country. In response, thereto, a number of representations/
memoranda were received. The representations while pleading for individual cases/grievances
also highlighted the drawbacks in the system and came out with suggestions for improvement in
PGRM.
3.7 The major points raised in various representations/memoranda are summarized as follows:—
1 A Committee should be constituted at Central/State/District/Block level for Redressal of
grievances of general public.
2. Weekly meeting of the said Committee should be held.
3. After Redressal of grievance, it should be published in the newspaper.
4. Provision of punishment for non redressal of grievances should be prescribed.
5. Holding of pensionary benefits of officials who misrepresent facts or cause delay.
6. Thrust should be accountability in receiving the documents and replying to those
documents in a time bound manner.
7. Track of movement of the documents should be ensured.
8. There should be a public grievance office to handle officials complaints/grievances of
citizen.
9. The officials should be vigilant, acknowledge the letter and dispose the grievance
promptly.
10. There should be advertisement in leading newspaper/radio about the establishment of
such office so that citizen can lodge the complaints and the facility for lodging
complaints on telephone and internet should be provided. In case the complaint is
found to be genuine the concerned public servant should be penalized.
11. The ombudsman concept in banks, Insurance etc. should be extended to Central
excise, Customs, P&T, Sales Tax, Railway and Education etc.
12. The Consumer Protection Act should be reviewed so that grievances can be handled
by a single judge with a firm deadline of maximum three months for disposal of cases,
the verdict should be binding to stop further litigation as the verdicts are either not
implemented or delayed in implementing the orders of Ombudsman. In exceptional
cases, the consumer or the department should be allowed to submit review petition
against the orders of the Ombudsman.
13. The Central/State Government Departments should be asked to maintain registers of
public complaints, the complaint should be acknowledged.
14. The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions should call for quarterly
report for the number of complaints and action taken by the Department.
15. It should be the accountability of the Ministry to keep vigilance that the complainant
is kept in good humour and not neglected.

18
16. In case of refusal to receive the grievance/complaint the official must be punished.
17. Grievance should be redressed in a time bound manner.
18. Official should be accountable and punished for delay or lapses and the victims should
be duly compensated and interest should be paid on any claims/dues.
19. In case the grievance is against any higher officer, no prior permission should be
required.
20. There should be a time bound policy in cases of promotion and transfers.
21. There should be a judicial body on the lines of consumer court for handling
grievances.
22. A customer focused approach to resolve complaints should be created.
23. Staff skills for working with customers should be improved.
24. The DARPG and DPG should remain under the control of PMO.
25. The Central Government may consider separate enactment of public grievances
Redressal mechanism.
Replies/views received from the Government
3.8 The representations received by the Committee which highlighted the system’s drawbacks
and contained suggestions were forwarded to the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and
Pensions (Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances) for their comments. In
response to the various points raised in the memoranda, a summary of the comments received trom
the Ministry is given below:
1. Grievance Redress and Monitoring system headed by a senior officer of the level of
Joint Secretary is available in every Ministry. The DAR&PG is monitoring the redressal
of public grievances through meetings chaired by Additional Secretary (AR & PG) and
Secretary (AR & PG) for prompt redress of gnevances.
2. A citizen can lodge his/her grievance to the designated nodal officers/Directors of
Public Grievances in each Ministry/Department or to DAR&PG from any geographical
location for redress. The names, address and telephone/Fax Nos. and e-mail addresses
of the nodal officers are published by DAR&PG in all the leading newspapers in the
country for the information of citizens and also on website darpg-arpg@nic.in
3. The Department of AR & PG is the nodal department for formulation of policy and
coordination of issues relating to redress of public grievances in general and grievances
pertaining to central Ministries/Departments/Organisations in particular. To fulfill this
mandate, this department has issued policy guidelines and a number of instructions
from time to time to institutionalize the public grievance redress mechanism.
5. As per the guidelines/instructions on receipt of the grievance an acknowledgement has
to be issued and the grievance to be redressed within a period of three months; in case

6. The DAR&PG has developed a Public Grievance Portal available at website http://
pgportal.gov.in which has been introduced in May, 2007. It has two interfaces one for
the citizens to lodge/monitor the status of grievance online and the other one is
Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRM), a grievance

19
redress monitoring tool for the exclusive use by the Ministries/Departments/
Government organisations. The portal is aimed at facilitating the receipt and handling
of grievances from aggrieved citizens online and thus to help scrutinized, forward and
monitor the action taken by the departments concerned as well as the nodal agencies

7. In response to one of the queries regarding setting up the PG office in the Collector’s

8. In response to another query regarding there should be a judicial body on the lines

(IRAI) etc.
9. When the Ministry was asked to give their comments on separate enactment on public
grievances redressal mechanism, the Ministry has replied that the public grievances are

Steps Taken By The Banks To Redress The Grievances Of The Customers
3.12 The Committee held the detailed discussions with the managements of these Banks. Issue,
emerged in the course of deliberations with there Banks are summarized below:
1. The Customer is the King
(i) The banks believe that Customer is the ‘King’. Every satisfied Customer gets at least
one more Customer whereas every dissatisfied customer informs 11 others about the
inadequate service. Hence, it is imperative and also their core objective to ensure that
every customer goes out of the Bank happily each time and every time. Many
customers who desert a particular bank may not even tell it the reason for their leaving
the Bank and hence receiving a complaint is better than losing a customer.

21
(ii) Marketing experts say that it takes 4 times more effort and energy to acquire a new
customer than retaining them. So, Customer Care for existing customers assumes
tremendous importance in the emerging highly competitive scenario. Thus the battle of
Marketing happens in the minds of the Customer and nowhere else. To win a
Customer from competition would not only be a challenge, but also the order of future
Retail Banking Business in the country.
(iii) Customer handling is a passion and it is more an attitude-related parameter than the
knowledge possessed by the employees. It is important to approach every customer
with passion at all times. Different Customers come to Bank for varied reasons.
Identifying their need would be the key to success in the front office.
2. Discipline and Attitude
(i) Staff members at the counters must treat the customers politely and with courtesy and
make them feel welcome. The attitude should be positive and pro-active.
(ii) Apart from this, being on time at the work place, dedicated to work during working
hours, completing the day’s work without keeping any pending work and seeking
permission in advance for late-coming or early leaving as also planning for leave would
help in our customer-centric approach. The staff members must prominently display
their identity during working hours.
3. Complaint Book/Complaint Box
Complaint Book provided to all branches should be made available to the customers.
Branches should ensure that Complaints/Suggestions Box is available in the Banking Hall. It is the
responsibility of Branch Managers to make the best use of the feedback received and improve the
quality of their branch functioning commensurate with the expectations of customers.
4. Complaint Handling:
(i) Complaints are a ticklish business. Nobody likes complaints, but every one complains
about something or the other, atleast sometimes.
(ii) The first step in handling complaints is to understand the underlying causes which
give rise to them and to develop an attitude to handle complaints in a business like/
objective manner without leaving any bitter after-taste. Leaving aside the small number
of people who complain about every thing to give vent to their own frustrations, it
may safely be assumed that most people who complain have a genuine problem.
(iii) When a complaint is laid on the desk, take it calmly, get the facts into the open and
look at them judiciously. No customer must ever be brushed off or made to feel
ridiculous.
(iv) Flippancy is quite out of place. The customer is not going to be satisfied if you tell
him ‘to err is human’ and attempt to pass of his criticism with a shrug.
(v) When a customer sees that you are making efforts to discover and rectify conditions
that annoy him, he will come over to your side. Most of us run into an internal block
when shown an error. We tend to buck and twist in an effort to avoid admitting it.
(vi) If you slipped out or the Bank had made a mistake, a straight forward apology is in
order. Don’t hesitate to express regret. Then make correction adjustment quickly,
tactfully and in a friendly way.

22
(vii) In handling complaints, the vital thing is to listen. Show respect for customer’s
point of view, even if you do not agree with it. Quite often, all that people want is
to have their opinions respected. It does not mean that you should always concede
that the customer is right, but only that you should make him feel that you can
understand how he came to take his position. Your listening assures him that you are
entirely fair and take a similar attitude.
(viii) Avoid being drawn into an argument. An argument is a contest in which some one
is to lose. If you win, you forfeit his goodwill and probably antagonise the customer.
5. Observance of Customer Day :
Branches/Administrative offices are observing 15th of each month as Customer Day
between 3 p.m. and 5 p.m. If, however, 15th happens to be a Saturday/Holiday, the succeeding
working day is being observed as Customer Day. On this day the bank functionaries at various
levels should make themselves available for meeting the customers without prior appointment. If
the Branch Manager is preoccupied due to some reasons on the Customer Day, the next person
officiating in his place should be present in the branch to receive the customers’ suggestions/
grievances and should redress the same.
6. Staff Meeting Joint Customer Service Committee Meeting :
To review the level of customer satisfaction at the branch and to have a frank and free
exchange of views on the working of the branch, each branch should hold a staff meeting at least
once a month. Joint Customer Service Committee Meetings should be held at the branch level and
suitable steps taken for improving the customer service at the branch. The staff meeting should
be held preferably one or two weeks after the Joint Customer Service Committee Meeting of the
branch so that any suggestions made in the Joint Customer Service Committee Meeting may be
discussed in the staff meeting.

8. Goiporia Committee Recommendations
The following 25 core recommendations made by the committee are of very great
importance to us:
• Commencement of employees working hours 15 minutes before commencement of
business hours can be made operative by banks at branches in metropolitan and urban
centres.
• All the customers who enter the banking hall before the close of business hours should
be attended to.
• Staff at the counters should undertake the following transactions during the extended
business hours (branches to indicate the timings).
• a. Non-V oucher generating transactions.
• Issue of passbook/statement of accounts.
• Issue of cheque book.
• Delivery of term deposit receipt/draft.
• Acceptance of share application form.
• Acceptance of clearing cheques/bills for collection.
• b. V oucher generating transactions.
• Issue of term deposit receipts (TDR).
• Acceptance of cheques of locker rent due.
• Issue of travelers cheques.
• Issue of gift cheques
• Acceptance of individual cheques for transfer credit.
• To ensure that no counter remains unattended during the business hours and
uninterrupted service is rendered to the customers.

counter, either exclusively or combined with other duties, located near the entry point
of the banking hall.

well as from non-customers for issuance of drafts, should engage the attention of
branch officials, controlling offices and the RBI; Customers may be taken into
confidence about such difficulties.

customer-friendly by proper training of employees on one hand and liberalization of
Note Refund Rules on the other.

address of the nominee in the account opening form. Publicity about nomination
facility is needed, including printing, compatible message on cheque book, pass book
and any other literature reaching the customer as well as launching periodical drives
to popularise the facility.

scope for conjecture of non-compliance), nomination should be a rule, to over all other
existing and new accounts.

• Issuance of statements of accounts and updating of pass books with correct and
legible particulars should attract bank’s constant attention.

3.14 Model For Grievances Redressal Procedure For Staff And Officers In Central Public
Sector Undertakings:
1. Objectives
The objective of the grievance redressal procedure is to provide an easily accessible
machinery for settlement of grievances and to adopt measures in Central Public Sector
Undertakings as would ensure expeditious settlement of grievances of staff and officers leading to
increased satisfaction on the job and resulting in improved productivity and efficiency of the
organization.
2. Applicability
The scheme will cover all staff and officers of the organisation except employees who are
deemed to be workers/workmen under the Factories Act, 1948/Industriai Disputes Act, 1947 or any
other legislation applicable to such categories of employees.
3. Grievance
‘Grievance’ for the purpose of this scheme would only mean a grievance relating to any
staff member/officer arising out of the implementation of the policies/rules or decisions of the
organization. It can include matters relating to leave, increment, acting arrangements, non-extension
of benefits under rules, interpretation of Service Rules, etc., of an individual nature.
4. Procedure
Subject to the above provisions, individual grievances of staff members and officers shall
henceforth be processed and dealt within the following manner:

27
(a) An aggrieved staff member or officer shall take up his grievance(s) orally with his
immediate superior who will give a personal hearing and try to resolve the grievance(s)
at his level within a week.
(b) If the grievance is not satisfactorily redressed, the aggrieved staff member/officer may
submit his grievance in writing to the Departmental Head concerned or to the
Personnel/Officer/Manager as may be determined by the Chief Executive of the
organization. Such Nominated Authority will record his comments on the representation
within seven days, and if need be refer it to the Grievance Redressal Committee in
case the grievance is not resolved or settled amicably. The recommendation of the
Grievance Redressal Committee will be conveyed within one month to the Deciding
Authority to be nominated by the Chief Executive and the decision of the Deciding
Authority will be final, subject to the provisions contained in succeeding para.
(c) In exceptional cases, with the concurrence of the Grievance Redressal Committee, the
aggrieved staff member/officer whose grievance has been considered and is not
satisfied with the decision of the Deciding Authority, will have an option to appeal
either to the Director concerned or to the Chief Executive. A decision on such appeals
will be taken within one month of the receipt of the appeal. The decision of the
Director concerned or the Chief Executive, as the case may be, will be final and
binding on the aggrieved staff member/officer and the management.
(d) Grievances in respect of the following two categories of officers will not fall within
the purview of the Grievance Redressal Committee. In their case, the procedure will
be as under:
(i) In the case of officers who are one step below the Board level, the individual
grievance may be taken up with the concerned Director.
(ii) Officers reporting directly to the Chief Executive may approach him for resolving
their grievances.
5. Composition
The C.M.D. of the organization may determine the composition and tenure of the Grievance
Committee.
• In the case of multi-unit organizations the C.M.D. may constitute Grievance
Committees at the Regional level and also nominate the Deciding Authorities. However,
if the supervisors/officers in such Regional units are not satisfied with the decision of
the Deciding Authority, then they may prefer an appeal to the Grievance. Redressal
Committee at the Headquarters. The committee should consider and take a decision on
the grievances within a period of one month failing which it should be brought to the
notice of the C.M.D. of the organization. The Grievance Committee should meet at
least once a month.
6. Management
(a) The Staff member/officer shall bring up his grievance immediately and in any case
within a period of 3 months of its occurrence.
(b) If the grievance arises out of an order given by the management the said order shall
be complied with before the staff member/officer concerned invokes the procedure laid
down herein for redressal of his grievance.

28
(c) Grievance pertaining to or arising out of the following shall not come under the
purview of the grievance procedure:
(i) Confidential Reports;
(ii) Promotions including DPC’s minutes and decisions;
(iii) Where the grievance does not relate to an individual employee or officer; and
(iv) In the case of any grievance arising out of discharge or dismissal of a staff
member or officer.
(d) Grievances pertaining to or arising out of disciplinary action or appeal against such
action shall be channeled to the competent authority as laid down under the Conduct,
Discipline and Appeal Rules of the organization and in such cases the grievance
redressal procedure will not apply.
(e) All grievances referred to the Grievance Committee shall be entered in a Register to
be maintained for the purpose by the designated officer(s). The number of grievances,
settled or pending, will be reported to the C.M.D. every month.
Findings of the Committee on Its Study Visits
3.15 After having the detailed and intensive discussions with the managements of the above
mentioned Public Sector Banks, Companies and the statutory bodies, the Committee observes the
following:
1. People are not aware that a system of grievance redressal exists in many of the
Government departments and its subordinate offices where they are required to visit.
2. Wide publicity to create awareness regarding the redressal mechanism among people
is the need of the hour.
3. Every office should display its organizational structure at a prominent place,
indicating names of officers and their functions, particularly in respect of the
grievance redressal officers.
4. Grievance handling system should be made simple and responsive.
5. As far as possible spoken language (State-wise) should be used in the banks, and the
Government bodies.
6. Application/complaint forms should be users friendly.
7. Time limits should be fixed for approval or rejection of applications.
8. There is a need to bring about a total change in the behaviour of public servants
towards redressal of public grievances.
9. Citizen’s Charters are not properly drafted and followed in Banks, PSUs, Trusts etc.
10. Redressal mechanism should be encouraged to provide feedback periodically for the
management of systemic reform.
11. The State Governments could consider setting up independent watchdog committees
at the district/block/village levels by involving civil society organisations, which are
acknowledged to be closer to the populace.
12. At all levels of the Government, time-bound redressal of public grievances must be
made mandatory.

29
13. Receipt of the grievances should be promptly acknowledged, and reply to the
complainant should follow the redressal without any delay.
14. This receipt-redressal-reply cycle should be kept going on at all levels in a
continuous quality improvement (CQI) mode.
15. The DPG should be authorized to ensure this across the board in the Government
offices.
16. All departments and Government offices must be made accountable for timely
redressal of public grievances under their jurisdiction.
17. The public grievances database should be analyzed at regular intervals to
understand the nature, volume, causes, etc., of the complaints and to give
meaningful feedback to the departments/authorities concerned. This exercise will
also help in keeping a finger on the pulse of the state of affairs in the State, which
could prove to be a valuable input in ensuring good governance.
The Committee impress upon the Government to take note of the Committee’s
abovementioned findings and desires Government to suitably incorporate them in redressal
mechanism of the Government sector Companies, Trusts and the Banks.

Ministry of Health and Familv Welfare
3.17 In its meeting held on 4th October, 2007 with the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare, the Chairman of the Committee had made the following observation:—
“...today, the Committee has to consider two issues. One of them is the ‘Public Grievance
Redressal Mechanism’, which is available in all the Departments and therefore, we are
calling all the Secretaries to know their opinion on this aspect. You know their opinion on
this aspect. You know that if the various programmes that the Government runs from time
to time are no implemented properly, then there will be some grievances that would come
up. If people are well informed about these programmes of the Government, then naturally
some grievances would be there. Therefore, if the delivery system is perfect, then whatever
programmes that the Government implements for the welfare of the people, it would benefit
them. But if the delivery system is not that efficient, then whatever the Government plans
or anything which it does would not reach the people and the people would say that this
Government is not doing anything for them. Therefore, the main thing is the delivery
system. Now, from the public redressal mechanism, we can find out how this delivery system
works. When a person is denied certain things to which he is eligible under some
programme run by the Government, he immediately complains to the concerned organisation
or the designated officers as per the direction of the Ministry of Personnel. They have to
look into the grievances and see that the problem is solved. If they are simply keeping the
petition in their record and sending a reply regretting that they can’t do anything, or, if they
are not replying at all, then it tells upon the Government. An officer in the Health
Department can simply spoil the entire system of the Government by no answering a
question. Therefore, we directly want to get the opinion of the Secretaries of the various

30
Ministries/Departments as to whether we can have a statute for this purpose like the Right
to Information Act. As you know the Right to Information Act has come into force very
recently. So, some people have used it for their benefit and some people have misused it.
But it is only giving the desired information to the people it is not giving redressal to the
people. However, many people feel that the Right to Information Act is helping them in
seeking the redressal also. I think, it is a wrong notion which has spread through the media
and also through the people. Therefore, the Committee prima facie feels that there should
be some statutory support for the Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism whereby we can
have a system perfectly made for this purpose. At the lowest level, the concerned officers
can immediately attend to the grievance. If they cannot do anything, they can, at least, give
a reply specifying the reasons why they could not redress the grievance. In that case, the
aggrieved person can resort to the inbuilt mechanism of First Appeal, and there also, if it
is not properly redressed, then he can go in for filing the writ petition. A lot of writ
petitions are pending throughout India because of non-reply at certain official levels. That
is the main issue. They are hearing the writ petitions and the Judges are sying that within
six weeks they should file a detailed reply or that they would hear them. Due to this,
umpteen cases are pending throughout India. Therefore, we want to reduce the number of
cases against Government also...”
