NOTES ON CLAUSES 
 Clause 1 deals with the short title, extent and the commencement of the legislation. The legislation 
will come into force on the one hundred and twentieth day of its assent by the President. 
 Clause 2 defines various words and expressions used in the Bill. 
 Clause 3 seeks to confer on the citizens a right of access to information held by public authorities. 
 Clause 4 seeks to entrust a duty on every public authority to maintain records and publish manuals 
rules, regulations, instructions, etc. in its possession. 
 Clause 5 provides for designation of Public Information Officers and Assistant Public Information 
Officers. 
 Clause 6 specifies the manner in which requests may be made by a citizen to the authority for 
obtaining the information. It also provides for transferring the request to the other concerned public authority 
who may hold the information. 
 Clause 7 lays down specific time limit with in which a public authority shall provide information and 
the fees to be paid for processing the request and for providing the information. 
 Clause 8 deals with various categories of information which shall be exempted from disclosure. 
 Clause 9 empowers the Public Information Officer to  reject a request for information where an 
infringement of a copyright subsisting in a person would be involved. 
 Clause 10 enables the public authority to severe and provide partial information which falls partly 
under the exempted categories and partly under the non-exempted categories.  
 Clause 11 provides for consultation with the third party where the request relates to or has been 
supplied by a third party and has been treated as confidential by that party.  
 Clauses 12 to 15 provides for constitution of Central Information Commission, the terms and 
conditions of service and the powers of the Information Commissioners and the Deputy Information 
Commissioners. 
 Clause 16 seeks to provides for first and second appeals,  the first appeals lies with the officer senior in 
rank to the Public Information Officer and the second appeal may be made to the Commission. 
 Clause 17 provides for imposition of penalty on a Public Information Officer for persistently failing to 
provide information without any reasonable cause within the specified period. The Commission may 
authorise any officer of the Central Government to file a complaint against such Public Information Officer 
before a Judicial Magistrate and on conviction, a penalty upto rupees twenty five thousand, or an 
imprisonment upto five years, or both, may be imposed. 
 Clause 18 bars the institution of legal proceedings against any person for things done in good faith 
under the Act. 
 Clause 19 seeks to make the legislation overriding in character so that the scheme is not subverted 
through the operation of other enactment. 
 Clause  20 seeks to bar the jurisdiction of the subordinate courts. 
 Clause  21 seeks to exempt certain intelligence and security organisations from the purview of the 
legislation but information pertaining to allegation of corruption, shall, without prejudice to the exemption, 
be provided. 
 Clause 22 provides for preparation of an annual re port by the Commission and laying of such report 
by the Central Government before each House of Parliament. 

 Clause 23 seeks to cast an obligation on the Central Government to develop and promote schemes for 
advancement of the information regime. 
 Clause 24 seeks to empower the Central Government to make rules so as to carry out the provisions of 
the legislation. 
 Clause 25 seeks to empower the competent authority to make rules so as to carry out the provisions of 
the legislation. 
 Clause 26 seeks to require the Central Government to lay the rules before each House of Parliament. 
 Clause 27 empowers the Central Government to remove difficulties in giving effect to the provisions 
of the legislation within a period of two years from the commencement of the legislation. 
 Clause 28 seeks to repeal the Freedom of Information Act, 2002.

1.  Sub-clauses (1 ) and (2) of clause 12 provide for constituting the Central Information Commission 
which shall consist of a Information Commissioner and such number of Deputy Information Commissioners, 
not exceeding ten, as may be deemed necessary. 
2.  Sub-clause (7) of clause 13 provides for a ppointment of officers and employees for assisting the

3.  An estimated recurring expenditure of rupees one crore eighty-six lakhs is likely to be incurred on the

4.  At this stage, it is not possible to give precise details of the expenditure to be incurred on material

5.  The Bill does not involve any other recurring or non-recurring expenditure. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION 
 Sub-clause (2) of clause 21 of the Bill empower s the Central Government, by notification in the 
Official Gazette, to amend the Schedule for including any other intelligence or security organisation 
established by the Central Government or omit therefrom any organisation already specified therein. 
 Clause 24 of the Bill empowers the Central Government to make rules to carry out the provisions of 
the Act. Sub-clause (2) of that clause enumerates th e matter with respect to which rules may be made under 
this clause. 
 These matters relate to, inter alia, the publishing of particulars of public authority, functions and duties 
of its officers, details of facilities available to citizens for obtaining information, fee payable to obtain an 
information from a public authority, salaries and allowances payable to and the terms and conditions of 
service of the officers and other employees, procedure for disposal of appeals and the authority before whom 
an appeal may be preferred against the decision of Public Information Officer. 
 Clause 25 of the Bill empowers the competent authority to make rules to carry out the provisions of 
the Act. These matters relate to, inter alia, the fee payable for obtaining the information from the Public 
Information Officer of a public authority; the appellate authority before whom an appeal may be preferred 
against the decision of the Public Information Officer and the procedure to be adopted by the Commission in 
deciding the appeals. 
 Clause 27 of the Bill empowers the Central Govern ment by order to remove certain difficulties which 
may appear to it to be necessary or expedient in giving  effect to the provisions of the Act within a period of 
two years from the commencement of the Act. 
 The matters in respect of which rules and the order may be made are matters of administrative 
details and procedure and, it is not practicable to make provisions for them in the Bill. The delegation of 
legislative power is, therefore, of a normal character.

 to provide for setting out the practical regime of right to information for people to secure access to

8. (1) Nothing in the foregoing sections shall compel any public 
authority to disclose the following:–– 
 (a)  information which, if disclosed will prejudicially affect the 
sovereignty and integrity of India or the defence and security of India or 
relations with foreign St ates and which has been classified as such in 
pursuance of any rule or order made by the appropriate Government; 
 (b) information, which has been expressly forbidden to be disclosed 
by any court of law or tribunal or the disclosure of which may constitute 
contempt of court: 
 (c) legitimate trade secrets, and commercial or financial information 
obtained from or furnished by a third party on condition of strict 
confidentiality; 
 (d) information the disclosure of which will lead to identification of 
an informer or his sources of information or which would endanger the 
life or safety of any person for having furnished material information 
useful to the Indian nation or would materially hamper investigations 
into crimes or other law enforcement activities; 
 (e) the Cabinet papers including records of deliberations of the 
Council of Ministers, Secretaries and other officers: 
 Provided that the decisions of the Council of Ministers, the reasons 
thereof and the material on the basis of which the decisions were taken 
shall be made public after the decisions has been taken, and the matters 
is complete, or over: 
 Provided further that those matters which come under the 
exemptions listed in this section shall not be disclosed; 
 (f)  information not related to operations of appropriate Government 
or its instrumentalities and disclosure of which would constitute a clear 
unwarranted invasion of privacy of an individual. 
 (2) Information which cannot be denied to Parliament or Legislature 
of a State, as the case may be, shall not be denied to any person. 
 (3) A public authority may, notwithstanding the exemptions 
specified in sub-section (1), allow access to information if public 
interest in disclosure of the information outweighs the harm to the 
public authority.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 
 In order to ensure greater and mo re effective access to information, the Government resolved that the 
Freedom of Information Act, 2002 enacted by the Parliament needs to be made more progressive, 
participatory and meaningful. The National Advisory Council deliberated on the issue and suggested certain 
important changes to be incorporated in the existing Act to ensure smoother and greater access to 
information. The Government examined the suggestions made by the National Advisory Council and others 
and decided to make a number of changes in the law. 
 The important changes proposed to be incorporated, inter alia, include establishment of an appellate 
machinery with investigating powers to review d ecisions of the Public Information Officers; penal 
provisions for failure to provide information as per law; provisions to ensure maximum disclosure and 
minimum exemptions, consistent with the constituti onal provisions, and effective mechanism for access to 
information and disclosure by authorities, etc. In view of significant changes proposed in the existing Act, 
the Government also decided to repeal the Freedom of Information Act, 2002. The proposed legislation will 
provide an effective framework for e ffectuating the right of information recognized under Article 19 of the 
Constitution of India. 
 The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

NOTES ON CLAUSES 
Clause 1  deals with the short title, extent and the commen cement of the legislation. The legislation will 
come into force on the one hundred and twentieth day of its assent by the President. 
Clause 2 defines various words and expressions used in the Bill. 
Clause 3 seeks to confer on the citizens a right of access to information held by public authorities. 
Clause 4 seeks to entrust a duty on every public authority to maintain records and publish manuals rules, 
regulations, instructions, etc. in its possession. 
Clause 5 provides for designation of Public Information Officers and Assistant Public Information Officers. 
Clause 6 specifies the manner in which requests may be made by a citizen to the authority for obtaining the 
information. It also provides for transferring the request to the other concerned public authority who may 
hold the information. 
Clause 7 lays down specific time limit with in which a public authority shall provide information and the 
fees to be paid for processing the request and for providing the information. 
Clause 8 deals with various categories of information which shall be exempted from disclosure. 
Clause 9 empowers the Public Information Officer to reject  a request for information where an infringement 
of a copyright subsisting in a person would be involved. 
Clause 10 enables the public authority to sever and provide partial information which falls partly under the 
exempted categories and partly under the non-exempted categories. 
Clause 11 provides for consultation with the third party where the request relates to or has been supplied by 
a third party and has been treated as confidential by that party. 
Clauses 12 to 15 provides for constitution of Central Information Commission, the terms and conditions of 
service and the powers of the Information Commissioners and the Deputy Information Commissioners. 
Clause 16 seeks to provides for first and s econd appeals, the first appeals lies  with the officer senior in rank 
to the Public Information Officer and the second appeal may be made to the Commission. 
Clause 17  provides for imposition of penalty on a Public Information Officer for persistently failing to 
provide information without any reasonable cause within the specified period. The Commission may 
authorise any officer of the Central Government to file  a complaint against such Public Information Officer 
before a Judicial Magistrate and on conviction, a penalty upto rupees twenty five thousand, or an 
imprisonment upto five years, or both, may be imposed. 
Clause 18 bars the institution of legal proceedings against any person for things done in good faith under the 
Act. 
Clause 19 seeks to make the legislation overriding in char acter so that the scheme is not subverted through 
the operation of other enactment. 
Clause 20 seeks to bar the jurisdiction of the subordinate courts. 
Clause 21 seeks to exempt certain intelligence and security organisations from the purview of the legislation 
but information pertaining to allegation of corruption, shall, without prejudice to the exemption, be provided. 
Clause 22 provides for preparation of an annual report by the Commission and laying of such report by the 
Central Government before each House of Parliament. 
Clause 23  seeks to cast an obligation on the Central Government to develop and promote schemes for 
advancement of the information regime. 

Clause 24 seeks to empower the Central Government to make rules so as to carry out the provisions of the 
legislation. 
Clause 25 seeks to empower the competent authority to make rules so as to carry out the provisions of the 
legislation. 
Clause 26 seeks to require the Central Government to lay the rules before each House of Parliament. 
Clause 27 empowers the Central Government to remove difficulties in giving effect to the provision of the 
legislation within a period of two years from the commencement of the legislation. 
Clause 28 seeks to repeal the Freedom of Information Act, 2002. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM 
1.  Sub-clauses (1) and 2 of clause 12 provide for constituting the Central Information Commission which 
shall consist of a Information Commissioner and such number of Deputy Information Commissioners, not 
exceeding ten, as may be deemed necessary. 
2.  Sub-clause (7) of clause 13 provides for a ppointment of officers and employees for assisting the 
Information Commissioner and the Deputy Information Commissioners as may be necessary for the efficient 
performance of their functions under the Act. 
3.  An estimated recurring expenditure of rupees one crore eighty-six lakhs is likely to be incurred on the 
salaries of the Informa tion Commissioner, Deputy Information Commissioners and other officers and 
employees of the Commission. 
4.  At this stage, it is not possible to give precise details of the expenditure to be incurred on material 
resources in terms of office accommodation, vehicles, telephones and other office equipments required by 
the Commission. Adequate provisions will have to be made in the annual grants of the Commission to meet 
this expenditure. 
5.  The Bill does not involve any other recurring or non-recurring expenditure. 
MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION 
 Sub-clause (2) of clause 21 of the Bill empow ers the Central Government, by notification in the 
Official Gazette, to amend the Schedule for includi ng any other intelligence or security organisation 
established by the Central Government or omit therefrom any organisation already specified therein. 
 Clause 24 of the Bill empowers the Central Government to make rules to carry out the provisions of the 
Act. Sub-clause (2) of that clause enumerates the matter with respect to which rules may be made under this 
clause. 
 These matters relate to, inter alia, the publishing of particulars of public authority, functions and duties 
of its officers, details of facilities available to citizens for obtaining information, fee payable to obtain an 
information from a public authority, salaries and allowances payable to and the terms and conditions of 
service of the officers and other employees, procedure for disposal of appeals and the authority before whom 
an appeal may be preferred against the decision of Public Information Officer. 
 Clause 25 of the Bill empowers the competent authorit y to make rules to carry out the provisions of the 
Act. These matters relate to, inter alia  the fee payable for obtaining the information from the Public 
Information Officer of a public author ity; the appellate authority before whom an appeal may be preferred 
against the decision of the Public Information Officer and the procedure to be adopted by the Commission in 
deciding the appeals. 
 Clause 27 of the Bill empowers the Central Government by order to remove certain difficulties which 
may appear to it to be necessary or expedient in giving effect to the provisions of the Act with in a period of 
two years from the commencement of the Act. 
 The matters in respect of which rules and the order may be made are matters of administrative details 
and procedure and it is not practicable to make provisio ns for them in the Bill. The delegation of legislative 
power is, therefore, of a normal character.

REPORT
Central Government Employees Consumer Cooperative Society Ltd., the largest consumer
cooperative society in the country popularly known as Kendriya Bhandar is a welfare project of
Government of India, under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. It was set
up in 1963 in pursuance of a Union Cabinet decision as a welfare project for the benefit of Central
Government employees and public at large. It is functioning under aegis of Ministry of Personnel,
Public Grievances and Pensions, Government of India and was registered with Delhi Registrar of
Cooperative Societies. Subsequently, it was registered with Central Registrar of Cooperative
Societies, Government of India as a Multi State Consumer Cooperative Society in September, 2000.
The objects of the Society are as under:—
(a) to obtain, distribute and market food stuffs, essential commodities and other consumer
goods at reasonable prices primarily for the benefit of Central Government Employees
and employees of subsidiary/autonomous organizations set up by the Government of
India/or Union Territory Administration and other consumers within its area of
operation and to undertake wholesale and retail trade in consumer goods and essential
commodities and to establish departmental stores, super markets and fair price shops;
(b) to supply to the Government Departments/Offices/Subsidiary organizations set up by
the Government and other customers, stationery, office equipments, machines of office
use and other items required by them;
(c) to establish and run manufacturing and processing units for production of consumer
goods for the benefit of members and other bonafide consumers;
(d) to open repairing and servicing facilities and shops to provide such service to members
in respect of articles supplied to them or as may be in common demand amongst them;
(e) to encourage thrift, self help and cooperation amongst members;
(f) to import and export consumer goods; and
(g) to provide any other services to members/consumers.
2. In furtherance of the objects set out above the Society is at liberty to:
(a) receive deposits including trade deposits and loans from members, cooperative
financing agencies and other Banks approved by the Registrar of Cooperative Societies
and from the Government;
(b) accept agency of any person or firm for wholesale and retail business;
(c) acquire land and buildings, vehicles, factory, workshop, machinery and equipment;
(d) import goods directly or through agents;
(e) undertake welfare activities for the members and employees and their children;
(f) become a member of Cooperative Bank or any other cooperative society and purchase
shares of such Societies; and
(g) generally do all such things as are incidental to or conducive to the attainment of any
or all the above objects.

2
3. The following are the business activities of Kendriya Bhandar:-
(a) Retailing and Institutional sales of grocery consumer and household items.
(b) Sales of Stationery items
(c) Sales of Medicines and allied items
(a) Retail and Institutional Sales
The grocery, consumer and household items are sold through Kendriya Bhandar retail outlets
located at convenient locations in Delhi in or around Government Colonies and other towns. Being
a co-operative and Welfare organization, items are reasonably priced by adding nominal margin to
meet administrative and other expenses. A large variety of branded products are available. Quality
standards are normally higher than PFA. Products pass through stringent laboratory testing.
Kendriya Bhandar supplies grocery/consumer items to several hotels, hostels, hospitals,
canteens, guest houses including prestigious institutions such as Rashtrapati Bhawan, PM’s
residence, Parliament House through Institutional Sales Unit (ISU) on regular basis. Laboratory
tested items are supplied at reasonable prices.
(b) Stationery products and Office equipment
Kendriya Bhandar has been supplying stationery and office equipments including furniture,
computers, photocopiers, fax machines, furniture etc. to Central Government Ministries/Department,
public sector undertakings, autonomous bodies etc. from its Stationery Office at R.K. Puram, New
Delhi and various Regional offices since 1981.
Over the period, Kendriya Bhandar has developed expertise in supply of the office stationery
requirements to Central Government organizations at competitive prices. The selling price prevailing
in Kendriya Bhandar is taken as benchmark for procurement of items by Government Departments.
As a unique service Kendriya Bhandar has developed a system of extending credit facility
to its regular customers from the Government by opening of credit accounts under where they can
procure items simply by raising an indent which ensures meeting of their requirements whenever
demand arises.
In purchasing of items from Kendriya Bhandar, the Government departments achieve
savings in terms of invitation, scrutiny and evaluation of tenders, collection of material from

etc.;

• Plastic Items;
• Crockery;

• Cleaning material;

• Tyres tubes, batteries, shoes;
• Computers along with peripherals, accessories. Printers and softwares.
(c) Medicine
All kinds of medicines and surgical items for institutional and retail customers are supplied
from Medical Division located at 23, Mahadev Road, New Delhi
NETWORK OF STORES/OFFICES
4. Presently, Kendriya Bhandar operates a network of 114 stores located in Delhi, Mumbai,
Chennai, Hyderabad, Banglore, Tiruchi, Cochin, Tirupati, Daman, Goa, Mussoorie, Lucknow,
Ghaziabad, Gwalior, Gurgaon, Faridabad, Kapurthala and Chandigarh. With the objective of providing
better shopping environment to customers, Kendriya Bhandar has modernized some of its existing
grocery and consumer stores like Netaji Nagar, Pandara Road, R.K. Puram-I, R. K. Puram-IV , Sarojini
Nagar–B Block, IARI Pusa, Pushpa Bhawan etc. Concerted steps are being taken for computerization
of godowns and installation of the latest Point of Sales (PoS) Machines at retail stores for ensuring
better supply chain management.
5. Some Milestones pertaining to Kendriya Bhandar :

6. Kendriya Bhandar being a cooperative society under the administrative control of Ministry
of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions has drawn the Committee’s attention in the past also.

4
The Committee in its 14th Report on the Demands for Grants (2007-08) of the Ministry considered
the functioning of the Kendriya Bhandar. Showing its concern for the organization, the Committee
had recommended as under:
The Committee fails to understand why the Ministry’ s control in the Governing Body
of Kendriya Bhandar is negligible when it holds 81.43% of shares. Also, it is not clear
whether the Ministry’ s nominees in the Board of Directors hold vital posts or  whether they
do not play an active role. The Committee has no objection to the functional autonomy
granted to Kendriya Bhandar; but is of the opinion that there should be strict and efficient
monitoring by the Ministry on the financial activities of the Kendriya Bhandar. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should look into the functioning of
Kendriya Bhandar so that it may not go the ‘Super Bazar’ way. The Committee also desires
to take up this issue separately after the receipt of action taken reply from the Government
in the matter. (21.5)
The Ministry, in a written reply stated that with the withdrawal of special dispensation of
Kendriya Bhandar from the procedure of inviting tenders/quotations by the Ministry of
Finance, Kendriya Bhandar may become prone to machinations and that there would be
uncertainity about Kendriya Bhandar being able to obtain the supply orders. (21.6)
The Committee is of the considered view that Kendriya Bhandar should upgrade itself to
compete with other players in tenders/quotations rather than being apprehensive of
competition. (21.7)
7. The Committee’s attention was to the problems being faced by the Kendriya Bhandar when
it received some petitions that Kendriya Bhandar has been asked to vacate the possession of those
properties or its retail outlets in the habitations of the Central Government employees. The Kendriya
Bhandar, which was working in different areas, that is, in the habitations of the Central
Government employees has also been asked to vacate the buildings from where they were
functioning. The vacation of these properties will threaten the very existence of Kendriya Bhandar
These properties are under the control of the Ministry of Urban Development and that Ministry is
now pressing for the vacation.
8. Considering the utility of services being provided on the Kendriya Bhandar, the Committee
decided to seek clarifications from the concerned Ministries. The Committee at its meeting held on
3rd June, 2008 heard the representatives of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and
Pensions, Ministry of Urban Development and the Kendriya Bhandar.
9. The Special Secretary, Ministry of Urban Development while explaining their stand informed
the committee:
“...I do sense the feeling of the Committee where they want to preserve Kendriya Bhandar
and that we have all recognized that the Kendriya Bhandar is giving some very useful
service to the community itself. However, Sir, I am sure you would also like to know why,
when the Kendriya Bhandar is rendering such a service, has such a strange decision been
taken to have them withdraw from the residential units handed by the Directorate of Estates.
Sir, there was a case filed in the Supreme Court, Shiv Sagar Tiwari Case, which laid down
the principle that residential units must be used for residential purposes and since the
Kendriya Bhandar activities are not of a residential nature this decision had to be taken
at the level of the Cabinet Committee on Accommodation in November 2005 the notice, that
is now being discussed, was issued to the Kendriya Bhandar. Having done that, Sir, that was
the easy part of the job, where a decision was taken and action was communicated, and
in compliance with that from about 42 units, which the Kendriya Bhandar was in
occupation of, they have now withdrawn from 16. That is a good number which has

5
happened. Managing Director, told you, this entire process is being done with a certain
amount of care and concern for the Kendriya Bhandar and the thoughts that Committee
Members have harboured are the same thoughts that went in the process of having to have
Kendriya Bhandar step out from occupying the residential units for non-residential purposes.
In the process, we, in the Directorate of Estates, also look after some markets where there
are certain shops and facilities for commercial activities, which is available.
Some of these places have been given to the Kendriya Bhandar where they have had
exemplary reaction on the entire market. It has enhanced the market’ s ambience and
environment. I am sure that the kind of visit on which has taken me to show a modern and
a well-run shop would very well create an exemplary good impression amongst the Members
themselves. Because much of the clientele of Kendriya Bhandar, we understand, are the
people who are living in the Government colonies, we tried to undertake an exercise to find
out whether there are any vacant and open spaces where Kendriya Bhandar can open up
a retail outlet and continue to provide service to those customers who have been used to
purchasing items from the Kendriya Bhandar. We have also tried to extend this exercise to
a further extent by saying, “Alright, Kendriya Bhandar, you seem to be very useful service
provider, can we link up a service between you and CPWD”. That is, if we build one unit
where the Kendriya Bhandar can operate on the ground floor and the CPWD centre can
operate on the first floor, it becomes useful for everybody.....
So, we have also tried to look at this kind of thing. The Master Plan prescriptions allow
a 20 sq. mtr. retail outlet for the kind of work that they are doing. So, the exercise is
underway. The Kendriya Bhandar has also inspected 22 other sites. So, with regard to the
balance amount of places that they require, hopefully, we should be in a position to try and
attain what the Committee is moving towards, and, at the same time, keep within the
bounds of ruling which we are faced with, which has brought about this situation where it
has become necessary for you to consider the requirements of Kendriya Bhandar...”
10. In his deposition before the Committee, the representative of the Department of Personnel
and Training made the following observation:
“...I would like to say that when we receive the decision of the Ministry of Urban
Department, we would go to the Cabinet for looking into this issue. We are taking the case
what the Kendriya Bhandar has suggested...”.
11. As regards the compliance to the order of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, a member of the
Committee observed as under:
“...there is one point that ‘user of premises’ is a matter of policy and it is the Government
not the Supreme Court which decides that policy. So the Government can take fresh policy
decision that a certain percentage of residential premises can be used for such activities and
that policy is final. The Supreme Court does not decide policies. Rent Act says something
and within that ambit, something happens where you are converting residential premises into
commercial one. That is not permitted by many Rent Acts. But, otherwise, being a user of
your own premises is a matter of policy. And, fortunately, today, the Supreme Court is not
deciding the matters of policy. Why don’t you take a policy decision at the highest level
and implement it.”
12. In the course of deliberations the Members of the Committee felt very strongly for the
cause of Kendriya Bhandar. The feelings of the Committee was conveyed by the Chairman of the
Committee as under:
“...At a time, when the prices prevailing outside are very high, I think, we need to maintain
them for our Government employees. I hope you have understood the feelings of the hon.

6
Members of this Committee. We would like to maintain this and we are in a mood to say
that its services should be extended to other habitations also. We have to enlarge its
services. We are having PDS throughout India run by the State Governments but the
Central Government also has to protect the interests of their employees. At least, this much
help should be provided by its own Department. We should not ask them to close it. If
these stores get closed, then these employees would be left with no alternative but to go
to the main shops and pay a higher price. Then they would come back and say that their
salary is not suitable for their day-to-day living. Therefore, we want that you try to express
our feeling to them”.
13. Subsequent to the above meeting of the Committee a letter was received from the
Chairperson and Managing Director, Kendriya Bhandar highlighting the grave problem threatening
survival of Kendriya Bhandar’. In his letter addressed to the Chairman of the Committee, the CMD
referred to the issue of eviction orders issued by the Ministry of Urban Development through their
Office Memorandum No. 12035/2/94-Pol.II dated 10th November, 2005. The relevant contents of
the letter are given below:
A. Ministry’s O.M incorporated the following:—
(a) No new unit of residential/office accommodation shall be allotted to Kendriya Bhandar
or to a similar organisation/retail outlet in future.
(b) The residential/office accommodation allotted to Kendriya Bhandar at various places
shall be got vacated in a phased manner over a period of three years. One third
accommodations to be vacated every year w.e.f. 1st November , 2005 onwards.
(c) Market rate of License fee as fixed by the Central Government from time to time
shall be charged from Kendriya Bhandar on all the accommodation w.e.f.
1st November, 2005 (till they are vacated).
B. Adverse impact of the above decision on Kendriya Bhandar
As a result of the above decision, Kendriya Bhandar has already surrendered one third
accommodations to Ministry of Urban Development i.e. out of 42 Nos. accommodations,
Kendriya Bhandar has already surrendered 16 nos. accommodations to the Directorate of
Estates in compliance of the above order (OM). This has resulted/caused great hardships
to the Government employees/their families residing in the above colonies, who have to
commute long distances to purchase their household requirements from other Kendriya
Bhandar stores or from open market. More so market rent of licence fees has also ben
imposed on Kendriya Bhandar retail outlets and also the office accommodation amounting
to Rs. 1.26 crore per year, which is a huge financial burden on Kendriya Bhandar.
C. Note prepared by the Ministry of Personnel, PG and Pensions for review by CCA:
We would also like to inform you that our Ministry i.e. Ministry of Personnel, Public
Grievances and Pensions are in the process of submitting a note before the Cabinet
Committee on Accommodations (CCA) to review its earlier decision dated 10th November, 2005
regarding withdrawal of Government Pool Residential and Office accommodations allotted
to Kendriya Bhandar.
D. Factual position about Kendriya Bhandar:
(a) Kendriya Bhandar is a Welfare Project of the Central Government and is operating
under the aegis of the Ministry of Personnel, PG and Pensions.

7
(b) It is providing good quality grocery, consumer and household items at reasonable
prices to the Government employees and the lower income segment of the society.
Due to meager profit margins, Kendriya Bhandar actually incurs a loss in grocery/
consumer retail business every year.
(c) The residential and office accommodations being utilized by Kendriya Bhandar have
been progressively allotted to Kendriya Bhandar over the last thirty years, consequent
to a decision of the Union Cabinet (in 1963).
(d) It is not a case of fresh/new allotment – but it is only a case retention of existing retail
stores and two office accommodations. A majority of the 28 accommodations allotted
to Kendriya Bhandar are in its possession for over 30 years.
(e) Kendriya Bhandar is constantly playing a major role in supporting the Government’s
efforts to contain rising inflation by selling essential items at lower than market price
through its retail stores.
14. The CMD requested the Committee to look into the matter and prayed that the issues raised
above need to be sympathetically considered and Ministry of Urban Development’s OM should be
suitably revised.
15. Keeping in mind the hardships faced by the Kendriya Bhandar and the views expressed by
the Members of the Committee in its meeting held on 3rd June, 2008, the Chairman of the
Committee wrote a D.O. letter to the Secretary, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and
Pensions (being the nodal Ministry).
“...as you are aware, the working of Kendriya Bhandar is presently under consideration of
the Committee of Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice and the Committee in its
meeting held on 3rd June, 2008 heard the Chairperson and Managing Director of Kendriya
Bhandar along with the officers of Department of Personnel and Training. During the
deliberations, the Members of the Committee had expressed their unanimous concern over
the development and felt that Kendriya Bhandar retail stores are rendering very useful
services not only to the government employees and their families but also the poor people
residing in the periphery of government colonies and for that purpose, Kendriya Bhandars
were allotted accommodations from the government pool in the residential colonies. These
days when the price rise and inflation is at its peak, the Kendriya Bhandars are giving the
much desired relief to the government employees and other common man. As such, the
Members were of the view that the Kendriya Bhandar should be allowed to continue in the
Government residential colonies in public interest.
I also feel that both the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions and the
Ministry of Urban Development should discuss the issue threadbare and take necessary steps
so that Kendriya Bhandars are allowed to function from their existing government pool
residential and office accommodation.”
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERV ATION OF THE COMMITTEE
16. The Committee feels that Kendriya Bhandar retail stores are rendering very useful
services not only to the Government employees and their families but also the poor people
residing in the periphery of Government colonies and for that purpose, Kendriya Bhandars
were allotted accommodations from the Government pool in the residential colonies. These
days when the price rise and inflation is at its peak, the Kendriya Bhandars are giving the
much desired relief to the Government employees and other common man. The Committee
therefore, recommends that the Kendriya Bhandar should be allowed to continue

8
functioning from their outlets in the Government residential colonies in larger public
interest which is the fundamental of a welfare State like ours.
17. The Committee also feels that Kendriya Bhandar is providing useful services to its
major clientele i.e. Government employees, the products are below market prices and are
of highest quality. Hence, effort should be in the direction of promoting and preserving
these units rather than closing, because closing will not serve the purpose. The Committee
therefore, recommends that Government should make an all out effort in the direction of
promotion of these units.
18. The Committee further feels that Kendriya Bhandar is a welfare project of the
Central Government and is operating under the aegis of the Ministry of Personnel, PG and
Pensions. It is providing good quality grocery, consumer and household items at reasonable
prices to the Government employees and the lower income segment of the society. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that such a society which is working for the benefit of
the common people should not be asked to vacate their present units rather the
Government should provide all necessary assistance to the Kendriya Bhandar since they are
fulfilling the daily household needs of thousands of Government employees every month.
19. The Committee also recommends that Kendriya Bhandar may be directed to make
payment of monthly license fee at flat rates equivalent to that payable by a Government
employee occupying the Government residential accommodation plus the average monthly
house rent amount (which is otherwise applicable to the Government employees of that
category). The market rent should be waived off and instead a monthly license fee at flat
rates should be prescribed on Kendriya Bhandar.
20. The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry of Urban Development should
either return the 16 nos. of surrendered accommodations to Kendriya Bhandar or
alternatively it should immediately provide alternative accommodations to Kendriya Bhandar
in lieu of the surrendered accommodations at nearby location.
21. The Committee feels that the residential and office accommodations utilized by
Kendriya Bhandar have been allotted to them, consequent upon the decision of the Union
Cabinet in the year 1963. Moreover, they are not requesting for new allotments rather what
they are pleading for is retention of existing retail outlets. The Committee feels that a
welfare project run by the Government sustains in today’s competitive environment only
when the organisation is protected/looked after well by the mother but if the mother start
giving step motherly treatment to a child whom it had nurtured for 30 years the survival
becomes difficult. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Kendriya Bhandar
should be allotted land in the Central Government colonies by the Ministry of Urban
Development at economical cost for construction of retail stores (on the same lines as
Mother Dairy) and after the construction of the retail stores they may be asked to
surrender the Government Accommodations in a phased manner.
22. The Committee further feels that the Kendriya Bhandar is the welfare face of the
Government and Government of India is holding more than 78% shares in the society then
why not the Kendriya Bhandar should have their own permanent building to carry out day
to day office work. It has also come to the notice of the Committee that the Kendriya
Bhandar had requested the Ministry of Urban Development to provide land for the
construction of its building in the year 2004 and the issue is pending till date. The
Committee expresses its displeasure to note that no concrete decision has so far been taken
with regard to providing land for construction of building for Kendriya Bhandar inspite of
the considerable time that has already lapsed. The Committee, therefore, recommends that

9
the Ministry of Urban Development should vigorously pursue the matter and ensure that
the vacant Government land should be allotted to the Kendriya Bhandar for construction of
its building without further delay. The Committee also recommends that Kendriya Bhandar
should be allowed to retain the existing office accommodations by paying rent equivalent to
that payable by post Offices etc. (Public utility departments), till such time suitable land at
economical rates is allotted to Kendriya Bhandar for construction of its own office.
23. The Committee desires that both the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and
Pensions and the Ministry of Urban Development should discuss the issue threadbare and
take necessary steps together so that as a relief Kendriya Bhandars are allowed to function
from their existing Government pool residential and office accommodation.
24. The Committee feels that the Ministry of Urban Development had taken this step
because of the judgment given by the Apex court in the Shiv Sagar Tiwari Case, which laid
down the principle that residential units must be used for residential purposes and since the
Kendriya Bhandar activities are not of a residential nature this decision had to be taken
at the level of the Cabinet Committee on Accommodation. The Committee feels that though
the Hon’ble Supreme Court had given its verdict in a particular case. The point that who
should be the ‘user of premises’ is a matter of policy and it is the Government, not the
Hon’ble Supreme Court, which decides that policy. So, the Government can certainly take
a fresh policy decision that a certain percentage of residential premises can be used for
such activities and that policy is final. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
Government should as early as possible bring forward a new policy that a certain percentage
of residential premises could be used for such activities as are being carried by Kendriya
Bhandar.
25. The Committee feels that if these Kendriya Bhandars are closed, the people who are
working there will lose their jobs and there will be unemployment. The Government
employees and members of the general public who are patronizing the Kendriya Bhandar
will be deprived of cheaper quality products and this will be a set back to the cooperative
movement of the nation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Kendriya
Bhandars should be protected and Government should start thinking in terms of extending
their services to other areas.
26. The Committee also feels that in today’s world when things are growing at rapid pace
there is an urgent need for the Government to plan/keep enough space for public utility
services at residential area/complex. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should earmark certain space for the public utility services in the upcoming
areas/localities/residential complexes so that the people can take benefit of these facilities.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel,
Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorized by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Thirty first Report on Action Taken by Government
on the recommendations/observations contained in the Twenty fifth Report on Demands for Grants
(2008-09) of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.
2. The Twenty fifth Report of the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of
Lok Sabha on 29th April, 2008.

on the Twenty fifth Report of the Committee on 16th September, 2008. The Committee considered
the draft Report and adopted the same at its meeting held on 16th December, 2008.

Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH
HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING
DEMAND NO. 78
Recommendation/observation
1. The Committee observes that the budgetary allocation for the Ministry of Personnel,
Public Grievances and Pensions has increased from Rs. 366.00 crore in 2007-08 to
Rs. 443 crore in the current year, reflecting a hike of Rs. 77.00 crore, i.e., 21.03% increase
over the previous financial year, whereas for UPSC, it has increased from Rs. 75.12 crore
to 77.81 crore reflecting a hike of Rs. 2.69 crore i.e., 3.58% increase over the previous
financial year. The Committee expects that this enhanced allocation would be optimally
utilised. Out of the total budgetary allocation of Rs. 443 crore, Rs. 305 crore is devoted to
Non Plan expenditure. A minimum sum of Rs.138 crore has been allocated for various Plan
schemes/programmes of the Ministry. The Committee notes that this Ministry is the nodal
agency for wide ranging crucial matters like personnel policy, recruitment, training,
administrative reforms, public grievances and pensions and in the absence of adequate
facilities and infrastructure, it practically becomes impossible to render these services.
Hence it is of the opinion that this Ministry has a very vital role to play in formulating as
well as implementing the Plan schemes in these fields, for which infrastructure and assets
are to be created. Therefore, the Committee feels that more focus should be given on Plan
expenditure. [Para 5.13]
Action Taken Reply
1.1 The observation of the Committee has been noted for compliance.
ANNUAL HEALTH CHECK-UP FOR ALL INDIA SERVICE OFFICERS
Recommendation/observation
2. The Committee appreciates such initiatives of the Ministry. It is pleased to note that
maintaining a healthy working environment and ensuring the welfare of employees are
accorded top priority by the Ministry. It hopes that the Ministry would assess the feedback
on implementational aspects of the above mentioned initiatives and take necessary follow
up action. The Committee recommends that similar welfare initiatives may also be explored
by the Government in case of other officers and employees as well. [Para 7.1]
Action Taken Reply
AIS Division
2.1 A new system of assessment of the performance of members of the All India Services has
been adopted by replacing the All India Services (Confidential Roll) Rules, 1970 with the All India
Services (Performance Appraisal Report) Rules, 2007. This system has been made applicable for
assessment from the year 2007-08.
2

3
2.2 The new system provides for mandatory health check up for all the members of the Indian
Police Service (IPS) and the Indian Forests Services (IFS) while it is mandatory for the members
of the Indian Administrative Services (IAS) above the age of 40. The concerned Cadre Controlling
Authorities of the three Services i.e. the Department of Personnel and Training for the IAS, the
Ministry of Home Affairs for the IPS and the Ministry of Environment and Forests for the IFS are
required to devise the modalities for conducting health check-up for the members of the Services.
2.3 The Department of Personnel and Training, in consultation with the Ministry of Health and
Family Welfare has fin alized the formats for the health check up of the IAS officers. 5 Government
hospitals and 16 private hospitals have been assigned the job of conducting health check-up of IAS
officers posted in the Centre as per the rates approved by them Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare.
2.4 Necessary instructions in this regard have been issued to all Ministries/Departments of the
Government of India in January, 2008. The system has also been made simple as instructions have
also been issued to the effect that for the purpose of health check-up, no prior reference of the
Authorised Medical Attendant is required. Copies of the instructions have also been sent to the State
Governments with the request to formulate similar arrangement in the State Government for IAS
officers posted under the States.
2.5 In order to avoid inconvenience, a comprehensive list containing the name and address of
the contact persons of the private hospitals alongwith their contact telephone numbers/fax etc. has
also been issued in February, 2008.
2.6 In the case of IAS officers working with Central Government outside Delhi, instructions have
also been issued to the Ministries/Department in June, 2008 that they have their medical check-up
done in the approved hospitals of the State Governments where they are currently posted. The
concerned Ministry/Department would reimburse their claims as per the rates prescribed by the
concerned State Governments for the IAS officers posted in connection with the affairs of that State.
2.7 The Ministry of Home Affairs and the Ministry of Environment and Forests have been
requested to take necessary action relating to formulation of formats and modalities for Health Check-
up for IPS and IFS respectively in consultation with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
2.8 The feedback received in this regard will be assessed from time to time.
CS Division
2.9 A proposal to prescribe an Annual Medical Health check-up for CSS officers is already
under consideration of the Government.
MID CAREER TRAINING FOR ALL INDIA SERVICE OFFICERS
Recommendation/observation
3. The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has envisaged such training
programmes. It hopes that such training would boost their self confidence and ensure that
the trainees hone their skills and capabilities and that modern management techniques are
infused into governance by the trainees. The Committee recommends that training
programmes should be visualized in such a manner that it should enhance the morale,
knowledge, accountability, democratic compulsions in delivery system and productivity of the
trainees. [Para 9.1]
Action Taken Reply
3.1 The Primary objective of the Mild Career Training Programme for IAS officers is to help
develop “next level competency” before the officers get promoted to higher positions. It is

4
envisaged that the training would contribute meaningfully to updating knowledge of the IAS officers
based on the rapidly changing global environment.
3.2 The course curriculum has thus been designed keeping in view specifically the need to
enhance the morale, knowledge, accountability, democratic compulsions in delivery system and
productivity of the officers. Thus the recommendations of the Committee have been followed.
Recommendation/observation
4. The Committee feels that time is a powerful segmentation variable for the Government
service as it is the only ‘objective’ dimension on which the citizen can gauge quality of
governance. It recommends that punctuality, duration, availability, speed of response and speed
of innovation in delivery system are to be inculcated in the in-service training. [Para 9.2]
Action Taken Reply
4.1 Government has realized that the entire career profile of an IAS officer has changed
substantially over the last 50 years, with far greater emphasis on policy formulation and programme
implementation now as against the emphasis on district administration earlier. The recommendations
of the Committee have been implemented in the design of the programme of Mid Career Training
of IAS Officers by incorporating the course content which lays more stress on the quick delivery
systems keeping in view the rapid advances in technology as well as the need for greater
transparency. It is believed that this training would enable the IAS officers to address the new
challenges before them with the speed of response and speed of innovation in the delivery system
as recommended by the Committee.

TONING OF STATE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
Recommendation/observation
6. The Committee desires that the Ministry should put in place an effective mechanism
to ensure that State PSCs which are the main recruiting agencies at the State level, should
be free from the shackles of nepotism and favouritism and function independently and in
a transparent manner. [Para 14.2]
Action Taken Reply
6.1 The State Public Service Commissions are constitutional bodies and the power to appoint
the Chairman and Members in the State Public Service Commissions is exclusively with the
Governor of the respective States. However, the Constitution has reserved the power to remove
the Chairman/Members in any State PSCs to the President of India subject to the provisions

5
contained in Article 317 of the Constitution. The DoPT has no role in the day-to-day administration
or internal functioning of the State PSCs. Whenever any proposal is received from the State
Government for removal of a Chairman/Member in the State PSC, further action is taken in this
Department keeping in view the provisions of Article 317 of the Constitution.
Committee’s further observation
6.2 The Committee knows the provision and legal frame work of State PSCs. Within the legal
frame work, UPSC and DoPT should discharge duties as leaders and guides at the National level
and for that, UPSC and DoPT are accountable morally for corruption and inefficiency at State
level PSCs .

CENTRALISED PUBLIC GRIEVANCES REDRESS AND MONITORING SYSTEM (CPGRAMS)
Recommendation/observation
15. The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has acted upon its
recommendation made in its 19th Report that the PGRAMS should be introduced in all
Ministries and Departments and that the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public
Grievances may pursue the matter with those Ministries who have yet to install PGRAMS
and to take expeditious steps to install the same without further delay. It appreciates that
this has led to the birth of Centralized PGRAMS, the implementation of which started in
June, 2007. [Para 28.3]
15.1 The Committee is happy to note that the CPGRAMS has been benefited by many
user organisations such as Railways and that its benefits are utilized by even the Zonal
Offices of the Railways. [Para 28.4]

8
Action Taken Reply
15.2 The old PGRAM System was server based and required investment in servers in each
Ministry/Department where PGRAM System was to be installed leading to delay. However, with the
birth of the new centralized PGRAMS which is web based and does not require investment in
servers for installing it in Ministries/Departments, this process has been expedited. This system was
introduced in June, 2007, wherein each of the Nodal Officer of 89 Ministries/Departments have
been given a user name and password through which they can access the CPGRAMS software
from the Centralised Server. The Ministries/Departments could also open accounts of their
subordinate offices which in turn can access the CPGRAMS software from the same Centralised
server. This has facilitated the usage of CPGRAM software in all Ministries/Departments of Central
Government and also the field attached offices under them. However, to ensure implementation of
CPGRAM system in all Ministries/Departments and its effective usage and in order to keep close
vigil on grievances, an Action Plan has been drawn up. This Plan includes organizing monthly
meetings of 20-25 Ministries under Chairmanship of Additional Secretary where grievances of these
Ministries/Departments are reviewed and progress of CPGRAM is monitored. Wherever necessary,
training with the help of NIC is being organized for better utilization of this system.
Committee’s further observation
15.3 The Committee is happy to note that the CPGRAM software is being used by the
Ministries/Departments of Government of India. The Committee also welcomes the Action Plan
drawn to monitor the effective implementation of the system. The Committee is, however, keen
to know whether the system is effectively working as the Committee understands that CPGRAM
is a devise to redress the grievances and to what extent this objective is being achieved.

STAFF SELECTION COMMISSION
Recommendation/observation
20. The Committee takes note of the steps taken by SSC to facilitate the physically
handicapped people. [Para 47.5]

10
Action Taken Reply
20.1 The Commission is grateful to the Committee for appreciating the steps taken by the
Commission to provide facilities to the Handicapped candidates including the Visually Handicapped
candidates. Scribes are provided to Visually Handicapped candidates including blind and partly blind,
free of cost. One invigilator is exclusively posted with every VH candidate. They are also allowed
extra time in examination for completing their paper. A few examination venues are dedicated to
such candidates where they are provided assistance by the Commission to reach their allotted seats
etc. with a view to provide them equal opportunity and full participation in the examination. The
question paper for VH candidate including the question paper on Arithmetic are specially modeled
which have no components of map/graphs, statistical data, diagrams, geometrical problems and
figures etc. Assistance is also provided to orthopedically handicapped candidates.
Recommendation/observation
21. The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken in this regard and recommends that
more innovative steps should be adopted to ensure cutting down on time and expenditure.
[Para 47.7]
Action Taken Reply
21.1 W ith a view to take further steps to reduce the time element and a number of separate
Examinations, the Commission is exploring the possibility of combining all the examinations where
the Essential Qualification (EQ) is Graduation and holding a combined Preliminary Examination. It
may be mentioned here that there are about eight such examinations where the EQ is Graduation
and one examination (Junior Hindi Translator exam) where EQ is Masters Degree. A Back Ground
Note was circulated to all the user Departments (Cadre Controlling Authorities). The basic structure
of the proposed Examination Schemes consists of two parts i.e., (i) Preliminary Examination
(ii) Main Examination.
21.2 The Preliminary Examination will be ‘Screening in Nature’ identifying target groups of
prospective candidates for different Main Examinations so that the number of candidates appearing

UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
Recommendation/observation
16. The Committee takes serious note of the enormous wastage of time between
advertising vacancies and declaring results, and recommends that the UPSC should consider
the viability of conducting examinations in the format adopted in Graduate Management
Admission Test (GMAT), IIT and IIM. The Committee is of the view that this would prevent
wastage of resources and time and would ensure transparency and instill greater confidence
of the candidates in the examination system. [Para 46.3]
Action Taken Reply
16.1 The UPSC is a constitutional body and clause (i) of Article 320 of the Constitution has
mandated that it shall be the duty of the UPSC to conduct examination for various appointments
to the services of the Union. The fathers of the Constitution realized that the democratic system
could be maintained only if the civil servants are appointed solely on the basis of merit by open
competition. The values of independence, impartiality and integrity are the basic determinants of the
constitutional conception of the UPSC. The UPSC has to keep in view the various provisions of
the Constitution in regard to the fundamental rights of the citizens for consideration to
appointments to the Public Services. Whereas the purpose of entrance examinations like GMAT/CAT
for management course and IIT for technical education is to assess the nature of the knowledge
held by the candidates on particular subjects and their aptitude for the intended academy courses,
in the case of recruitment to public services, the merit cannot be simply concluded on the basis
of the procedure adopted for the GMAT etc. The Commission has to test not only the academic
worth of a candidate on a subject but also his potential for Civil/Public Services and his personality
with reference to his familiarity with important national/international issues vis-a-vis natural

CAPACITY BUILDING AND AWARENESS GENERATION FOR RIGHT TO INFORMATION
AND IMPLEMENTATION OF THE ACT
Recommendation/observation
6. The Committee opines that the application under RTI Act should not be rejected for
non payment of fee at the initial stage and then incur expenditure for defending cases in
High Courts. Instead the applications should be entertained and the fee may be added at
the time of receiving the information in such cases. [Para 26.5]

33
Action Taken Reply
6.1 The RTI Act does not put a bar on consideration of requests received from any
person otherwise than under the Act. Such requests are replied to by the Public Authorities
in normal course. However, if an application under the RTI Act, is not accompanied with
the requisite fee, it, accordingly to the provisions of the Act, is invalid application. It is felt
that for smooth functioning of a law, provisions of the law should not be allowed to be ignored
by any party.
Committee’s further observation
6.2 The Committee is not convinced by the reply given by the Department of Personnel and
Training to the Committee’s recommendation and feels that it is against the very spirit of the
Right to Information Act, 2005 itself which calls for proactive dissemination of information. The
Act does not provide for payment of fee at the initial stage. It provides for the cost of payment
towards the procurement of printed copies or information in electronic format. The provision of
Rs.l0/- as fee for first entertaining the application has been provided in the Rules made by the
Government. Therefore, in the opinion of the Committee, treating an application “invalid” on
the basis of Rules, is not justified.
6.3 The Committee’s recommendation is based on its experience/input received while
interacting with various Governmental bodies/PSUs/Banks. The Committee came across cases
where the application was rejected mainly for not paying Rs.l0/-. Later on, when such denial
was taken up at the level of Central Information Commission or High Court, considerable
money was spent by the organizations/Government Department to defend themselves. The
Committee feels that the wastage of money and time could have been avoided had the
information been duly supplied or the application not been rejected.
6.4 The Committee, therefore, takes strong exception to the reply of the Department of
Personnel and Training and feels that their reply appears to be based on the Rules and not the
Act. The Committee, therefore, observes that if a rule/instruction/order goes against the spirit of
the Act, it may accordingly be quashed or amended.
6.5 The Committee feels it important to clarify that in its recommendation, it is nowhere
suggested that the cost of printed and electronically formatted information may not be recovered
as it has been provided in the Act. The Committee is against the rejection of an application
under RTI merely on non-payment of Rs.10/-.

8.1 The proposal is under consideration of the Government.
Committee’s further observation
8.2 The Committee notes that the proposal of CBI to exempt them from the request of prior
approval of Screening Committee for filling of direct vacancies, is under consideration of the
Government. The Committee further notes that the proposal is under consideration of the
Government for a considerably long time and the Committee, in its previous Reports on
Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions had
recommended that the proposal should be considered expeditiously. The Committee fails to
understand why the proposal is kept pending for so long. The Committee feels that it is one of
the major reasons for hampering the professional efficiency of CBI; it is but imperative that the
proposal should be given urgent consideration. The Committee wishes to be apprised of the
action taken in this regard in the ATN.
SEPARATE ENACTMENT FOR CBI
Recommendation/observation
9. The Committee, however, fails to agree and strongly feels that the absence of a
separate statute for CBI is a major hindrance for effective functioning of the organisation.
It observes that if we aspire CBI to transform into an organisation of international
standards, an effective statutory support is inevitable. The Committee, has time and again,
felt the necessity for a separate enactment for CBI. It is of the opinion that the
Constitution of India itself envisages the same, as has been observed by this Committee in
its 24th Report. [Para 41.2]
9.1 In view of the above, the Committee would appreciate the avoidance of such evasive
replies and recommends that this matter should instead be urgently examined at the
highest level. The Committee wishes to be apprised of the action taken in this regard at
the earliest. [Para 41.3]
Action Taken Reply
9.2 A separate and exclusive enactment for CBI is already in existence namely the DSPE Act,
1946. CBI derives its powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946 as
amended by CVC Act, 2003. This mechanism viz. the CBI’s functioning under the DSPE Act has
allowed CBI to maintain its reputation of a premier investigating agency of the country functioning

35
with credibility and impartiality within the federal structure of our polity. As such, it has not been
considered necessary to have another statute for the same purpose.
Committee’s further observation
9.3 The Committee reiterates its recommendation on the issue and desires that the
Government may earnestly consider the independent statutory provision in this regard. The
Committee is of the strong view that lack of a separate enactment for CBI is a major hindrance
in the effective and impartial functioning of the premier investigating agency in the country.
The Committee notes that the Ministry has not even apprised the Committee of the action taken
in pursuance of the recommendation of the Committee. The Committee again strongly
recommends that the Ministry should explore the possibilities of a separate enactment for CBI
and take concrete action in this direction.

CENTRALISED PUBLIC GRIEV ANCES REDRESS AND MONITORING SYSTEM
(CPGRAMS)
Recommendation/observation
6. The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has acted upon its
recommendation made in its 19th Report that the PGRAMS should be introduced in all
Ministries and Departments and that the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public
Grievances may pursue the matter with those Ministries who have yet to install PGRAMS

39

user organizations such as Railways and that its benefits are utilized by even the Zonal

Ministry/Department where PGRAM System was to be installed leading to delay. However, with the

from the Centralised Server. The Ministries/Departments could also open accounts of their
subordinate offices which in turn can access the CPGRAMS software from the same Centralised
server. This has facilitated the usage of CPGRAM software in all Ministries/Departments of Central
Government and also the field attached offices under them. However, to ensure implementation of
CPGRAM system in all Ministries/Departments its effective usage and in order to keep close vigil
on grievances an Action Plan has been drawn up. This plan includes organizing monthly meetings
of 20-25 Ministries under Chairmanship of Additional Secretary where grievances of these
Ministries/Departments are reviewed and progress of CPGRAM is monitored. Wherever necessary
trainings with the help of NIC is being organized for better utilization of this system. A list of 89
Ministries/Departments where CPGRAM System is functioning is enclosed.
Committee’s further observation
6.3 The Committee is happy to note that the CPGRAM software is being used by the
Ministries/Departments of Government of India. The Committee also welcomes the Action Plan
drawn to monitor the effective implementation of the system. The Committee is, however, keen
to know whether the system is effectively working as the Committee understands that CPGRAM
is a devise to redress the grievances and to what extent this objective is being achieved.
STATUTORY SUPPORT FOR PUBLIC GRIEVANCES REDRESSAL MECHANISM
Recommendation/observation
7. The Committee is not satisfied with this reply. It is of the opinion that the
Ministries/Departments should keep a close vigil on grievances and that they should be
redressed in a time bound manner. It could gather that Government is the major litigant
in Courts of law, resulting in vast expenditure of public money, Governmental resources and
time. It is of the view that the essence of good governance is defeated in the absence of
efficient and timely redressal of grievances. If the grievances are redressed timely at the
level at which they arise, the aggrieved will not approach Court of Law. This will save
resources and time, of both the aggrieved and the Government. [Para 29.2]
7.1 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should make a study
as to the nature of cases pending in Courts mainly because of non-application of in built
Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism and make the erring office accountable and
punished. This will reduce the cases in Courts due to non-application of mind and soul into
the dispute. [Para 29.3]
7.2. The Committee is of the view that public service delivery system is inefficient unless
it caters to the needs and issues of the common man. In order to assuage the concerns of
the people regarding the efficiency of the public services, it is pertinent that their
grievances are redressed promptly. [Para 29.4]

40
7.3 The Committee strongly feels that enacting a statute for PGRM will go a long way
in ensuring participatory governance and the Ministry should seriously examine this issue
and the Committee be apprised of the outcome therefrom. [Para 29.5]
Action Taken Reply
7.4 The Department is acting on the recommendation of the Committee and the issue of
envisaging Public Grievance Redress Mechanism (PGRAMS) in a statutory form is being examined
in consultation with Ministry of Law. Apart from providing statutory support to the Public
Grievance Redress mechanism which is being examined in consultation with Ministry of Law it was
also felt that the Redress and Monitoring System for Ministries should be strengthened to ensure
efficient and timely redressal of grievances. With the introduction of the CPGRAM systems, a
handy tool has been provided in the hands of Director of Public Grievances (Joint Secretary) level
officers in each Ministry/Department to monitor grievances sent for redress to their subordinate
offices. The system provides suggestive categories under which the Ministries/Departments can
categorise the grievances for making systemic improvements. The CPGRAMS has many facilities
for the citizens like lodging complaints online and getting a unique registration number for further
reference. Acknowledgement is provided by e-mail and citizens can send the grievances directly to
Ministries/Departments. Grievances received directly by post are registered on behalf of the citizen
by DARPG and complaint is scanned and forwarded to Ministry concerned for its timely redressal.
Since the grievances are organized at a decentralized manner, the usage of the system by all
Ministries/Departments up to their attached, field and subordinate officers will help in efficient and
timely redressal of grievances. The Department agrees that if the grievances are redressed timely
at the level at which they arise they will not approach Court of Law and resource and time of
both Government and aggrieved would be saved.
7.5 In the light of the recommendation of the Committee the Ministry of Law and Justice has
been requested to conduct a study as to the nature of cases pending in Courts simply because of
non-application of in-built Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism and make the erring office
accountable and punished.
7.6. The Department has noted the recommendation of the Committee and will continue to
endeavour to strengthen the Public Grievance Redress and monitoring Mechanism in all Ministries/
Departments of the Central Government.
7.7 The recommendation of the Committee was regarding enacting a statute for PGRAM on the
lines of RTI Act 2005, that could make it mandatory on all Departments/Ministries/Organisations to
pursue the grievance till their logical end. The Department has examined the above recommendation
and prepared a detailed concept paper for seeking the comments of Ministry of Law.
Committee’s further observation
7.8 The Committee endorses the view of the Government that Public Grievances Redressal
Mechanism needs to be strengthened. The Committee appreciates the introduction of CPGRAM
system enabling the citizens to lodge their complaints online and forwarding the grievance to the
respective Department electronically for a timely redressal. It is just a beginning and the efficacy
of the system is yet to be established. The Committee feels that efficiency, fairness and timely
redressal of the grievance is the key to the whole issue and hopes that the Government
Ministries/Departments and the Organizations falling under their administrative control will be
able to meet this enshrined objective.
7.9 The Committee also welcomes the view of the DARPG that timely redressal at the level
where complaint arises will reduce the burden of the Courts and thereby, save the resources of
the Government as well as those of the aggrieved person. The Committee, however, awaits the

41
details of the study undertaken by the Ministry of Law and Justice as to the nature of cases
pending in the Courts because of non-application of inbuilt PGRM and making the erring office
accountable and punished. The Committee desires that the details may be made available by the
Ministry in their ATN.
7.10 The Committee notes that its suggestion regarding enacting a statute for PGRM in the
lines of the Right to Information Act is being considered by the Department in consultation with
the Ministry of Law and Justice. The Committee eagerly awaits the details of the Concept Paper
alongwith the comments of the Ministry of Law and Justice. The Committee further urges the
DARPG to pursue the matter vigorously with that Ministry.
7.11 The Committee takes note of the communication dated 4th November, 2008 received
from the Secretary, Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, in which it
was stated that there could not be single authority/Act to deal with all the issues that are raised
through public grievances pertaining to different Ministries/Departments.
7.12 In this regard, the Committee is of the strong view that enactment of a law for Public
Grievances Redressal Mechanism will ensure accountability and lend enforceability to the
inherent right of a citizen as a consumer of the services rendered by the Government. The
Committee would like to emphasize that the recommendation of the Committee was for an
inbuilt Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism for “customer satisfaction”, rather than an
external mechanism. The Committee recommends that the Government should examine the
recommendation in right earnest.

Recommendation/observation

delivery. They should also provide adequate support to formulate Citizens’ Charter and

V ACANCIES IN CBI
Recommendation/observation
12. The Committee is of the view that the number of vacancies existing in CBI is
alarming. It recommends that the causes/reasons for the vacancies should be thoroughly
examined and should be addressed immediately. It is of the opinion that such large number
of vacancies will affect the operational efficiency of the organisation and the existing staff

44
will be hard pressed to deliver results. The vacancies of 30.8%, 66.2%, 58.8% in the ranks

observes that when we aspire CBI to evolve into an organisation of international standards,
there is no scope for such vacancies which will adversely affect the pace of investigation and
trial. [Para 39.1]

12.1 Continuous efforts are being made to fill up the vacancies in all ranks, especially at
investigating officer level. Occurrence and filling up of vacancies is a continuous process. The

the posts to be filled up by direct recruitment/ promotion are filled up.
• The induction at the level of Inspectors has been decentralized by the CBI for speedy
induction.
12.3 An i ncentive allowance to the executive cadres of CBI @ 25% upto Sr. SP level and
@ 15% for officers above that rank has been approved.

ensure speedy filling up of vacancies in different ranks. However, it is of the opinion that a close

Recommendation/observation
13. The Committee appreciates such efforts and is of the opinion that this would
maximize the conviction rate and minimize expending of resources and time. [Para 40.1]
13.1 The Committee is concerned about the pendency of cases under trial especially those
which are pending for 10 years and more. It observes that pendency is one of the major
concerns, which should be addressed urgently and recommends that concrete steps should
be taken in a time bound manner to minimize the backlog of cases. [Para 40.2.]

13.2 CBI’s performance is being monitored on a monthly basis and they have been advised to
pay special attention to reduce pendency to minimize the backlog of cases.

45
Committee’s further observation
