BUDGETARY CONCERNS OF CBI
Recommendation/observation
14. The Committee strongly feels that such shortfall will adversely affect the welfare of

SOME AREAS OF CONCERN HIGHLIGHTED IN THE ANNUAL REPORT OF CVC
Recommendation/observation
18. The Committee recommends that the issues/concerns raised by CVC and reflected in
its Annual Report (2006) should be addressed urgently in order to ensure independence,
impartiality and credibility of the Apex Body. [Para 51.5]
Action Taken Reply
18.1 The proposal of the CVC to appoint full time CVO’s in Ministries/Departments was
examined by this Department in consultation with Major Ministries/Departments and the CVC. The
proposal has evoked mixed response as indicated by the comments received so far from various

47
Ministries/Departments. Meanwhile, the CVC has been requested to provide some empirical data (on
the quantum of cases pending handled in these Ministries) in support of its proposal.
18.2 The proposal of the Commission for appointment of ‘outsiders’ as CVO in Departments
like Railways, Telecom, CPWD, P&T, CBDT and CBEC was examined in consultation with
the concerned Ministries/Departments. It was decided to refer the matter first to the Committee
of Secretaries (CoS) for its recommendations. After deliberations in its meeting held on
19th October, 2007, the following decisions were taken by the CoS:—
(i) CVC may consider vigilance audit in the four departments viz., Railways, Posts, CBDT
and CBEC. Appropriate action can be initiated based on the findings.
(ii) The long-term objective should be posting of outsiders as CVOs as per the proposal
of CVC.
18.3 The CVC has been requested to take further action accordingly.
18.4 As regards the Commission’s recommendations that the selection of the successor CVO
should be completed in time, some posts for which eligible officers are not available remain
unfilled. However, the concerned Ministries/Departments with the concurrence of CVC entrust
additional charge of these posts to some other CVO under their administrative control.
18.5 The recommendation of the CVC for incorporating a clause in the CSS (CCA) Rules
mandating consultation with the CVC in cases involving ‘vigilance angle’ is under consideration.
18.6 As regards making the Commission’s First Stage Advice mandatory for all Government of
India organizations under the purview of the CVC, the issue would require further examination.
18.7 As regards doing away with the consultation mechanism with UPSC regarding the quantum
of punishment to be imposed on the Government officials and overlapping of authority with the
UPSC, it is submitted that the Constitution has envisaged specific role to the UPSC and disciplinary
matters affecting the persons serving under the Government of India in a civil capacity is one
among them. Consultation with the UPSC in specific matters mandated by the provisions of
Article 320(3) of the Constitution and the relevant provisions to the effect have been incorporated
in the CCS (CCA) Rules and the CCS (Pension) Rules and corresponding Rules applicable to
Railway employees. However, the UPSC’s function is purely advisory. Not only is its advice not
binding upon the Government, the Government cannot act mechanically upon such advice also
without applying its mind on the matter in question. The expression “disciplinary matters” is wide
enough to include any kind of disciplinary action proposed to be taken under the disciplinary rule
except where such consultation is specifically exempted by the UPSC (Exemption from
Constitution) Regulations. The fathers of the Indian Constitution realized that democratic system
could be maintained only if the civil servants could carry on administration without fear and favour
and values of independence, impartiality and integrity are the basic determinants of the
Constitutional conception of the Public Service Commission. In view of this, the existing provision
relating to consultation with the UPSC as envisaged in the Constitution may continue.
18.8 As regard the pr oposal of the Commission for strengthening of its resources, it is submitted
that the Commission on the basis of an internal work-study had proposed creation of 51 additional
posts in the Commission. The proposal was examined in consultation with the Ministry of Finance
and creation of 6 posts of officers in the grade of Deputy Secretary/Director has been approved.
Committee’s further observation
18.9 The Committee is of the opinion that appointment of full time CVOs in Ministries/
Departments is a pre-requisite to ensure a robust vigilance mechanism. Therefore, it would like

48
to impress upon the Ministry that the proposal of CVC to appoint full time CVOs should be

for incorporating a clause in the CSS (CCA) Rules mandating consultation with the CVC in cases
involving ‘vigilance angle’ should be given urgent consideration and should be duly implemented.

CERTAIN ISSUES HIGHLIGHTED IN THE ANNUAL REPORT OF CIC
Recommendation/observation
22. The CIC, in its Annual Report, has highlighted certain issues which need to be
tackled by the stakeholders concerned:—
(i) Setting up a citizens’ council of RTI User Groups/Sector Panels to oversee the
implementation of the Act and act as a bridge between the public and
Government.
(ii) Public authorities engaging in dialogue with applicants can be a constructive
process to strengthen the freedom of access to information. Every Ministry
could consider setting up a mechanism within public authorities under its
jurisdiction to address this.
(iii) In keeping with the above suggestion, each Ministry may suo moto  develop a
mechanism in consultation with the Commission to deal with RTI matters in
any Government Department.
(iv) Suo moto disclosure by public authority.
(v) Expand the modes of depositing the fee for making an RTI application.
(vi) Seeking information using e-mail.
(vii) All Head Post Offices should be designated as Assistant Public Information
Officers to receive RTI applications for public authorities.
(viii) Government and public authorities must set aside a specific budget for
dissemination of knowledge amongst citizens so that the provisions of the Act
can be utilized at all levels of society, through heightened public awareness.
(ix) All public authorities may include a chapter titled “Implementation of RTI
Act, 2005” in their Annual Reports.
(x) Strengthening the grievance redressal mechanism of public authorities so that
citizens/employees do not have to resort to the RTI Act.
(xi) Monetary remuneration to the Public Information Officers.
(xii) Financial and administrative autonomy of the Commission.
(xiii) Contempt powers should be given to the Commission.
(xiv) T raining of Public Information Officers.
(xv) The Government may set up a Centre for Accountability and Transparency for
undertaking activities relating to research in best practices in creating an open
access regime and other such related activities that would effectively strengthen
the Commission in pursuing its mandate. [Para 53]
Action Taken Reply
22.1 The RTI Act, 2005 has created 28 establishments in the country, one Central Information
Commission and 27 State Information Commissions, which, in fact are the bridges between the
appropriate Governments and the Citizens. The Commissions have power to receive and enquire

50
into complaints, receive and decide appeals and impose penalties on the CPIOs etc. As regards
setting up of Citizens’ Council of RTI Users etc., it is felt that such a role can effectively be played
by the NGOs. In this regard this Department has requested all the States/UTs to involve the Non-
Government Or ganizations working in their States to spread awareness about the Act vide letter
No.F.1/26/2007-IR, dated 9th January, 2008. The Government has taken following steps to ensure
smooth implementation of the provisions of the Act which cover the points raised by the
Commission as well:
(i) All the Ministries/Departments have been requested for appointment of CAPIOs vide
DOPT OM 34012/13(S)/2005-Estt.(B) dated 6th October, 2005.
(ii) All the Ministries/Departments have been requested vide  DOPT OM dated
23rd March, 2007 to post the details of CPIOs on the website etc.
(iii) Instructions have been issued vide OM dated the 9th July, 2007 clarifying that the
function of the first appellate authorities is quasi-judicial in nature and that the
appellate authority should see to it that justice is not only done but it also appears to
have been done. The OM further clarifies that the AA should pass speaking order
giving justifications for the decision arrived at.
(iv) All the Ministries/Departments have been requested to prepare an exhaustive list of
public authorities under them and to upload the same on the RTI portal and to keep
it updated (OM dated 31st July, 2007).
(v) A clarification regarding disclosures of the ACRs of any employee has been issued
vide OM dated 21st September, 2007.
(vi) All the Ministries/Departments etc. have been requested to comply with the provisions
contained in Section 4 of the Act, which relates to  suo-motu discloser of information
(OM dated 21st September, 2007).
(vii) It has been clarified vide OM dated 31st October, 2007 that sub-section (3) of section
8 does not require retention of records indefinitely.
(viii) All the public authorities have been advised to update their records, improve their
infrastructure and bring out necessary manual (OM dated 14th November, 2007).
(ix) All the Or ganizations specified in the Second Schedule of the Act have been advised
to designate CPIOs and first appellate authorities and publish the details thereof (OM
dated 14th November, 2007)
(x) All the public authorities having more than one PIO have been requested to create a
Central Point within the organization where all the RTI application and appeals addressed
to the first appellate authority may be received (OM dated 14th November, 2007).
(xi) All the public authorities should designate the first appellate authorities and publish their
particulars along with the particulars of the PIOs (OM dated 14th November, 2007)
(xii) A letter has been written to all the States/UTs on 9th January, 2008 requesting them
to involve the Non-Government Organizations working in their States to spread
awareness about the Act.
(xiii) Guidelines for the officers designated as Central Public Information Officer have been
issued (OM dated 27th February, 2008).
(xiv) Guidelines for the first appellate authorities have been issued (OM dated 25th April, 2008).
(xv) Guidelines for the public authorities have been issued (OM dated 25th April, 2008).

51
(xvi) Clarification has been issued regarding transfer of RTI applications which are the
subject matter of more than one public authority. (OM dated 12th June, 2008).
(xvii) All the Ch ief Secretaries of the States/UTs have been informed about the best
practices initiated by the Government of Andhra Pradesh for effective implementation
of the RTI Act, 2005 (Letter dated 23rd June, 2008).
(xviii) All the public authorities were requested again to ensure suo-moto  disclosure
as provided in the RTI Act and to remain courteous with the information seekers
(OM dated 24th June, 2008).
22.2 The Act enables the citizens to send application through e-mail. The Government, in due
course of time, may consider developing a system of accepting fee through e-mode etc.
22.3 The Government already has a public grievance redressal system. The RTI Act, however,
supplements the redressal system in as much as citizens have now a statutory right to get
information.
22.4 Regarding imparting training, it may be stated that the Training Division of this Department
has been continuously conducting training programmes for CPIOs with updated training modules.
22.5 The CIC or the SICs are not courts of records and don’t have contempt power.
22.6 The PIOs are performing their role as PIOs as a part of their duty. Though it is an
additional responsibility, it is not proposed to pay for this work separately.
Committee’s further observation
22.7 The Committee takes note of the reply furnished by the Ministry. It feels that though the
Ministry has taken some steps on certain issues, proactive steps need to be taken on matters
given in para nos (viii), (ix), (xii) and (xv). The Committee, therefore, desires that these matters
should be given due consideration for effective implementation of the RTI Act.
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES
Recommendation/observation
23. The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has acted upon its
recommendation made in its 19th Report that the PGRAMS should be introduced in all
Ministries and Departments and that the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public
Grievances may pursue the matter with those Ministries who have yet to install PGRAMS
and to take expeditious steps to install the same without further delay. It appreciates that
this has led to the birth of Centralized PGRAMS, the implementation of which started in
June, 2007. [Para No. 28.3]
23.1 The Committee is happy to note that the CPGRAMS has been benefited by many
user organizations such as Railways and that its benefits are utilized by even the Zonal
officers of the Railways. [Para 28.3 and 28.4]
Action Taken Reply
23.2 The old PGRAM System was server based and required investment in servers in each
Ministry/Department where PGRAM System was to be installed leading to delay. However, with the
birth of the new centralized PGRAMS which is web based and does not require investment in
servers for installing it in Ministries/Departments, this process has been expedited. This system was
introduced in June, 2007, wherein each of the Nodal Officer of 89 Ministries/Departments have
been given a user name and password through which they can access the CPGRAMS software

52
from the Centralised Server. The Ministries/Departments could also open accounts of their
subordinate offices which in turn can access the CPGRAMS software from the same Centralised
server. This has facilitated the usage of CPGRAM software in all Ministries/Departments of Central
Government and also the field attached offices under them. However, to ensure implementation of
CPGRAM system in all Ministries/Departments its effective usage and in order to keep close vigil
on grievances an Action Plan has been drawn up. This plan includes organizing monthly meetings
of 20-25 Ministries under Chairmanship of Additional Secretary where grievances of these
Ministries/Departments are reviewed and progress of CPGRAM is monitored. Wherever necessary
trainings with the help of NIC is being organized for better utilization of this system. A list of 89
Ministries/Departments were CPGRAM System is functioning is enclosed.
Committee’s further observation
23.3 The Committee is happy to note that the CPGRAM software is being used by the
Ministries/Departments of Government of India. The Committee also welcomes the Action Plan
drawn to monitor the effective implementation of the system. The Committee is, however, keen
to know whether the system is effectively working as the Committee understands that CPGRAM
is a devise to redress the grievances and to what extent this objective is being achieved.
STATUTORY SUPPORT FOR PUBLIC GRIEVANCES  REDRESSAL MECHANISM
Recommendation/observation
24. The Committee is not satisfied with this reply. It is of the opinion that the
Ministries/Departments should keep a close vigil on grievances and that they should be
redressed in a time bound manner. It could gather that Government is the major litigant
in Courts of law, resulting in vast expenditure of public money, Governmental resources and
time. It is of the view that the essence of good governance is defeated in the absence of
efficient and timely redressal of grievances. If the grievances are redressed timely at the
level at which they arise, the aggrieved will not approach Court of Law. This will save
resources and time, of both the aggrieved and the Government. [Para No. 29.2]
24.1 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should make a study
as to the nature of cases pending in Courts mainly because of non-application of in-built
Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism and make the erring office accountable and
punished. This will reduce the cases in Courts due to non-application of mind and soul into
the dispute. [Para No. 29.3]
24.2 The Committee is of the view that public service delivery system is inefficient unless
it caters to the needs and issues of the common man. In order to assuage the concerns of
the people regarding the efficiency of the public services, it is pertinent that their
grievances are redressed promptly. [Para No. 29.4]
24.3 The Committee strongly feels that enacting a statute for PGRM will go a long way
in ensuring participatory governance and the Ministry should seriously examine this issue
and the Committee be apprised of the outcome therefrom. [Para No. 29.5]
Action Taken Reply
24.4 The Department is acting on the recommendation of the Committee and the issue of
envisaging Public Grievance Redress Mechanism (PGRAMS) in a statutory form is being examined
in consultation with Ministry of Law. Apart from providing statutory support to the Public
Grievance Redress mechanism which is being examined in consultation with ‘Ministry of Law it
was also felt that the Redress and Monitoring System for Ministries should be strengthened to

53
ensure efficient and timely redressal of grievances. With the introduction of the CPGRAM systems,
a handy tool has been provided in the hands of Director of Public Grievances (Joint Secretary)
level officers in each Ministry/Department to monitor grievances sent for redressal to their
subordinate offices. The system provides suggestive categories under which the Ministries/
Departments can categorise the grievances for making systemic improvements. The CPGRAMS has
many facilities for the citizens like lodging complaints online and getting a unique registration
number for further reference. Acknowledgement is provided bye-mail and citizens can send the
grievances directly to Ministries/Departments. Grievances received directly by post are registered
on behalf of the citizen by DARPG and complaint is scanned and forwarded to Ministry concerned
for its timely redressal. Since the grievances are organized in a decentralized manner, the usage of
the system by all Ministries/Departments up to their attached, field and subordinate officers will
help in efficient and timely redressal of grievances. The Department, agrees that if the grievances
are redressed timely at the level at which they arise they will not approach Court of Law and
resource and time of both Government and aggrieved would be saved.
24.5 In the light of the recommendation of the Committee the Ministry of Law and Justice has
been requested to conduct a study as to the nature of cases pending in Courts simply because of
non-application of in built Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism and make the erring office
accountable and punished.
24.6 The Department has noted the recommendation of the Committee and will continue to
endeavour to strengthen the Public Grievance Redress and monitoring Mechanism in all Ministries/
Departments of the Central Government.
24.7 The recommendation of the Committee was regarding enacting a statute for PGRAM on the
lines of RTI Act 2005, that could make it mandatory on all Departments/Ministries/Organisations to
pursue the grievance till their logical end. The Department has examined the above recommendation
and prepared a detailed concept paper for seeking the comments of Ministry of Law.
Committee’s further observation
24.8 The Committee endorses the view of the Government that Public Grievances Redressal
Mechanism needs to be strengthened. The Committee appreciates the introduction of CPGRAM
system enabling the citizens to lodge their complaints online and forwarding the grievance to the
respective department electronically for a timely redressal. It is just a beginning and the efficacy
of the system is yet to be established. The Committee feels that efficiency, fairness and timely
redressal of the grievance is the key to the whole issue and hopes that the Government
Ministries/Departments and the Organizations falling under their administrative control will be
able to meet this enshrined objective.
24.9 The Committee also welcomes the view of the DARPG that timely redressal at the level
where complaint arises will reduce the burden of the Courts and thereby, save the resources of
the Government as well as those of the aggrieved person. The Committee, however, awaits the
details of the study undertaken by the Ministry of Law and Justice as to the nature of cases
pending in the Courts because of non-application of inbuilt PGRM and making the erring office
accountable and punished. The Committee desires that the details may be made available by the
Ministry in their ATN.
24.10 The Committee notes that its suggestion regarding enacting a statute for PGRM in the
lines of the Right to Information Act is being considered by the Department in consultation with
the Ministry of Law and Justice. The Committee eagerly awaits the details of the Concept Paper
alongwith the comments of the Ministry of Law and Justice. The Committee further urges the
DARPG to pursue the matter vigorously with that Ministry.

54
24.11 The Committee takes note of the communication dated 4th November, 2008 received
from the Secretary, Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, in which it
was stated that there could not be a single authority/Act to deal with all the issues that are raised
through public grievances pertaining to different Ministries/Departments.
24.12 In this regard, the Committee is of the strong view that enactment of a law for Public
Grievances Redressal Mechanism will ensure accountability and lend enforceability to the
inherent right of a citizen as a consumer of the services rendered by the Government. The
Committee would like to emphasize that the recommendation of the Committee was for an
inbuilt Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism for “customer satisfaction”, rather than an
external mechanism. The Committee recommends that the Government should examine the
recommendation in right earnest.
CITIZENS’ CHARTER
Recommendation/observation
25. The Committee recommends that the Department of Administrative Reforms and
Public Grievances should encourage all Ministries/Departments to include Citizens’ Charter as
an item in their Annual Report and to implement the Citizens’ Charter for effective service
delivery. They should also provide adequate support to formulate Citizens’ Charter and
implement the same. Special emphasis should be given to formulate and implement the
Citizens’ Charter in newly created Ministries/Departments. The Department should encourage
other Departments, Organizations and Institutions to coin a “slogan” and to create a “logo”
reflecting their role, functions and motto, in the pattern of private companies and corporate
houses, and which can be comprehended by the common man. [Para 32.1]
Action Taken Reply
25.1 The instructions regarding inclusion of Citizens’ Charter in the Annual Report has already
been included in Para No. 157 of the Central Secretariat Manual of Office Procedure (CSMOP)
which is the basis of functioning of all Government Ministry/Department. In case of newly created
Ministries/Departments instructions have been issued for formulating the Citizens’ Charter within
six months and instructions contained in Manual of Office Procedures Chapter 18 para 157,
regarding inclusion of Citizen Charters’ in their Annual Report have been reiterated (copy enclosed).
These newly created Ministries have also been provided support for formulation of Citizen Charters.
25.2 The Department is providing regular support to the Ministries/Departments for formulation
of Citizens’ Charter. The second ARC in its fourth report on “ethics in governance” has also
recommended that “Citizen Charters’ should be made effective by stipulating the service levels and
also the remedy if these service levels are not met”. In the light of these recommendations
instructions have been issued to all Ministries/Departments regarding setting of a mechanism or
system in each Government Department/Organisation to ensure monitoring of Standards of services
defined in the Citizens’ Charter. The Citizen’s Charter should be reviewed periodically after taking
the feedback from users and stake holders and they should be involved in review of the Charter.
25.3 As regards the Committee’s recommendation regarding coining a “slogan” and create a
“logo” reflecting their role, functions and motto, this recommendation of the Committee has been
circulated to all Ministries/Departments.
Committee’s further observation
25.4 The Committee observes that the pace with which the Ministries/Departments of
Government of India are formulating their Citizens’ Charter is not encouraging. The Committee,

55
during its interactions with the Central Ministries/Departments and also with the Public Sector
Undertakings and other statutory bodies, noted that many of them were yet to formulate their
Citizens’ Charter. The Committee, therefore, directs the DARPG to impress upon the respective
Ministries to expedite the formulation of the Citizens’ Charter. The Committee also directs the
DARPG to submit the list of Ministries/Departments and also the Organizations who have not
so far prepared their Citizens’ Charter.
25.5 The Committee has also been impressing upon the Public Sector Banks/ Undertakings
and statutory bodies, which it interacted with in the course of its business, to mention the topic
in their Annual Reports. The Committee directs the DARPG to impress upon the Ministries to
ensure that their Organizations invariably include this as an item in their Annual Report.
25.6 The Committee desires that the recommendation of the Committee with respect to
“slogan” and “logo” should be implemented, in the benefit of the common man.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel,
Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorised by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Thirty-second Report on Action Taken by Government
on the recommendations contained in the Twenty-sixth Report on Demands for Grants (2008-09)
of the Ministry of Law and Justice. The Action Taken Report contains only those paragraphs which
entailed recommendations/observations of the Committee.
2. The Twenty-sixth Report of the Committee was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the
Table of the Lok Sabha on 29th April, 2008. Draft Report on the replies of the Government to the
recommendations/observations contained in this Report were considered and adopted by the
Committee in its meeting held on the 16th December, 2008.
DR. E. M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN
N
EW D ELHI; Chairman,
16th December, 2008 Committee on Personnel, Public
Grievances, Law and Justice.

1
REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by Ministry of Law
and Justice on the recommendations/observations of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice in its 26th Report on Demands for
Grants (2008-09) of the Ministry. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table
of Lok Sabha on 29th April, 2008.
2. Action Taken replies have been received from the Ministry of Law and Justice (Department
of Legal Affairs, Legislative Department and Department of Justice) in respect of the
recommendations contained in the above mentioned report. These replies have been categorised as
follows:
Chapter – I – The recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the Ministry in
respect of Paras 5.8, 5.38, 4.49, 4.69. The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has
accepted its recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter–I of the report.
Chapter – II – The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue
in view of the replies given by Department of Justice in respect of Paras 5.9, 5.19, 5.20, 6.28,
6.93, 6.94, 6.98, 7.2,4.12, 4.13, 4.40, 4.43, 4.54, 4.55, 4.66, 4.67, 4.68, 4.82. The Committee is
convinced with the explanations advanced by the Ministry of Law and Justice and does not want
to pursue as of now.
Chapter – III – The recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not accepted
replies given by Ministry of Law and Justice with regard to Paras 5.10, 5.11, 5.14, 5.24, 5.36,
6.24, 6.33, 6.42, 6.43, 6.46, 4.6, 4.7, 4.9, 4.16, 4.21, 4.26, 4.27, 4.48, 4.76. The Committee
expresses its concern for not accepting the recommendations of the Committee contained in
Chapter–III of this report and desires that Ministry should furnish logical explanations in respect
of these recommendations.
Chapter – IV – The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry
of Law and Justice have not been received with regard to Paras 5.27, 5.33, 6.12, 6.51, 6.65, 6.72,
6.73, 6.75, 6.81, 6.89, 6.96, 6.36, 6.37, 6.38, 4.36, 4.56, 4.61, 4.83. The Committee observes that
Ministry has furnished interim replies and the Committee desires that Ministry should furnish action
taken notes in respect of recommendations categorised in Chapter–IV .
3. The recommendations/observations of the Committee in its 26th report, the ATRs furnished
by Ministry of Law and Justice and the Committee’s further recommendations/observations have
been dealt with in the succeeding chapters.

2
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY
THE MINISTRY
DELIMITATION COMMISSION
Recommendation/observation
1. The Committee notes that the President of India has issued notification specifying
the dates of implementation of the Commission’s order and future elections of all the said
States will now be held on the basis of new Delimitation Order. The Committee feels that
the delimitation work with respect to the North-Eastern States of Arunachal Pradesh,
Assam, Manipur and Nagaland which was deferred will also be completed as early as
possible. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry to submit the status report in this
regard at the time of furnishing the Action Taken Replies. (Para 5.8)
Action Taken Reply
1.1 The Delimitation Act, 2002 was amended to insert two new sections 10A and 10B in the
Act. Section 10A of the Delimitation Act, 2002 empowers the President to defer the Delimitation
exercise in a State, in view of the situation whereby unity and integrity of India is threatened or
there is a serious threat to the peace and public order. The situation in respect of North-East States
of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur and Nagaland have been assessed by the Ministry of Home
Affairs and they have suggested the deferment of delimitation exercise in those States, as the
conditions prevailing there have not been conducive for the conduct of delimitation exercise by the
Delimitation Commission. Accordingly, four Orders to defer delimitation exercise in the above said
States have been issued on the 8th February, 2008.
1.2 Now, consequent upon the completion of the delimitation exercise in the entire country, the
Chairman, Delimitation Commission has demitted office on the 31st May, 2008 and Ministry of Law
and Justice vide notification dated 23rd May, 2008 has specified the first day of June, 2008 as
the date on which the Delimitation Commission shall cease to exist.
1.3 Further, as a consequential requirement, the Representation of the People (Amendment) Act,
2008 (10 of 2008) amending the Representation of the People Act, 1950 was enacted and made
effective from the 16th April, 2008. As per sub-section (1) of section 8A of the Representation of
the People Act, 1950, if the President of India is satisfied that the situation and the conditions
prevailing in the States of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur or Nagaland are conducive for the
conduct of delimitation exercise, he may, by order, rescind the said deferment orders in relation
to that State and provide for the conduct of delimitation exercise in the States by the Election
Commission. Further, as per sub-section (2) of section 8A of the Representation of the People
Act, 1950 the Election Commission of India is empowered to undertake fresh delimitation in respect
of the aforementioned four States as soon as may be after the deferment orders in respect of these
States are rescinded.
1.4 In  view of the aforesaid fact, it may be stated that a fresh delimitation exercise will be
initiated as and when conditions prevailing in these States become conducive for the conduct of
delimitation exercise.
2

3
Recommendation/observation
SIMPLIFICATION OF LEGISLATIVE LANGUAGE
2. The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry has taken steps in the direction
of simplification of laws. But still the Committee feels that it is an ongoing process and
efforts should be made for simplifying the legal language, which is quite often difficult to
understand. It feels that, laws should be drafted in national or regional languages to convey
the purpose and intent thereof rightly comprehended by those meant for. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should find ways and means to simplify laws so
as to be understood even by the people having no specialized knowledge of legal
formulations. (Para 5.38)
Action Taken Reply
2.1 With a view to find out ways to simplify laws so as to be understood by the common man,
the subject matter has been deliberated upon by the Government draftpersons under the guidance
of the Secretary. In this connection it was considered appropriate to issue instructions to the
draftpersons to take it as an ongoing process in simplifying the texts of the draft legislations
prepared and finalised by them. In addition, it has been decided to conduct regular workshops on
monthly basis to discuss, train and develop the skills of legislative drafting in simple language
amongst the officers of the Legislative Department to simplify the legal language so as to be
understood by the general public easily. In the said workshop some of the important and social
welfare laws having frequent interface will be taken-up for transforming/drafting into simple legal
language and thereafter, the draft of the simplified law will be forwarded to the concerned
administrative Ministry for their comments. Once the draft is finalised, the approval to replace the
existing law with the newly prepared simplified law, by following due Parliamentary procedure, will
be obtained. This whole exercise will be beneficial in two ways; firstly, identifying certain laws
with complex language and redo it in a simple text and secondly, the draft person will be adequately
trained for the purpose in undertaking any future legislation in simple and plain language.
2.2 Further, the terms and expressions used in Hindi version of Central Laws were decided and
approved by the various experts of the then Official Languages (Legislative) Commission. This
Commission consisted of legal and language experts of all India repute and finalized translation of
most of the major Acts. We cannot deviate much from these terms and expressions as it would
result into affecting the interpretation of law. However, now a days, we are simplifying the
language where the strict compliance of the earlier settled technical words is not necessary so that
Hindi text may be more comprehensible to the extent, common man could be in a position to
understand the spirit of law. Since law making process is a continuous one, no drastic changes
can be made. Official Languages Wing, earlier Official Languages (Legislative) Commission, is not
drafting the laws in Hindi, but is translating them into Hindi and other regional languages.
2.3 Information regarding simplification of legislative language, as far as it relates to Regional
Languages Unit, is given below:—
2.4 The translation of Central Acts in certain regional languages as enshrined in the 8th
Schedule to the Constitution is undertaken by the respective State Governments through the
Agencies/Departments under their control by using the terminology prevalent and understandable in
that particular region so that the common man is able to understand the law in the language, he
understands. Moreover, while finalizing the terminology used in the translation of “a particular
Central Acts in the Working group meeting, which is attended by the representative from the
respective State Government, the weightage is given to their suggestions for using simple language
in order to fulfil the purpose of rendering translation of Central Acts into regional languages.

4
Recommendat ion/observation
LEGAL EDUCATION AND RESEARCH
3. The Committee also recommends that Indian Law Institute which is country’s
premier research institute in the field of law should carry out research on the subjects like
needs and difficulties faced by the subordinate judiciary, revamping our legal education,
research on Judicial Impact Statement etc. which will not only help the institute to grow
but also help their studies to be utilized by others. Regular or short terms courses should
allow the serious participants rather than casual persons for getting certificates. Quality of
faculty, course material etc. should be of international level. The students and in service
trainees should be made to do research and give papers, rather than whiling away the time
and get certificates. It should work more as think tank to the State. (Para 4.49)
Action Taken Reply
3.1 It is indeed true that Indian Law Institute (ILI) is a premier research Institute in India.
Right from its inception, it has been the aim of the Institute to conduct research into the area,
which are of interest of the legal fraternity including the functionaries in the subordinate Judiciary.
When the research on the appellate judiciary is conducted naturally the needs and difficulties of the
subordinate judiciary are also enquired into. During 2007 in pursuance of advice by the then
President of India, the ILI undertook an empirical study involving the subordinate judiciary to
identify the causes for delay in the Administration of criminal justice in the country. The areas of
difficulties were identified and the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India/President, ILI wrote to all Chief
Justices of the High Courts in the country urging the need for avoiding delay and suggesting
various measures therefor. The Institute continues to take interest in the affairs of the
administration in the subordinate judiciary.
3.2 As regards revamping legal education, it may be noted that recently ILI has written to the
National Knowledge Commission to initiate steps for conducting an International seminar on Indian
Legal Education, so that new ideas on the subject may come up for discussion and adoption. The
ILI has been considering the possibility for adopting various measures for revamping legal
education. Its LL.M. programme which is research based has become very popular. Its products
are finding employment as teachers in various law schools. Training they receive at the Institute
make them to work hard for revamping legal education and research. The Institute have recently
devised a LL.B. LL.M. (integrated) 4 years programme to produce enough law teachers. This is
intended to avoid our students seeking foreign shores in search for LL.M. degree. The idea is to
offer LL.B. curriculum of 3 years after graduation and to offer advanced courses for one year to
enable them to get LL.M. within a year i.e. during the final year of 4 year course. The approval
of BCI and the U.G.C. is awaited. We think it will go a long way in producing enough law teachers
for our country.
3.3 There is already a Committee which went into the question of judicial impact statement.
Depending upon its recommendations and the Government of India’s follow-up action ILI would
be very much happy to get involved in undertaking research connected with judicial impact
statement.
3.4 Recently ILI has conducted three major projects having national importance. The report
made in pursuance of the directions Minorities Commission was very much appreciated. The World
Bank Project on ADR Systems in India is a major one. They are also engaged in a study on
“Judiciary’s Impact on Parliamentary Practices in India” on behalf of the Rajya Sabha Secretariat.
It will be of much importance in nation-building.

5
3.5 ILI’s academic programme have always been associated with the requirement of students
doing ample research before they obtain a degree from the ILI whether it is LL.M. or PG Diploma
course offered by it. In almost all the PG Diploma courses it is necessary for the certificates to
do research and produce a dissertation before he/she is granted the certificate. The requirement is
very important in the case of LL.M. Course. Some of the research papers produced by its students
in the LL.M. class have already been published in the internationally reputed journal of the JILI.
It is a matter of satisfaction that some of its student have started publishing their articles in foreign
journals also.
Recommendation/observation
INTERNATIONAL CENTRE FOR ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION (ICADR)
4. The Committee is happy to note that its recommendation for timely audit of accounts
of ICADR is now being carried out regularly. The Committee further hopes that ICADR,
which is the premier institute in the field of arbitration, should be made fully accountable
and transparent in terms of every aspect of its functioning to enhance its appeal to the
public, and for that matter, every effort should be invested by the Ministry. The Committee
further desires that the ICADR should optimally utilize the building constructed for the
purpose. The Committee also recommends that ICADR, which has the ability to be the best
institute of the world, should make all out efforts to attract foreign arbitration cases and
try to become the hub of international arbitration. (Para 4.69)
Action Taken Reply
4.1 ICADR is making sincere efforts to attract both international and domestic arbitration cases.
The World Bank has given a grant of US $ 4.80 lakhs for “Strengthening ADR in India”. Under
the said project of the World Bank, the Indian Law Institute has been given the work of preparing
a Report on “ADR Status/Effectiveness Study”. The draft final Report of the Indian Law Institute
has been already discussed by the Officers of the World Bank and the Members of the Committee
of ICADR with the Director of Indian Law Institute and the Research Professors associated with
the preparation of the draft Final Report. The draft Final Report has been extensively discussed and
various suggestions have been made to the Indian Law Institute to revise the said Report. The said
Report contains various suggestions/recommendations, e.g., creation of public awareness, training
of arbitrators and mediators, further research on ADR, adoption of ADR as a part of formal
education, conducing community mediations, establishing good rapport with V oluntary
organisations/Universities in spreading the message of ADR and evolving a Code of Conduct and
Professional Ethics for arbitrators, mediators and others, etc. On the presentation of the said
Report, ICADR will prepare further plans for upgrading its services and implementation of the
suggestions made by the Indian Law Institute. Similarly under the aforesaid project of the World
Bank, ICADR has given to the Centre for Effective Dispute Resolution (CEDR), London, U.K. the
work relating to preparation of Business Plan for development of ICADR and for conducting
training of mediators in India. The CEDR have already conducted the programme for Training of
Mediators in India from April to June, 2008. Two Foundation Courses for training of about 60
mediators were held in the premises of ICADR located at Plot No.6, Vasant Kunj Institutional Area,
Phase-II, New Delhi from 9th – 12th April, 2008 and 14th – 17th  April, 2008. An Advanced Course
for Training of Mediators was conducted from 12th  – 14th May, 2008, wherein 24 candidates
(selected out of 60 candidates who attended the Foundation Courses) were given further training.
Thereafter the Masters Trainer Course was held from 3rd - 5th June, 2008, wherein 12 candidates
selected out of 24 candidates who attended the Advanced Course were given Training. In addition
to these 12 candidates 13 Additional District and Sessions Judges and one Advocate, nominated by
the Mediation Committee of the Supreme Court, were also trained. Thus as a result of the said

6
programme for Training of Mediators, 26 Mediators for giving further training of mediation are
available.
4.2 The draft Final Business Plan for the Development of ICADR, as prepared by CEDR, has
also been discussed by the Officers of the World Bank and the Members of the Committee of
ICADR with the representatives of CEDR and a number of suggestions for revising the said draft
Final Business Plan have been made. The said draft Final Business Plan also contains a number of
suggestions for upgrading the services of ICADR so as to attract international arbitration cases and
international mediation cases in India. Further the Members of Committee of ICADR have also
undertaken a Study Tour of Singapore International Arbitration Centre, Singapore, CEDR,  London
Court of International Arbitration (LCIA), Chartered Institute of Arbitrators and Eversheds (a
leading law firm dealing in international arbitration and mediation), all located in London, U.K. We
sincerely hope that the cumulative effect of the aforesaid activities undertaken by ICADR in
association with Indian Law Institute, CEDR  and the World Bank will show result over the next
few years in upgrading the services and other infrastructure of ICADR which will attract
international arbitration cases and international mediation cases and enable ICADR to emerge as an
Institute of repute in the field of arbitration and mediation in India.

7
7
CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE
DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES
GIVEN BY DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
Recommendation/observation
PHOTO ELECTORAL ROLLS
1. The Committee appreciates that Election Commission has taken many steps like
introduction of Booth Level Officers, Computerisation of electoral rolls, introduction of
photo electoral rolls etc. to hold free and fair elections in the country. The Committee
hopes that with the introduction of these innovative methods the Commission would
certainly put a check on number of issues like duplicity, mistaken identity, faulty electoral
rolls etc. The Committee further feels that though the Commission has taken some
measures but it should also send its team of officers on a surprise visit to cross check the
working of BLOs. On computerization of electoral rolls, the Committee feels that with the
computerization of electoral rolls the Commission would be able to solve the problems of
the electorate in a better and efficient manner. (Para 5.9)
Action Taken Reply
1.1 The Election Commission has taken note of the Committee’s observation about sending its
team of officers on a surprise visit to cross check the working of BLOs. The Commission has
started deputing senior officers as “Roll Observers” who, inter alia , check and report on the
quality of BLO’s work. However, issues like mistaken identity (of voters) leading to impersonation
and bogus voting can be addressed much better only if the EPIC is made compulsory.
Committee’s further observation
1.2. The Committee takes note of the reply furnished by the Ministry. The Committee may be
apprised of the status as the time frame as set up by Election Commission is already over. The
Committee desires a status note including Assam, J&K and Nagaland on the subject may be
furnished along with ATN.
Recommendation/observation
ELECTRONIC VOTING MACHINES
2. The Committee is happy to note that the technical committee formed to decide the
technical worthiness of the 1989-90 model EVMs has submitted its report to the
Government. The Committee therefore, recommends the Government should immediately
start the weeding out of old EVMs and chalk out a definite time-frame for upgradation and
procurement of new EVMs. The Committee hopes this will help to get the election results
early and in a speedy manner. (Para 5.19)
Action Taken Reply
2.1 Identification process of less reliable EVMs of 1989-90 batches is going on. The inputs

8
received from the manufacturers and the field functionaries involved in this exercise indicate that
a large number of such EVMs may no longer be usable in future elections. However, the final
figures will be known very shortly.
2.2 The Election Commission has approached the Government of India for procurement of 1.80
lakhs of upgraded EVMs and replacement of roughly 1.5 lakh 1989-90 models EVMs, in order to
save the time and to be in readiness to handle the Lok Sabha poll of 2009 without any difficulty.
Committee’s further observation
2.3 The Committee impresses upon the Government to meet the requirement of Election
Commission for conducting the 2009 Lok Sabha elections smoothly.
Recommendation/observation
3. While taking note of the steps taken by the Commission in educating the people in
the use of EVMs, the Committee desires that the Ministry may focus more attention in
educating the rural poor and the masses in the far flung interior villages of the country.
It further opines that propagation of the usage of EVMs by way of flyers and posters will
go a long way for areas that have no access to audio-visual means. (Para 5.20)
Action Taken Reply
3.1 The Election Commission has taken all necessary steps in educating the voters. Propagation
of the usage of EVMs by way of flyers and posters is one of them. During Lok Sabha Election
2004, some Compact Discs were prepared through DAVP for voter awareness and training of
officials. The same are being reviewed and is under active consideration of the Commission for
further improvement.
COMPUTERISATION OF JUDICIARY
4. The Committee records its appreciation with the pace of computerization. However,
it feels that Ministry should fix a target for completion of computerization in a time-bound
manner. The Committee is of the view that computerization of judiciary would be an
effective tool to bring down pendency of cases as has been experienced in the Apex Court.
The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry should ensure
that necessary budget allocations for this purpose should be made and the targets set to
computerize the entire judicial system are met. (Para 6.28)
Action Taken Reply
4.1 The Central Government is implementing the Central Sector Plan scheme of computerization
of District and Subordinate Courts as a Mission Mode Project.
4.2 Under the scheme laptop computers have already been provided to 13365 Judges and 12074
laser printers have also been provided. 11005 judicial officers and 44020 court staff have been
trained in the use of ICT tools. Internet connectivity through broadband or dial-up facility has been
provided at the residences of 9524 Judges. 478 District Court complexes and 1203 Subordinate
Court complexes have also been provided with such connectivity.
4.3 The site preparation in the court complexes has commenced with the National Informatics
Centre having disbursed funds to those High Courts that have furnished the estimates for site
preparation work as per the guidelines. The matter of obtaining complete information on site
preparation estimates from all the High Courts is being pursued. The Department has been closely

9
monitoring the progress of site preparation work which is a key component in the implementation
of the project and is making efforts to sort out the issues/problems with a view to implement the
project on time.
4.4 A budget provision of Rs.125 crore has been made for the year 2008-09 which will ensure
that the requirement of funds of the National Informatics Centre for implementing the scheme
through 2008-09 is fully met.
4.5 The scheme is scheduled to be implemented by February 2009. The key activities
under the scheme are also being monitored regularly against specific timelines.
Recommendation/observation
ROLE OF REGISTRY OF SUPREME COURT
5. The Committee recommends that Registry, Supreme Court should work out some
mechanism like annual conference/forum where Registries of High Courts and
Administrative Head of Subordinate/Lower Courts can participate to ventilate and narrate
the problems faced by them. (Para 6.93)
5.1 The Committee also recommends that some mechanism should be worked out or
developed so that some kind of control over the District, Subordinate and High Courts in
the states should be there. Mere acknowledgement that the Registry doesn’t exercise or
have any control on the working of other Courts will not serve the purpose but rather
complicate the whole issue. The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry of Law
and Justice in consultation with the Chief Justice of India should try to formulate some
means/mechanism to exercise some control over the Munsif, District, Subordinate
Judiciaries and High Courts in the States which would work as a watchdog and keep tab on
their functioning. (Para 6.94)
Action Taken Reply
5.2 The above recommendations were forwarded to the Supreme Court Registry who have
informed that no further action is required to be taken by the Supreme Court Registry.

1. The Committee appreciates that the Commission has completed the exercise of Photo

smooth manner. But, Committee also advises the Election Commission to take extra
measures to ensure that the Photo Electoral Rolls are error free and serve the purpose for
which it has been made otherwise the whole exercise will be a failure. Each year there are
numbers of complaints regarding faulty rolls, missing names etc. In such cases, a person
having a bonafide “Voter Identity Card” should have legal rights to vote. (Para 5.10)
Action Taken Reply
1.1 The Election Commission has set an initial time frame of 31.08.08 to complete the exercise
of photorolls. Some States/Union territories however, due to prevailing ground situation may need
more time. The Commission is closely monitoring the exercise. Due to prevailing circumstances,
PER is not being taken up in Assam, Jammu and Kashmir and Nagaland for the present.
1.2 According to the extant provisions of law (sub-section (1) of section 62 of the RP
Act, 1951), only those who are enrolled as an elector in the electoral roll of a constituency can
exercise their vote. Therefore, to be registered as a voter in electoral roll is the first and foremost
requirement for exercising the right to vote. EPIC are issued for the purpose of verification /
identification of the bonafide of that registered voter. Electors Photo Identity Card, once issued is
a valid identity for the purpose of exercising ones franchise irrespective of whether a person has
moved from place where EPIC was originally issued provided the person is registered as a voter
at that point of time in that place. On the date of poll, a person is allowed to vote in a particular
polling station of a constituency if his/her name is in the Electoral Roll and his/her identity is
established through a bonafide document (EPIC). For polling purposes, the basic document used
would be the Electoral Roll and EPIC is only an instrument of identification to ensure that the
person appearing in a polling station to vote is same what he claims to be. Every person who is,
for the time being entered in the electoral roll of any constituency shall be entitled to vote in that
constituency. Therefore, if the “V oter Identity Card” holder is enrolled in the electoral roll in force,
only then he can exercise his vote, otherwise not.
Committee’s further observation
1.3 The Committee’ s concern was that a registered voter having the valid voter identity card
should not be denied of his right to vote. It is the responsibility of the State to remove the
inaccuracy in the electoral rolls and that can be done by taking extra measures/precautions ensuring

17
that photo electoral rolls are free of errors. The Committee is keen to know what extra measures
have been taken to remove the errors and what has been its outcome.

Courts in the country. It feels that the Ministry should take up the matter with State
Governments and fix a target for establishing at least one Family Court in each district so
as to resolve family disputes and related matters expeditiously and if need be amend the
relevant provision of the Family Court Act, 1984 pertaining to eligibility criteria of
population exceeding one million for setting up of a family court, so that at least one family
court is set up in each district particularly. (Para 6.33)
Action Taken Reply
7.1 In so far as the matter of establishing more Family Courts is concerned, Minister for Law
and Justice has written to the Chief Ministers/Administrators of all State Governments/Union
Territories pursuant to a request received from the Chief Justice of India that Family Courts may
be established in all Districts of the country.
7.2 The Government has also written to the State Governments requesting for the cost
estimates for setting up such Family Courts.
7.3 A number of States and UTs have responded over a period of time. While some Chief
Ministers have informed that they are having the matter looked into, the Governor of Karnataka
informed that the matter was under consideration of the High Court. The Chief Minister of West
Bengal has informed that steps are being taken to establish Family Courts in five Districts in

21
consultation with the High Court of Calcutta, his Government having decided to set up Family
Courts in the remaining Districts. The Chief Minister of Delhi has mentioned that the matter of
setting up of Family Courts is under active consideration of a Committee of Judges in the Delhi
High Court, the premises for setting up of Family Courts at two locations is likely to be ready
shortly. The Chief Minister of Maharashtra has informed that his State agrees in principle to set
up Family Courts in all the Districts and the concerned High Court has identified eleven places
where Family Courts can be set up. The Government of Rajasthan has informed that fourteen
Family Courts are to be set up.
7.4 The Administrator of UT of Andaman and Nicobar Islands has informed that the
infrastructure for a court building for the Family Court has already been built and a proposal is
shortly being submitted for establishing Family Court. The Administrator of the UT of Chandigarh
has informed that they are awaiting the framing of the rules by the State of Punjab that is expected
to be completed shortly.
7.5 The Chief Minister of Arunachal Pradesh has mentioned that the State does not have a
single town or city whose population exceeds one million and also that all family disputes are
settled as per customary and personal law of the indigenous population of Arunachal Pradesh.
Establishment of Family Courts in Arunachal Pradesh is not considered necessary.
7.6 The Government of Goa has mentioned that it has no town or city having a population of
one million. All matters pertaining to family disputes are being dealt with by regular civil courts
(senior divisions) in accordance with the common civil code applicable throughout the State
irrespective of caste, race, religion and that there appeared to be no requirement for establishment
of Family courts in the State of Goa.
Committee’s further observation
7.7 The Committee feels that with this speed, it will take long time to set up at least one family
court in each district. Responses from the State/UT Governments are not very encouraging as only
a very few of them have initiated the process. The Committee impress upon the Department of
Justice to vigorously pursue this issue with all the State and UT Governments to set up family court
in each district. The Committee desires that Government may explore the possibility as to how the
process can be expedited.
Recommendation/observation
PENDENCY OF CASES
8. The Committee notes with concern that year after year, the pendency of cases has
been steadily increasing. The trend is continuing even after taking recourse to other
alternative measures like setting up of fast track courts, family courts and permanent Lok
Adalats. The Committee has also been apprised that the Government has been constantly
reviewing accumulation of the arrears in Courts and the problem is sought to be tackled
by constitution of specialized benches and organizing Lok Adalats at regular intervals;
encouraging alternative modes of disposal, establishing Fast Track Courts even at the level
of Magistrates Court etc. The Committee finds that specialized. (Para 6.42)
8.1 Lok Adalats and Fast Track Courts, though created as an alternative mode of
disposal of arrears of cases, have been suffering due to infrastructural lacunae or financial
constraints and thus are not able to meet the desired targets. The Committee hopes that
with the establishment of Gram Nyayalayas the pendency will come down drastically. The
Committee therefore reiterates its earlier recommendation that the Ministry should
carefully analyze the factors responsible and look for viable solutions in addition to the

22
existing arrangements. The Committee further desires that since the pendency is mounting
by the day despite various measures taken in that regard, the Government, should request
the Law Commission of India to look into the whole gamut of the problem in an holistic
manner with help of ILI and Research Departments of Law Universities and submit its
Report as expeditiously as possible. (Para 6.43)
Action Taken Reply
8.2 The Committee’s recommendation that the Ministry should carefully analyze the factors
responsible for increasing pendency is one which has been the concern of the Government for
quite some time. Various Committees in the past have gone into the question of arrears, delay in
disposal and pendency of cases in courts. The Law Commission has also gone into the question
of pendency of cases in courts and made recommendations in this regard in the 77th and 79th
Report given in 1979 and 124th Report given in 1988. The Terms of Reference of the 18th Law
Commission inter-alia include “to keep under review the system of judicial administration to ensure
that it is responsive to the reasonable demands of the times and in particular to secure elimination
of delays, speedy clearance of arrears and reduction in costs so as to secure quick and economical
disposal of cases without affecting the cardinal principle that decisions should be just and fair”.
In view of this, the matter of requesting the Law Commission to look into the whole gamut of
the problem of pendency in a holistic manner is being examined in the Department.
8.3 Further, the Department has taken up a new Plan scheme which is shortly to be taken up
for approval in the Standing Finance Committee. This scheme proposes a component of studies by
reputed institutions in the country like the Indian Law Institute, research departments of various
Law Universities on different facets of judicial reforms including one on causes of increasing
pendency and measures to be taken to reduce it. This initiative of the Government is likely to fulfil
the Committee’s desire mentioned in Para 6.42.
Committee’s further observation
8.4 The Committee takes note of the initiative taken by the Government to address the problem
of pendency of cases. However, the reply does contain the details of new plan scheme. The
Committee directs the Department of Justice to furnish the details of scheme.
Recommendation/observation
V ACANCY OF JUDGES
9. The Committee notes with concern that there has not been any worthwhile
improvement with regard to filling up of vacancies of Judges in Supreme Court and High
Courts. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry to immediately take steps to fill the
remaining vacancies so that the same can help in reducing the mounting level of cases at
various levels. The Committee, therefore, calls upon the Ministry to come forward with an
alternative like the pre 1993 arrangement by involving the Executive, instead of allowing
the judiciary alone to choose the Judges. The aspirants of various vacancies should be
allowed to apply and appear before the Selection Committee. The closed system prevailing
now is not getting meritorious persons called to the Bench. Transparency, inclusiveness and
merit should be the way of appointing Judges. Till the warrant of appointment is issued by
President of India, it is maintained as secret. It is against democratic principles. The
aspirants’ names, merit and selection process should be made public and transparent,
through the High Court and Supreme Court website. The Report, at various levels in
Departments of Justice and Home and other stages, should be on the website of their
department till the final stage of issuing warrant of appointment. (Para 6.46)

23
Action Taken Reply
9.1 Filling up of vacancies in the High Courts is a continuous process. Vacancies do keep
arising on account of retirement, elevation or resignation of Judges. The Central Government has
been making every effort to fill up the existing vacancies in the Supreme Court and High Court.
The Minister of Law and Justice has been periodically reminding the Chief Justices of the High
Courts, to initiate proposals for filling up all vacant posts of Judges in the High Court. The
proposals received by the Department are processed expeditiously for approval of the competent
authority.
9.2 The existing system of appointment of Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts is in
pursuance of Supreme Court Judgment dated October 6, 1993 in the Supreme Court Advocates-
on Record and Anr vs. Union of India read with the Advisory Opinion of October 28, 1998. Any
change in the present system would require amendment of the Constitution or a review of their
judgment by a larger Bench of Supreme Court. There is at present no proposal before the
Government for bringing any change in the system of appointment of Judges.
9.3 It is the view of the Department as taken in the court that the records of deliberations
between the Chief Justice of India, Minister of Law and Justice, Prime Minister are in the nature
of advice tendered by the Cabinet to the Hon’ble President and hence, being privileged, cannot be
disclosed.
9.4 So far as making the appointment process transparent is concerned, it is the view of the
Department that public disclosure of names of candidates during the appointment process may be
an impediment in the dispassionate consideration of the names.
Committee’s further observation
9.5 The Committee is not convinced with the reply given by the Department of Justice. The
Committee has already addressed the issue of appointment, accountability and transparency in
appointment of Judges of Supreme Court and the High Courts in its 21st Report on ‘Judges
(Inquiry) Bill, 2007’, 27th Report on ‘Action Taken Replies on Law’ s Delays: Arrears in Courts’,
and 28th Report on ‘Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill: 2008’ and impressed
upon the Government to take necessary steps in restoring the pre-1993 arrangement by involving
the executive.
9.6 In its report on ‘Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2007’ the Committee suggested for bringing a
comprehensive legislation not only providing for the appointments of Judges by entrusting the
appointment to a body other than the collegium with representation both from the judiciary and the
executive. The Committee is of the considered opinion that it could be entrusted to the proposed
“Empowered Committee” which could initially screen the names and thereafter, refer the same to
the National Judicial Council for final recommendations.
9.7 Similarly the Committee in its 27th Report recommended for the restoration of the primacy
of the Executive in the matter so that judicial vacancies are filled up promptly and expeditiously.
9.8 Again in its 29th Report the Committee stressed on the Government to ensure the
compliance to the recommendations of the Committee in its previous Reports. The Department of
Justice while furnishing their action taken reply to the Committee’ s recommendation (para 6. 5)
stated:
“The appointment of Judges of the High Court and Supreme Court is being made in
accordance with the Supreme Court’ s judgment of October 26, 1993  and their Advisory
Opinion of October 28, 1998.  Any Change in the present system may required amendment
of the Constitution. The matter is being examined in the Department.”

24
9.9 The Committee takes note of the reply furnished by the Ministry. It is noteworthy that the

in Supreme Court and High Courts as the collegium system has failed. The Committee strongly feels
this is the time the Government should take initiative. The Committee therefore hopes that
Government will now give due consideration to the Committee’s recommendations made in its
reports to save the judiciary by strengthening transparency and accountability regime to which it
