Recommendation/observation
DELINKING OF DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE FROM THE MINISTRY OF HOME AND
CREATION OF A SEPARATE DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE WITH A FULL TIME SECRETARY
OF JUSTICE
3. The Committee feels that the rationale behind keeping Department of Justice under
the control of Home Secretary was logical at the time when this decision was taken during
the year 1971 but in view and of the drastic changes in last ten fifteen years, the rise in
the incidents of terrorism, birth and growth of naxalism in the country; the growing
complexity of modern crimes, handling natural calamities throughout India are becoming
difficult for the Home Secretary to devote time specifically for the Department other than
the Home. In nearly all the Government Departments there is a separate post of Secretary
to carry out the work of the Department in an efficient manner. Moreover, the Department
of Justice has been assigned a distinct task under the Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961, and the Department has been performing sensitive functions
pertaining to judicial appointments, service conditions of Judges and the administration of
justice. Viewed in this context and also of the fact that there are about 3 crore cases
pending in different Courts and about 100 High Court vacancies are to be filled and
thousands of vacancies exist in subordinate judiciary, thus corroding the faith of the people
in the judicial system, it would be more appropriate if the Department is accorded a distinct
identity including strong administrative structure of its own. It is in this context that the
Committee is of the considered opinion that for the sake of administrative efficiency and
exigency, the Department is separated from the Home Ministry and provided with a full-
fledged Secretary. (Para 6.12)
Action Taken Reply
3.1 The administrative efficiency and the service delivery of the Department of Justice have not
been compromised on account of the Department not having an independent Secretary and the
Home Secretary also being the Secretary of the Department. As has been mentioned earlier in
respect of the 20th Report, though the administrative arrangements of the Department of Justice
are through the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Justice is an independent Department
delinked and separated from the Home Ministry in terms of its functions and functional
independence as also in respect of budgetary allocations for both Plan and Non Plan schemes. The
Department of Justice is implementing Plan and Non Plan schemes for improvements in
administration of justice independent of any restrictive/budgetary control from the Home Ministry.
These schemes are aimed at reducing the pendency of cases in the courts and facilitating
improvements of efficiency of courts. Reduction of pendency is a matter predominantly within the
domain of the judiciary. Filling up vacancies in the subordinate judiciary is a matter with which
State Governments are concerned. These are matters which are not affected by the Department not
having an exclusive separate Secretary. On the contrary since the Ministry of Home Affairs is
responsible for Criminal Laws such as Indian Penal Code and Criminal Procedure Code and for
Prisons, it is advantageous to the Department of Justice to have the Home Secretary also as the
Secretary of Justice, more so as a lot of coordination is often required between the judiciary, the
police as also the prisons. Further the Ministry of Home Affairs is responsible for issuing advisories

31
to the State Governments and thus having the Home Secretary as Secretary (Justice) facilitates
better coordination with State Governments. The fact of the Home Secretary also heading the
Department of Justice as Secretary allows the Department of Justice leverage while dealing with
the other Ministries and Departments of the Government. This considerably facilitates the resolution
of issues and problems for the Department of Justice. The Department of Justice often needs and
use the services of agencies which work under the Ministry of Home Affairs. The fact of Home
Secretary as Secretary (Justice) facilitates cooperation of these agencies in the performance of
tasks assigned to the Department of Justice.
3.2 In view of the above distinct advantages in having the Home Secretary also as Secretary
of the Department of Justice, the Committee is requested not to press for a change in the existing
arrangement.
Committee’s further observation
3.3 The Committee is not in agreement with the view of the Government and still firmly
believes that Department of Justice has to be independent of the control of Ministry of Home
Affairs and needs to be headed by separate Secretary. The Committee is however constrained to
observe that Government has not given any weightage to the Committee’ s recommendations made
in this regard.
3.4 The Committee strongly believes that judicial administration is all together different affair
than the general administration and it needs to be managed by a professional who is exclusively
trained and experienced in handling judicial matters. Contrarily, the Justice Department has been
deprived of independence in managing its own affairs. Instead, the government of India has
preferred to club this department with the Home Ministry depriving to have a separate Secretary,
as nearly all the Government Departments have, to carry out the work of the Department in an
efficient manner and thereby ignoring the distinct task it has to perform under the Government of
India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, and the sensitive functions pertaining to judicial
appointments, service conditions of Judges and the administration of justice.
3.5 The Committee further observes that the Central Government provides for the grants for
development and regulation of judiciary and the funds from International Institutions are also
earmarked for certain institutions/activities. Besides, there is a strong need for making more funds
available to judiciary by enabling the Supreme Courts and the High Courts to generate revenue
themselves which can also be utilized by the subordinate judiciary in the States. Further, the
vacancies in the Supreme Court and the High Courts remain un filled for a long time which needs
to be filled in on the date of retirement as it can be closely monitored and planned in advances.
Judicial reforms have to be implemented. The Committee feels that such matters calls for instant
and continuous involvement of the Head of the Department. The Home Secretary being the incharge
of Internal Security supervises the law and order in the country. Besides this he is involved in
numerous responsibilities like managing natural calamities and because of this he does not find
enough time to manage the affairs of Justice Department. It is in this context the Committee
recommends that Justice Department must be headed not only by separate Secretary but also
professional, exclusively trained in judicial matters.
Recommendation/observation
BENCHES OF THE SUPREME COURT
4. The High Court benches in various places in addition to the State capital is much
appreciated by people for easy accessibility to justice to the poor and needy, on reasonable
expenditure. The Committee is not happy with the persistent opposition for establishing

32
benches of the Supreme Court in other parts of the country without advancing any
convincing reason or justification therefore. Even the Constitution of India makes
provisions for it under Article 130 of the Constitution. The Committee, therefore, endorses
its earlier view that establishment of benches of the Supreme Court atleast in Chennai on
trial basis and then in other parts of the country would be of immense help to the poor who
cannot afford to travel from their native placed to Delhi. The Committee, therefore, feels
that the Ministry should come forward with a necessary Constitutional amendment to
address this deadlock. (Para 6.51)
Action Taken Reply
4.1 Article 130 of the Constitution provides that “the Supreme Court shall sit in Delhi or in such
other place or places as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President, from
time to time, appoint”.
4.2 The matter of setting up of Supreme Court Benches outside Delhi has been taken up the
Chief Justices of India from time to time, However, the Supreme Court has not agreed to setting
up of Bench of Supreme Court at any place outside Delhi. The Chief Justice of India, in his letter
dated 12th August, 2007, informed that after reconsideration of the matter, the Full Court, in its
meeting held on 7th  August 2007, found no justification for deviating from its earlier resolutions
on the subject.
4.3 The Supreme Court of India have recently introduced a system enabling the Advocates-on-
Record/petitioner-in-person to file cases in the Supreme Court of India through internet to obviate
the difficulties faced by the litigants.
4.4 The recommendation of the Committee is being examined in consultation with the Ministry
of Law and Justice.
Committee’s further observation
4.5 The Committee reiterates its recommendations vide para 6.51  of 26th Report. However, the
report and action taken as per para 4 of the action taken reply is awaited. The Committee will
like to make its observation in the light of that report.
Recommendation/observation
SEPARATE HIGH COURTS FOR NORTH EASTERN STATES
5. In that backdrop, the Committee feels that there is a valid justification for each of
the North Eastern States for a separate High Court in each States. The Committee also
feels that when re-organisation of the North-Eastern region by the North Eastern Area
(Re-organization) Act, 1971 was passed, a common High Court was established for the five
North-Eastern States, i.e. Assam, Nagaland, Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura and the two
Union Territories (Union Territory of Mizoram and the Union Territory of Arunachal
Pradesh) and called as the Guwahati High Court which was established for administrative
convenience. Though, six outlying benches of the Guwahati High Court were also established
in the other States they are but benches of High Court. Moreover, nearly 3 crore of cases
are pending in different courts of the country which needs immediate attention which has
in turn diffused people’s faith in the judiciary. The law prevailing in the North Eastern
States is mainly the tribal laws existing in that area and mostly uncodified. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the government may, after thoroughly studying all the issues,
explore the possibility of establishing separate High Courts for each of the North Eastern

33
State which will, in turn play the role of evolving codification of the tribal laws existing
amongst the people of those States. It further feels that such a step would ensure that the
judgments of the High Courts will be treated as precedents, which with passage of time, can
evolve into written law. The interpretations given to the existing uncodified rules/laws by
the High Courts, can in future, be consolidated and this will result in codified laws and
uniformity of judgments. (Para 6.65)
Action Taken Reply
5.1 The recommendation of the Committee regarding establishing separate High Court for each
of the North-Eastern States is being examined.
Committee’s further observation
5.2 The Committee awaits the final decision of the Ministry in the matter and would like to
make its comment in the light of that report.
Recommendation/observation
FAST TRACK COURTS
6. The Committee is of the opinion that, the Department of Justice should devise
concrete ways and means to increase the efficiency of Fast Track Courts. It has come to
the notice of the Committee that Fast Track Courts are very often criticized for taking
decisions in a hurried manner, the Committee impresses upon the Ministry to monitor
performance of Fast Track Courts so that innocent persons are not convicted for the
offences not committed by them. The Committee also recommends that necessary Central
financial support may be accorded to the Fast Track Courts and their numbers may also be
augmented for speedy dispensation of cases. The Committee further exhorts the Ministry
to ensure that the FTCs resort more to fair trials and judgements and not only focus on
raising the statistics of disposal of cases. (Para 6.72)
6.1. ...This has not addressed the future of Judges after the ad-hoc period is over. Hence
Committee recommends to regularize the ad-hoc  judges and make FTC being managed
by the sitting judges rather than ad-hoc Judges, using the funds under the head of FTC.
[Para 6.73]
6.2 The Committee expresses its disappointment that the Fast Track Courts which were
made functional as a major reform initiative to lessen the burden on the already
overburdened Judiciary were not fully functional. The Committee fails to comprehend that
on one hand the Government has made tall claims that the FTCs have played a vital role
in reducing the ever mounting pendency of cases and on the other hand it has allowed some
functioning FTCs to dwindle out to the status of being non-functional and opines that if the
pillars of justice are shaken like this what would be its impact on the over all judicial
system. The Committee directs the Ministry to immediately look into the matter and
ensure that by the time of furnishing the Action Taken Reply all the non-functional FTCs
should start working. The Committee also recommends that in order to make these FTCs
functional, the Government should immediately start providing infrastructure, lucrative
salaries, permanent posts of Judges etc. otherwise the purpose with which it was established
would be defeated. (Para 6.75)
Action Taken Reply
6.3 The Government provides financial assistance to the State Governments for Fast Track

34
Courts (FTCs) and also has commenced providing support for enabling the judges with laptop
computers, broadband/dial-up connectivity for accessing the internet and has taken up both training
of both judicial officers and the staff in the courts with the overall view of improving the
efficiency in the courts including the FTCs.
6.4 The Government is committed to providing financial support to the FTCs upto 2010 and
also to facilitate improvement of court efficiency through application of Information and
Communication Technology.
6.5 The individual performance of the Judges of the FTCs and judgement delivery is a matter
outside the domain of the Government being entirely with the respective High Courts. The
Committee’s feelings on the issue of fair trials and judgements in the FTCs are, however, being
brought to the notice of the Chief Justices of the High Courts.
6.6 Judges of the Fast Track Courts (FTCs) are appointed by the State Governments in
consultation with the concerned High Courts in accordance with the directions given by the
Hon’ble Supreme Court in the Brij Mohan Lal case. The scheme of FTCs is presently up to
31.3.2010 a date up to which the Central Government will provide funds to the States.
6.7 State Governments have been requested to make all the non-functional FTCs functional on
priority basis. Financial assistance is being provided for FTCs as per the norms of the scheme
approved by Government on the lines of the recommendations of the Finance Commission. The
number of FTCs being assisted by the Central Government is restricted to 1562 i.e. the number
of FTCs operational on 31.3.2005.
Committee’s further observation
6.8 The Committee takes note of the reply furnished by the Department of Justice but is
constrained to observe that impact of FTCs is far from satisfactory. The desired results are yet to
be achieved. The Committee apprehends that with this pace of performance the status of pendency
is hardly going to clear by the year 2010. Hence there is need to augment the number of FTCs.
6.9 The Committee agrees that performance of FTCs comes within the domain of respective
HCs. The Committee wishes that Department of Justice continue to pursue with the respective State
Governments and HCs to ensure that FTCs not only expedite disposal of cases but also ensure fair
trial.
Recommendation/observation
RETIREMENT AGE OF JUDGES
7. The Committee therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation that Government
should immediately bring forward a Constitutional Amendment Bill to raise the retirement
age of Judges of High Courts from 62 to 65 i.e. at par with the retirement age of Judges
of the Supreme Court without any further delay. (Para 6.81)
Action Taken Reply
7.1 The concerned Departments have been consulted on this issue and the proposal is currently
under examination for seeking Government’s approval.
Committee’s further observation
7.2 The Committee will like to comment only after the final reply of the Government is
received.

35
Recommendation/observation
LANGUAGE OF THE COURTS
8. The Committee feels that the Chief Justice of India had rejected the proposal
without considering the benefits for those people who are poor, living in rural areas and who
cannot afford education and cannot speak any language other than their mother tongue.
The Committee feels that these factors should be borne in mind while making any
observation. Even Tamil language also contains legal terms/terminologies and the
Constitution of India has been translated in Tamil. Since the matter has been referred to
the Law Secretary for his comments, the Committee would appreciate if the Ministry would
furnish details thereof at the time Action Taken Reply by implementing the
recommendation. (Para 6.89)
Action Taken Reply
8.1 Department of Justice has again requested Department of Legal Affairs to provide their
comments on the subject matter which are still awaited. As soon as comments are received from
the D/o Legal Affairs, further necessary action will be taken.
Committee’s further observation
8.2 The Committee awaits the final reply of the Government and will like to make observation
after the receipt thereof.
Recommendation/observation
ALL INDIA JUDICIAL SERVICE
9. The Committee notes the views of the States for establishment of All India Judicial
Service as furnished so far. However, the Committee is of the view that creation of All
India Judicial Service on the line of Civil Services Examination in the country will attract
the best of talent in the country to join the prestigious Indian Judicial System and will
naturally improve upon the deteriorating quality of language used in judgments delivered
these days by the Courts excluding the Apex Court. The Committee also notes that the Law
Commission of India had in its 1st, 8th and 11th Reports had inter-alia recommended the
formation of All India Judicial Service and even the Supreme Court of India had also
recommended vide its judgments delivered on 13th November, 1991 in W.P. No.1022 of 1989
and 24th August, 1993 in Review Petition No.249/92 in the matter of All India Judges
Association for setting up of an All India Judicial Service in the country. The Committee
reiterates its earlier recommendation that all out efforts, including an amendment in the
Constitution, if necessary, may be taken up expeditiously to set up All India Judicial
Service. Till the consensus is arrived by the States and High Courts, the selection at State
level by the participation of Judicial Member, Pradesh Public Service Commission Member
and State should be formulated and followed uniformly in all States. This State Judicial
Services will further blossom as National Judicial Services for all National, Regional
Tribunal Chairman and Member appointments of various discipline. (Para 6.96)
Action Taken Reply
9.1 The suggestion that “till the consensus is arrived by the States and High Courts, the
selection at State level by the participation of Judicial Member, Pradesh Public Service Commission
Member and State should be formulated and followed uniformly in all States” is presently under
examination.

36
Committee’s further observation
9.2 The Committee awaits the final reply and would like to comment after the receipt of the same.
Recommendation/observation
NATIONAL JUDICIAL ACADEMY
10. The Committee expresses its anguish that despite its recommendations as contained
in its 15th Report and 20th Report, the NJA has so far failed to furnish its comments in
respect of the adverse observations/queries made by the Statutory Auditors in their Audit
Report. The Committee reiterates that the NJA should furnish its comments expeditiously.
(Para 6.36)
10.1 The Committee further feels that National Judicial Academy, which imparts training
to the judicial officers, court administrators and ministerial officers of the Supreme Court,
should open its gates/run programmes for Government officers dealing with administration
of justice. (Para 6.37)
10.2 The Committee is constrained to note that the grants given to the National Judicial
Academy were not fully utilised and were kept in a bank. The Committee desires that
the grants given in the year for a particular purpose must be utilized to its optimum.
(Para 6.38)
Action Taken Reply
10.3 The above recommendations/views of the Committee have been forwarded to the National
Judicial Academy for appropriate action.
Committee’s further observation
10.4 The direct the Department of Justice to pursue with the National Judicial Academy and
apprise the Committee of action taken in the matter.
Recommendation/observation
LOK ADALATS
11. In so far as the observation in Para 6.36 is concerned, the National Judicial Academy
(NJA) has commented that it is making efforts to furnish its comments to the Auditors.
(Para 6.36)
11.1 The NJA has informed that the amendment of the NJA Memorandum of Association
to include training of Government officers dealing with the administration of justice is not
currently envisaged as NJA is now focusing on fulfilling its core mandate. However, NJA will
continue to involve, as appropriate, Government officers in NJA academic programmes for
the judiciary in the capacity of resource persons and experts and foster a dialogue amongst
all of them on administration of justice. As part of NJA’s research and policy development
work, NJA has also held conferences and sponsored programmes along with Government
agencies in which such Government officials have participated. This will continue. In the
longer term, NJA will consider expanding its activities to provide training to other officials
involved in the administration of justice. (Para 6.37)
11.2 The NJA has informed that the comment is fully accepted and all necessary action
is being taken to comply with it. NJA has a clearly identified programme to utilize available

37
funds and a time table to complete utilization as much as possible within the current
financial year has been drawn. However, approval procedures required to be followed by
NJA take their own time. NJA will do its part in ensuring expeditious utilization of funds.
(Para 6.38)
Committee’s further observation
11.3 The Committee is constrained to note that NJA is yet to furnish the comments to the
statutory authority and wonders how long it will take to do so. This is a reflection on the State
of affairs in NJA. The Committee directs the Department of Justice to impress upon NJA to
expedite the matter.
11.4 The Committee also expresses its concern over the non-utilisation of funds by NJA and
impress upon it to rationalise its procedures to avoid delay in taking decision. The Committee
further directs the Department of Justice to advise/assist the NJA in improving its procedures so
that funds are not only properly utilised but also within the stipulated time. The Committee would
like to apprise of the steps taken by Department of Justice and NJA in this regard.
Recommendation/observation
12. The Committee notes that some States could not establish permanent Lok Adalats
due to paucity of funds and infrastructure. It is of the view that Government should explore
the possibility of establishing permanent Lok Adalats in all the States, so that common man
has access to speedy, inexpensive and substantial justice. (Para 4.36)
Action Taken Reply
12.1 The remaining State Legal Services Authorities have been directed by NALSA to take
necessary steps and persuade their respective State Governments for creation of infrastructural
facilities for establishment of Permanent Lok Adalats for Public Utility Services under the said Act.
Committee’s further observation
12.3 The Committee directs the Ministry to apprise the Committee of the steps taken by NALSA
along with the outcome thereof while furnishing the ATN.
Recommendation/observation
BAR COUNCIL OF INDIA
13. The Committee also recommends that in order to check the mushrooming of law
colleges coming up in different parts of the country and to maintain the standard of legal
education in India, the Bar Council should take immediate steps like uniform system of law
examination in the country, etc., with this the Committee believes that the deteriorating
standard of legal education in India can be checked to some extent. If possible, the proper
training for the lawyers who entered the profession may be given after according degree and
after enrolling in the Bar. (Para 4.56)
Action Taken Reply
13.1 It is certainly necessary to check the mushrooming of law colleges in the country. Bar
Council of India is taking all possible steps to put a break to this tendency. State Governments are
also responsible for mushroom growth of law colleges as the State Governments under political or

38
other compulsions forced to grant NoC to institutions which lack basic infrastructural facilities
and’” the Universities without taking these short comings into proper consideration grant affiliation
to such institutions.
13.2 When the matters come before the Bar Council of India it becomes difficult for the Council
to deal with these colleges as they resort to litigation. In spite of this unpleasant situation, Bar
Council of India has been taking utmost care in granting approval of affiliation to new law colleges.
BCI’s policy is to weed out sub-standard law colleges and establish only institutions which have
adequate infrastructure for imparting proper legal education. They have been advocating for
reintroduction of training for law graduates before their enrolment. In fact they had introduced
such a scheme some time ago but the scheme was challenged in various High Courts in the
country and ultimately the Hon’ble Supreme Court struck down the scheme on the ground that the
Advocates Act does not empower the Bar Council of India to prescribe a training programme for
law graduates as a pre condition for enrolment. Bar Council of India suggests that necessary
amendments in the advocates Act be carried out to enable the re- introduction of pre enrolment
training to the law graduates.
Committee’s further observation
13.3 The Committee expresses its concern over the deteriorating standard of legal education
throughout the country and is not satisfied by the efforts being made for improving the standard.
The Committee strongly feels that Bar Council of India has a definite role to play in checking the
mushrooming growth of Law Colleges without adequate infrastructure. The BCI must not allow such
colleges to have affiliation with it. BCI should also approach the State Governments impressing
upon them to check the growth of such colleges.
13.4 As regards the issue of training for the lawyers before entering the profession, the Committee
impresses upon the Ministry to bring out a bill proposing requisite amendment in Advocates Act.
Recommendation/observation
INSTITUTE OF CONSTITUTIONAL AND PARLIAMENTARY STUDIES (ICPS)
14. As it appears, there is total lack of co-ordination between the Ministry and the ICPS,
which is disappointed. The Committee, therefore, exhorts the Ministry that it should take
all out efforts to bridge cordial co-ordination with agencies under its administrative control.
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take up the issue with the concerned
agencies and the Secretariats of Parliament who are facing space crunch and may share the
costs in case some space is provided to them and ensure that the construction work is
started at the earliest. The Committee also direct Ministry to furnish a status report at the
time of Action Taken Reply. The Committee further recommends that Institute of
Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies (ICPS) should regularly organize capsule courses
in Parliamentary Privileges, Debates, Questions etc. for the benefit of newly elected
Member of Parliament. (Para 4.61)
Action Taken Reply
14.1 ICPS Building — As this Department has already informed to Hon’ble Committee that a
meeting was held on 14.08.2007 by the Department of Legal Affairs with ICPS in association with
the officers of  Land and Development office, M/o Urban Development, Legislative Department and
officer of integrated Finance Wing of Ministry of Law and Justice to discuss the further course
of action in respect of construction of ICPS building and arrangement for the sharing of the space.
The meeting ended with the understanding that a detailed proposal for Grant-in-aid in this regard

39
will be submitted by the ICPS which will be considered in this Department as per the rules relating
to Grant-in-aid. The ICPS has recently submitted a draft EFC proposal for sanction of funds for
construction of building for ICPS in some detail to this Department on June 17, 2008. The same
is being examined in this Department.
14.2 Capsule Courses– As recommended by the Committee, ICPS has planned to organize
following capsule courses for the benefit of elected MPs. It is proposed to invite senior — i.e.,
three time MPs or those who have already volunteered, to lecture.
14.3 The secretarial assistance in preparation of materials is being explored before the dates can
be finalized. If ICPS get relevant authorizations and funds from within or outside the Institute, they
may be able to hold the programmes as follows:
Topic T entative Dates
1. Parliamentary Privileges During Monsoon Session — August – September, 2008
2. Questions and Debates During Winter Session — December, 2008
3. Election Laws Budget Session — February, 2009
Committee’s further observation
14.4 The Committee takes note of the status report on the action taken in respect of construction
of building for ICPS. However, the Committee is worried over the inordinate time being taken by
the Ministry in the matter. The Committee would like to review the progress in the matter at the time
of consideration of demands for grants of the Ministry. The Committee hopes that by then the
Ministry would approve the EPC proposal for sanction of funds for construction of ICPS building.
14.5 The Committee in its meeting held on 4th December, 2008 heard the Secretary, Legislative
Department and Director, ICPS and impressed upon them to take initiative in the matter. In the
course of deliberation, the Secretary stated that ICPS would be given money for the preparation
of the plan of the building and that token money will be given after the procedural clearance by
the Standing Finance Committee. The Director, ICPS stated that ICPS was agreeable to share the
space with Law Ministry/Parliament against rent as determined by CPWD norms instead of market
rent which would be exorbitant seeing the location of plot. The Committee recommends that the
Ministry and ICPS should arrive at a consensus on this issue at the earliest in order to ensure that
the functioning of ICPS does not suffer due to space crunch.
14.6 The Committee heard the Secretary, Ministry of Urban Development on 16th December, 2008
on the issue of allotment of land to ICPS. The Secretary informed the Committee that land was
handed over to the Institute in 1976 and possession was handed over to them. As per the terms
and conditions of the lease deed, the Institute was given two years’ time to construct the building.
Thereafter, the ICPS was granted extension of time for fourteen times, the last being upto
20th March, 2008 for completing the construction of the building. The Institute has sought further
extension for three years, which is pending before the Ministry of Urban Development.
14.7 The Director, ICPS then apprised the Committee that they had already entrusted the task of
preparation of maps and drawings to the School of Planning and Architecture, which is scheduled
to complete the job by 15th January, 2008. Besides, the Ministry of Law and Justice has also
assured to assist and provide requisite funds for the building.
14.8 The Committee expects that the Ministry of Urban Development will facilitate the ICPS and
Ministry of Law and Justice in the construction of their building and accordingly consider their
further request for extension of time.

40
Recommendation/observation
MUSHROOMING OF ARBITRATION CENTRES IN INDIA
15. The Government should direct that all departments and PSEs should refer ICADR as
arbitrator in the Arbitration clause in the event of dispute between the parties in the
commercial contracts entered between them. More so, dual role played by working officials
as arbitrators should be converted as reference to ICADR. (Para 4.83)
Action Taken Reply
15.1 In pursuance of a decision taken in the meeting of Committee of Secretaries held on
4th March 2008, instructions have been issued to all ministries/departments relating to settlement
of commercial disputes between Government. Departments/Public Undertakings and private parties
recommending utilization of the services of ICADR vide this Department’s OM No.F.32(2)/05-Judl.
Dated 24.04.2008 (copy enclosed).
Committee’s further observation
15.2 The Committee wishes that the Ministry should continuously impress upon the Ministries/
Government Departments and also the PSEs to refer ICADR in respect of dispute arising with their
parties.

41
MINUTES

42

INTRODUCTION
I, The Chairman of the Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and
Justice, having been authorised by the Committee to submit this Report on its behalf, do hereby
present its Thirty-third Report on the Representation of the People (Second Amendment) Bill, 2008.
The Representation of the People (Second Amendment) Bill, 2008 (Annexure-A) seeks to amend the
Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee, the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred
♣ the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha
on the 24th October, 2008 and pending therein, to this Committee on the 31st October, 2008 for
examination and report.
3. Keeping in view the importance of the Bill, the Committee decided to issue a press
communique to solicit views/suggestions from desirous individuals/organisations on the provisions
of the Bill. Accordingly, a press communique was issued in major newspapers and dailies on
22nd November, 2008 in response to which memoranda containing suggestions were received by
the Committee.
4. The Committee considered the Bill in five sittings and heard the presentation of the
Secretary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice on the Bill in its meeting held on
19th November, 2008. The Committee heard the oral evidence of the representatives of Outlook,
Star News, Aajtak and NDTV India on 16th December, 2008; NDTV on 29th December, 2009; and
the Indian Express and the Week Magazine on 7th January, 2009. The Committee also interacted
with the representatives of the State Governments, Political Parties and media persons on the Bill
during its study visit to Kochi, Bangaluru and Hyderabad from 18th to 24th January, 2009.
5. While considering the Bill, the Committee took note of the following documents/information
placed before it:—
(i) Background note on the Bill received from the Government;
(ii) Proposals on Electoral Reforms forwarded by the Election Commission of India to the
Government of India in July, 2004; and
(iii) The comments of the Legislative Department on the views/suggestions contained in
the memoranda received from various organisations/institutions/individuals/experts on
the provisions of the Bill.
6. The Committee adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 16th February, 2009.
7. For the facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

CHAPTER–I
The Representation of the People (Second Amendment) Bill, 2008 (Annexure-A) seeks to
amend the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
2. The Representation of the People (Second Amendment) Bill, 2008 was introduced* in the
Rajya Sabha on 24th October, 2008. It was referred by the Chairman, Rajya Sabha to this
Committee, namely the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public
Grievances, Law and Justice on 31st October, 2008 for examination and report.
3. The background note, furnished by the Ministry of Law and Justice on the Bill, stated as
follows:
“...In July 2004, the Election Commission of India had forwarded a set of 22
proposals on electoral reforms to the Government of India for consideration. While the said
proposals were under consideration of this Department, the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
referred the entire matter of electoral reforms to the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice for examination and
report.
Meanwhile, while considering the proposals of the Election Commission, it was
considered appropriate to examine certain formal proposals in respect of some of the
actionable points and to make requisite amendment to the relevant laws. In the process,
four issues had been examined, which relate to (a) simplification of procedure for
disqualification of a person found guilty of corrupt practices; (b) appointment of the
appellate authority within the district against the orders of the electoral registration officers;
(c) increase in security deposit of the candidates; and (d) inclusion in section 123(7) of the
RP Act, 1951 of all officials appointed in connection with the conduct of elections...”
3.1 The Secretary, Legislative Department while making a presentation before the Committee on
the Bill stated thus:
“...the Representation of the People (Second Amendment) Bill, 2008 seeks to amend the
Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Representation of the People Act, 1951. As
the Hon’ble Members are aware, electoral reform was taken up by the Election Commission
way back in 2004. Around 22 proposals were forwarded to the Government for
consideration. It has been the consistent view of the Government that unless there is a
consensus amongst all the political parties, we shall not take up any step for implementing
it because we need to carry all the political parties with us. So, we examined a few of them
and we thought that on a few of them where there is an agreement, we can implement
them...”
4. Keeping in view the importance of the Bill, the Committee decided to invite views/
suggestions from desirous individuals/organisations on the Bill. It, accordingly, authorised the
Secretariat to issue a press release inviting views/suggestions. In response to the press release
published in major English and Hindi dailies and vernacular newspapers all over India on 22nd
November, 2008, a number of representations/memoranda were received.
4.1 The Committee forwarded the memoranda so received from the individuals and
organisations to the Ministry of Law and Justice (Legislative Department) for their comments
thereon. The comments of the Ministry (Annexure-B) were received on 3rd February, 2009.

4.2 The major points raised in the memoranda are summarized as follows:
(i) Section 126(A) which is to restrict publication and dissemination of result of exit
polls, proposed to be inserted by clause 7 of the Bill, gives a sense of imposing restrictions for
conducting any exit poll. Therefore, this provision could be challenged in the Court of Law as it
is in violation of right to freedom of expression as enshrined in our Constitution.
(ii) The restriction proposed in the Bill, as regards to publication having regard to
provisions of section 126A(l) and 126A(2) seem to be reasonable. However, it has been proposed
that period may commence from beginning hours fixed for poll on the first day of poll and
continue till half an hour after closing of the poll, in all States and Union Territories. In case of
general election, the polling usually takes place in phases on the different dates in each State which
is geographically large. There will be usually a gap between each phase of polling. Therefore, the
aforesaid section would not achieve the objective because during this gap there would be
dissemination of exit poll results, which would influence the voters in the subsequent phase polling.
In other words, the voters will not caste the vote according to dictates of their conscience.
Therefore, clause (a) of Section 126A(2) needs an amendment by way of insertion on the first day
of poll in the “first phase” and till half an hour after closing of the poll in the “last phase”, in all
States and Union Territories, where polling takes place in phases. This provision appears to have
been made assuming that there is single phase of polling.
(iii) A provision should also be made for registration and accreditation of poll survey
agencies with the Election Commission in order to ensure a fair survey of exit polls, so as not to
influence pattern of voting during the period of polling.
(iv) As regards amendment of section 8A of the Representation of People Act, 1951, the
object is not for simplification of procedure for disqualification of a person found guilty of corrupt
practices. But this will provide some breathing time to such guilty person to move to the Court
of Law against any adverse order which may have been passed against him, by specifying a period
of three months during which a case shall be submitted to the President for determination of
question as to whether such person shall be disqualified or not. Therefore, this amendment will
have ample scope for prolonged proceedings in the Court of Law, and continue till the expiry of
term of Assembly or Parliament, as the case may be. Therefore, true objective of this amendment
is to provide suitable opportunity for aggrieved person to move the Court of Law. It is the function
of the Election Commission to ensure that elections are conducted in fair manner, hence obviously
powers to admit the case of every person found to be guilty of corrupt practice, for determination
of the question as to whether such person shall be disqualified or not, should also go to the
Election Commission. It is felt that the President as executive head should not be vested with such
powers. The powers of the President is to appoint or dismiss a Minister from the Council of
Ministers. This function of President is to deal with post election situation such as constitution of
Council of Ministers. Hence the proposal needs to be examined in light of nature of powers given
to President.
(v) Amendment of section 24 of the Act is unnecessary, as the main provision is clear
and correct.
(vi) The increase in security deposits shall be in public interest of eliminating self-
propelling candidature having no spirit of public service in them.
(vii) With reference to amendment of section 34 for increase in the security deposit of
the candidates nominated for elections, there are millions of people in this country who are well-
meaning but financially not well-off, who can contribute towards the enhancement of legislative
activity in the Parliament as country needs highly disciplined legislators who can give better
legislative output.

3
(viii) Only disciplined and well educated people can give a better legislative performance.
Accordingly, the proposed increase in security deposit should be deferred and it is suggested that
the educational qualifications of the candidates should be paid more attention to. The highest
amount of security deposit should not be more than Rs.10,000/-. It shall encourage well-meaning,
but not economically well-off people to join politics.
(ix) Regarding insertion of new sections 126A and 126B in the Representation of People
Act, 1951, it was opined that it is a welcome step. It was further stated that the All India Radio
and Doordarshan should be asked to work in a fair manner as soon as elections are declared.
Generally, a news item giving positive publicity to the ruling party is aired juxtaposing it with a
news item giving negative publicity to the Opposition.
(x) In respect of banning of exit poll, the guidelines from the Press Council of India
already exist, asking newspapers not to publish exit poll surveys until the last day of the polls. In
this regard, it was suggested that the authority to decide and enforce this issue, should be left with
the Election Commission of India.
(xi) In respect of amendment of section 24 of the Representation of People Act, 1950
it was proposed that the first appeal should be made to lie with the District Election Officer (DEO)
instead of Additional District Magistrate or District Magistrate, as they are the Officers of the State

(xii) In respect of increasing security deposit, it was suggested that it should be
Rs. 1,00,000/- and Rs.50,000/- for election to Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly respectively;
whereas, the amount would be half in case of SC/ST candidates. It was further suggested that the
power to increase the security deposit amount should vest with the Election Commission.
(xiii) Conducting and publishing Exit Polls were supported. However, it was opined that
the opinion poll surveys prior to the election should be prohibited, after the close of campaign.
(xiv) In respect of amendment for banning exit poll, apprehension was raised that it would
be violation of fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 19 of the Constitution and ultra vires
to Article 324.
(xv) The amendment in respect of increasing security deposit may be made in such a way
that it should be Rs.50,000/- and Rs.30,000/- for Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly respectively
for candidates belonging to recognized National/State political parties. The amount should be
half in case of candidates belonging to Female/SC/ST. Further, for all other candidates it should
be Rs.2 lakh and Rs. 1,50,000/- for Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly respectively, whereas, the
amount would be Rs. 25,000/- and Rs.15,000/- for Female/SC/ST candidates.
(xvi) Section 123(7) should cover not only the period of re-voting stage, but also should
cover the period from the day of election process till the election result is declared.
(xvii) There should be an appellate authority in the Taluka instead of District against the
order of Electoral Registration Officer.
(xviii) The person found guilty of corrupt practices should be made disqualified within the
time limit/period of three months by simplification of procedure based on the petitions of
documentary evidence etc.
(xix) The Security deposits should be as under:-
For Parliamentary Elections:-
(a) Gen. Cat. – Rs. 200000/-
(b) SC/ST – Rs.100000/-

For Assembly Elections
(a) Gen. Cat. – Rs.100000/-
(b) SC/ST – Rs.50000/-
(xx) The official found guilty of having been involved in corrupt practice should be fined
for not less than Rs. 1,00,000/- as well as removal from his job so as to create permanent fear
complex among such corrupt officials.
(xxi) The amendment in respect of the restriction of exit polls has been supported. Also,
it is of the view that the pre-poll survey and opinion polls should be banned/prohibited during the
applicability of model code of conduct.
(xxii) There should not be any restriction on media in respect of the exit polls as it would
tantamount to curbing freedom of expression of an independent and vibrant press as enshrined in
the Constitution.
(xxiii) The banning of exit polls is unconstitutional and infringement of the freedom of
press guaranteed under Article 19(1) (a) of the Constitution. There is no empirical evidence to
prove that on the whole, voters would be affected by Exit polls result.
(xxiv) V ast majority of the voting population is exposed to more than one Newspaper and
News Channel, thereby leaving little scope for the voter to get influenced. In a way, multiple
opinions will help the voter take unbiased and independent decision. The Election Commission
should issue regulatory guidelines to streamline the publication and telecast of Opinion polls.
(xxv) To dispel the apprehensions that Opinion polls are “motivated and not impartial”,
publication/telecast of any such opinion poll should be mandatorily followed by a claimer. For
example, a box on Page 1 with specific font size, the details the agency employed to conduct the
survey, sample size vis-a.-vis actual size, methodology adopted, period of survey, etc. would enable
the reader/viewer judge the credibility of the publication/TV station and the Opinion polls published/
telecast.
