Separate enactment for CBI 
27.1. The issue of separate enactment for CBI has been 
engaging the attention of this Co mmittee for a very long time. 
The Committee, in its Reports on Demands for Grants of the 
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances a nd Pensions and                 
24th Report on “Working of CBI” , strongly recommended that a 
separate statute may be enacted for CBI. 
27.2. In reply to the questionn aire furnished on Demands for 
Grants (2010-11), the Ministry has stated that the existing 
enactment “The Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946” 
is an exclusive and separate Act for CBI which has been found 
to be adequate. 
27.3. While deposing before th e Committee, the Director, CBI 
stated: 

 58
"……..when we are in a situation where criminals 
are not respecting even Stat e boundaries and district 
boundaries, national and inte rnational boundaries, we are 
still being governed by the sa me geographical jurisdiction 
of the SHO of the district or St ate. So, it is high time we 
thought of, what the Committee has already recommended, 
having a CBI Act. And I feel that the judgement of the 
Supreme Court is in the right direction. ……….." 
27.4. The Committee is not sati sfied with the written reply 
furnished by the Ministry. Th e Committee is in agreement 
with the view of Director CBI and impress upon the 
Ministry to have a fresh look and come out with a separate 
Act for CBI. 
27.5. The Committee fails to understand how this premier 
investigation agency can be exp ected to function efficiently 
and impartially in the absen ce of an effective statutory 
backing. The Ministry should appreciate that the DSPE Act 
which was enacted in 1946 is no t sufficient to cater to the 
requirements of organisa tion whose mandate and 
responsibility have increased manifold during the years. 
27.6. The Committee strongly feels that in the current 
scenario, wherein crimes perv ade state, national and 
international boundaries, CBI which was established by a 
resolution dated April 1, 1963  and which draws powers to 

 59
investigate from the DSPE Ac t, with the existing legal 
framework, cannot be expect ed to fulfill the high 
expectations placed on it by the entire political, judicial and 
social spectra.  
27.7. The Committee is of the firm  view that such an Act of 
Parliament is sine qua non to the functioning of CBI as an 
independent and accountable ag ency which specializes in 
prevention, investigation and prosecution of crime. The 
Committee is of the considered view that apposite legal 
empowerment of CBI, in t une with the corresponding 
Entries in the Union List, Stat e List and Concurrent List, is 
in public interest. 
27.8. The Committee further no tes the deposition of the 
Secretary, DoPT that on 23 rd March, 2010 fresh proposals were 
received from CBI regarding independent legislation. 
27.9. The Committee recommends that this proposal should 
be considered at the earliest and quick action should be 
taken on the same.

44.1.1. The Department, in its reply to the questionnaire, has 
stated that the Impact Assessment study of the Pensioners' Portal 
through an external agency has been commissioned by 

 78
Department of Information Tech nology and that the report is 
awaited. 
44.2. The Committee appreciates this initiative and hopes 
that the report will be submitted at the earliest and that its 
recommendations will be implemented without delay.

REPORT 
CHAPTER - I 
BRIEF OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY 
1.0 The Union Ministry of Law and Justice comprises of three 
Departments, namely th e Department of Legal Affairs, Legislative 
Department and Department of Justi ce and through the said Departments, 
the Ministry assists in the process of orderly change directed towards 
realization of the objectives set out in the Constitution. 
Department of Legal Affairs 
1.1. The Department of Le gal Affairs is essentially  a services Department 
that renders advice to various Ministri es/Departments of the Government of 
India on legal matters and carries out  the conveyancing work in various 
Courts, including the Supreme Court. Besid es this, it is also concerned with 
appointment of Law Officers, namely  the Attorney General of India, 
Solicitor General of India and the Add itional Solicitor Generals of India, 
entering into treaties with foreign countri es in matters of Civil law inclusive 
of Hague Convention Matters, execu ting contracts and assurances of 
property on behalf of the President of In dia. It is also the nodal authority in 
respect of Appellate Tribunal for Foreign Exchange, the Income Tax 
Appellate Tribunal and National Tax Tribunal. 
1.2. The Department of Legal Affair s has a two tier set up, namely, the 
Main Secretariat, New Delhi and th e Branch Secretar iats at Mumbai, 
Kolkata, Chennai and Bangalore. The na ture of duties discharged by the 

 8
Main Secretariat as well as Branch Secretariats can be broadly classified into 
two areas - Advice work and Litiga tion work. Advice caters to Central 
Government Department/Offices at Cen tre and in States/UTs. Litigation 
work relates to CAT, High Courts and Supreme Court. 
1.3. The following are the organiza tions/institutions, which come under 
the overall supervision of Department of  Legal Affairs and get Grant in aid 
for their research works:- 
(a) National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) :- The National 
Legal Services Authority has b een constituted under the Legal 
Services Authorities Act, 1 987 to monitor and evaluate 
implementation of legal aid programmes and to lay down policies 
and principles for making legal se rvices available under the Act. 
The NALSA issues guidelines fo r the State Legal Services 
Authorities to implement the le gal aid programmes which are in 
turn discharged through the following services:- 
(i) Free Legal Services : Includes court fees, process fee and 
all charges payable or incurred in connection with any legal 
proceedings, providing Advocate in legal proceedings, 
obtaining and supply of rectified copies of orders and other 
documents in legal proceedings, preparation of appeal, 
paper book including printing and translation of documents 
in legal proceedings. 
(ii) Lok Adalats: -  Lok Adalat is a foru m where the disputes/ 
cases pending in the court of law or at pre-litigation stage 
are settled/compromised amicably.  The Lok Adalat has 

 9
been given statutory status  under the Legal Services 
Authorities Act, 1987.  Under th is Act, an award made by a 
Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court and is 
final and binding on all partie s and no appeal lies against 
thereto before any court. 
(b) Law Commission of India: - The Law Commission of India is a 
non-statutory body, constituted by the Government once in three 
years. The Commission was first c onstituted in 1955. It consists 
of a Chairman, three full-time Members, one Member-Secretary 
and three or more part-time Members, depending upon the nature 
of work. Law Commission Reports are considered to be primary 
source of law reforms for Parliame nt, as well as the judiciary. 
Law Commission presents its Report to the Government, the 
Government then lays these Reports on the Table of both the 
Houses of Parliament. 
(c) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) : - Section 252 of the 
Income Tax Act, 1961 provides that the Central Government 
shall constitute an Appellate Tr ibunal consisting of as many 
Judicial Members and Accountant Members as it thinks fit, to 
exercise the powers and discharg e the functions conferred on the 
Appellate Tribunal by said Act. 
(d) Appellate Tribunal of Foreign Exchange : - The Appellate 
Tribunal of Foreign Excha nge was established on 1 st June 2000 
vide Government of India Notification No. S.O. 531 (E), dated 

 10
1.6.2000 issued under section 18 of the Foreign Exchange 
Management Act, 1999 (FEMA),  
(e) Indian Law Institute (ILI):- The Indian Law Institute registered 
under the Societies Registration Act,  1860 is engaged in research 
in the field of law.  The Depart ment of Legal Affairs has been 
sanctioning annual recurring Grant in  aid to the Institute for its 
activities of legal research. 
(f) International Centre for Alt ernate Dispute Resolution 
(ICADR):- The International Centre for Alternate Dispute 
Resolution was registered under the Societies Registration Act, 
1860 on 31 st May 1995.  It is an autonomous organisation 
working under the aegis of the Ministry of Law and Justice 
(Department of Legal Affairs). It has been established to 
promote, organise and propagate alternative dispute resolution 
methods to facilitate early resolu tion of disputes and to reduce 
the burden of arrears on Courts.  
(g) Bar Council of India (BCI) : - The Bar Council of India is a 
statutory body constituted under the Advocates Act 1961.  The 
Council has been receiving annual Gr ant in aid from Department 
of Legal Affairs. 
(h) Institute of Constitutional  and Parliamentary Studies 
(ICPS):- The Institute of Constit utional and Parliamentary 
Studies is a private body engaged in research in the field of 
Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies and came into existence 

 11
in 1965.  The Department of Le gal Affairs has been sanctioning 
recurring annual Grant in aid to the Institute for the purpose. 
Legislative Department 
1.4. The Legislative Department is entr usted with legislative matters and is 
responsible for drafting of all Government Bills and Ordinances and scrutiny 
and vetting of subordinate legisla tions sponsored by various Union 
Ministries/ Departments.  It is admi nistratively concerned with the Election 
Commission and Election laws connected  with election to Parliament and 
State Legislatures and to the offices of  the President and the Vice-President.  
Legislative Department is also admi nistratively concerned with certain 
matters such as the Code of Civil Procedure, Limitation and Arbitration, 
Contracts, Personal Laws, Evidence and Transfer of Property as regards 
legislation.  There are over hundred  Central Acts falling under these 
subjects. 
1.5. The Department has two wings under it mainly:- 
(i) Institute of Legislative  Drafting and Research : With a view 
to increase the availability of tr ained legislative draftsmen in 
the country, the Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research 
was established as a Wing of  the Legislative Department, 
Ministry of Law and Justice in January, 1989. The Institute has 
been imparting theoretical as well as practical training in 
legislative drafting. 
(ii) Official Languages Wing and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan : The 
Official Languages Wing is a successor Organisation of the 
Official Languages (Legis lative) Commission under the 

 12
Legislative Department.  It has been entrusted with the 
functions such as, (a) to prep are and publish a standard legal 
terminology for use, as far as  possible, in all Official 
Languages; (b) to prepare authoritative texts in Hindi of all 
Central Acts and Ordinances a nd Regulations promulgated by 
the President; (c) to prepare aut horitative texts in Hindi of all 
rules, regulations and orders made by the Central Government 
under any Central Act or any Ordinance or Regulation 
promulgated by the President; (d) to prepare authoritative texts 
of all Central Acts and Or dinances and Regulations 
promulgated by the President in the respective Official 
Languages of the States and to a rrange for the translation of all 
Acts passed and Ordinances promulgated in any State into 
Hindi, if the texts of such Acts or Ordinances are in a language 
other than Hindi; and (e) to perform such other duties as may be 
assigned to it by the Government of India from time to time. 
Department of Justice 
1.6. The duties of the Department of Justice include the administration of 
justice and the processing of appointme nt of judges of the Supreme Court 
and High Courts. 
1.7. The following institutions/autonom ous bodies/policy initiatives  come 
directly under the overall supervision of Department of Justice: 
 (a) Supreme Court of India:-  Demand No.64 in the detailed 
Demands of Grants of the Ministry pertains to the Supreme Court 

 13
of India. The expenditure to be incurred on the Supreme Court of 
India is ‘Charged’ expenditure.  
(b) National Judicial Academy :- The National Judicial Academy 
was registered as a Society unde r the Societies Registration Act 
and came into existence with effect from 17 th august, 1993. The 
affairs of the Academy are ma naged by a Governing Council, 
which is chaired by the Chief Justice of India. The registered 
office of the Academy is in Supreme Court Building at New 
Delhi and another office was es tablished in August, 2000 at 
Bhopal. The main objectives of  the Academy are to impart 
training to the Judicial Officers of the States/Union territories and 
to study the court management and administration of justice in 
States and Union territories. 
 (c) Fast Track Courts :- The Fast Track Courts were started on the 
basis of the recommendation by the 11 th Finance Commission for 
the period of five years (till 2000-05) which was later extended to 
2010. The overall functioning of th e Fast Track Courts is the 
primary responsibility of the re spective State Governments and 
the concerned High Courts. The cas es are transferred to Fast 
Track Courts under the directions of the respective High Courts.  
(d) Family Courts:- The Family Court Act, 1984 was enacted with a 
view to providing for establishment of Family Courts, to promote 
conciliation in and secure speedy settlement of disputes relating 
to marriage, family affairs and related matters. These Courts are 
civil in nature, establishment of which has direct bearing on the 

 14
reduction of pendency of civil su its in various High Courts. In 
accordance with the provisions of  section 3 of the Act, the 
State/UT Governments can establis h Family Courts in the areas 
comprising districts, towns, city in the States having population 
of ten lakhs. Even the States/UTs  are competent to establish such 
court in those areas with the State/UT having a population less 
than ten lakhs in consultation with the concerned High Court.  
(e) The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 :-  The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 
2008 has been enacted by the Parliament to provide for the 
establishment of the Gram Nyayalayas at the grass roots level for 
the purpose of providing speedy and inexpensive access to justice 
to the citizens at their door steps. In so far as the Central 
Government is concerned, it is committed to provide assistance 
to the State Governments for me eting the non-recurring cost of 
establishment of the Gram Nyay alayas. The Central Government 
would also meet 50% of the recurring expenses to be incurred on 
these courts in the first three years subject to a ceiling of Rs. 3.20 
lakhs per annum. 

 15

AN OVERVIEW OF THE BUDGET ALLOCATIONS DURING 2010-11

 Demand No. 63 pertains to th e Supreme Court of India,

COMPUTERISATION OF ITAT 
4.8. The  Annual Report for 2009-10 of the  Ministry of Law and Justice 
states that the task of computeriza tion of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal by 
way of a pilot project at ITAT Delhi through NIC is likely to be completed 
shortly.  After successful completion of  this project at Delhi, other zonal 
Headquarters and Single Bench stations  would also be covered. Personal 
Computers have been provided to a ll Members and different section of 
offices all over India.  The officers a nd staff are also being given computer 
training. Computers have also been  provided to all Senior Private 
Secretary/Private Secretary and staff Members in order to minimize paper 
work. Matter of computerization in IT AT is being persuaded vigorously and 
Computerization and interlinking of all zonal offices and single bench 
offices is expected to be completed with in very short period.

Ministry has cited that the inadequ acy of the funds wa s the main reason

Ministry has informed that due to successive reductions in the grants allotted 
for the year 2008-09 under the Sub Head  'Office Expenses' (which includes 
the allocation for computerization as we ll) the target of computerization and 
interlinking of all zonal offices and single bench offices of ITAT could not 
be achieved as per the scheduled time frame.  Yet in the reply the 
Department emphasizes that the process of computerization and interlinking 
of all zonal offices and single bench o ffices of ITAT is expected to be 
completed during 2009-10.  

 30
4.10. The Committee takes note of  delay in consideration of 
computerization and interlinking of  all the zonal offices and single 
bench of ITAT for want of suffic ient funds. In view of this, the 
Committee is apprehensive whether the amount sanctioned during the 
year 2009-10 has been adequate to  address the requirement. The 
Committee, therefore, impress upon th e Department of Legal Affairs to 
make available adequate funds to IT AT so that the work is completed 
without further delay.

th 
September, 2009, about  99.29 lakh persons were benefited through legal aid

Scheduled Caste, 4.74 lakh persons of Scheduled Tribe, communities more

eligible for seeking legal aid under the NALSA, the annual income limit 
fixed by the Central Government for th e cases before the Supreme Court is 
Rs. 50,000.

Kashmir, Nagaland, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Daman& Diu and Lakshadweep 
all states and UTs have raised the income ceiling limit of Rs. 50,000/- per 

 31
annum to provide free legal aid. In  reply of the questionnaire of the

State Legal Services Authorities and State Governments to increase the 
income ceiling limits for the purpose of  Clause (h) of Section 12 of Legal 
Services Authorities to Rs.100,000- per annum.

Chairpersons, Member Secr etaries of State Legal se rvices Authorities, Law 
Secretaries and Finance Secretaries of  State Governments, it was resolved 
that the States shall attempt for rais ing the income ceiling to Rs. 1,00,000. 
The States of Jharkhand, Orissa, Tamil Nadu and Utta r Pradesh have 
increased the income ceiling limit to Rs.1,00,000/- per annum under Section 
12 (h) of the Act.  The States of Sikkim and Assam have increased the 
income ceiling limit to Rs.75,000/- pe r annum under Section 12 (h) of the 
Act.

NALSA is in the process of setting up a web-based monitoring system to 
monitor the activities down up to the Ta luk Legal Services Committees, all 
over the country, with the software and web portal to be installed with the 
help of National Informatics Centre. Discussion with National Informatics 
Centre and NICSI - a subsidiary organiza tion of NIC is in progress and this 
system will be put in place very soon  and thereby a daily monitoring of the 
activities throughout the country will be possible at NALSA. 
4.16. The Committee is constraine d to note that under the Head 2052 
the actual expenditure was only Rs. 0.28 crores against the amount of 
Rs. 2.98 crores allocated at the RE  stage. The Committee expresses 

 32
serious concerns over such a low p ercentage of utilization of the 
allocated funds as allocations for the other schemes of the Ministry are 
affected.  The Committee, therefor e, recommends that the Ministry 
should make concerted efforts fo r proper utilization of the funds 
allocated for the purpose and demand for the allocations at RE stage 
accordingly.    
4.17. The Committee is pleased to no te that in accordance with the its 
recommendations made in its earlier Reports, the Government has been 
persuading the State authorities to increase the income ceiling limit for 
getting free legal services. Appr eciating the steps taken by the 
Government, the Committee feels that the coverage of population under 
the free legal service should be en larged. Thus, the Committee insists 
that the Department and NALSA shou ld keep on their efforts to 
persuade the States until the desired criteria of the income ceiling limit 
to Rs.1,00,000/- per annum is achieved throughout the country.  
4.18. In response to the query of th e Committee relating to uniformity and 
rationalization in fee structure of Le gal Aid Counsel, it was informed that 
the Ministry had constituted an expert  committee comprising of three Senior 
Judges of High Courts. The said  expert committee had made 
recommendations to enhance the free st ructure of the legal lawyers in the 
lines of the recommendations of th e Department related Standing 
Committee.  
4.19. In reply to the que stionnaire of the Committee,  the Ministry apprised 
that the State Authorities were reque sted by NALSA to increase the fee-
structure of the legal aid lawyers as recommended by the expert Committee 

 33

persuade the State Governments to increase the fee-structure of the

structure of the Legal Aid Counsels sh ould be suitably enhanced so that

higher fees such as Rs. 20,000/- in the case of Sessions Cases which 
ended in acquittal, and Rs. 5000/- in the case of conviction, will motivate 
the counsel to work hard in favour of the accused who cannot afford a 
lawyer, with all sincerity.

been the core of the Co mmittee’s recommendations in its earlier Reports. In

 34

Department illustrates that no physical target could be fixed to monitor 
the progress of work under CSS as th e construction of court buildings 
etc. was to be decided by the State s. Though the Comm ittee takes into 
account the reason provided by the  Department in this regard, the 
Committee still feels that fixing of the ta rgets is an integral part of any 
planning process and also provi des benchmark to assess the 
achievements made during a plan period. Moreover, the Committee 

 62
finds that the failure to fix the target s under the CSS is an indicative of 
a common structural constraint that has diminished the prospects of

coordination between Center and States. The fate of a lot of 
Government schemes requiring the cooperation between Centre and 
State are in limbo owing to the reluct ance of either side in fulfilling the 
assigned responsibilities. 
6.12. To overcome this structural co nstraint, the Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Government sh ould continuously make all out 
efforts to persuade the State Gove rnments. There is also a need to 
identify the reasons of non complianc e by the States in this regard. The 
Committee opines that the Departme nt should explore the ways and 
means to motivate the States to comply with the responsibilities assigned 
in the scheme and extend more assistance to the States, if needed so.  
COMPUTERISATION OF JUDICIARY 
6.13. Rs.120 crore has been allocated for the scheme in Budget Estimates 
stage for the year 2010-11. The Committ ee was apprised that this allocation 
of Rs 120 crores was made against the demand of Rs 390.0 crore. The 
amount was reduced by the Planning  Commission while approving the 
Annual Plan of the Department of justice. The committee was further 
apprised that Ministry of law and Justice had written to Prime Minister, 
Finance Minister and Deputy Ch airman, planning commission for 
enhancement of the allocation. The Fi nance Ministry, however, has assured 
the Ministry of Law and Justice that the request may be considered at the RE 
stage 

 63
6.14. Budget Estimates 2008-09 for th e Scheme was Rs.125.00 crore which 
was reduced to Rs.26.40 crore at RE stage. The Committee was apprised that 
till February 2010, a total of 678 Dist rict Court complexe s and 430 Taluka 
Court complexes reported site prepara tion work as completed.  Respective 
hardware vendors have be en asked to conduct site readiness and LAN 
surveys at these Taluka and District Court complexes. Site readiness surveys 
have been completed at 587 District Court complex sites.Broadband Internet 
connectivity has been provided at 9773 judges' residence, 469 District 
Courts and 896 Taluka Cour t complexes.  In addition, Dial up internet 
connections have also been provided at the home offices of 971 Judicial 
Officers, 17 District Courts and 376 Ta luka Courts.  The connectivity has 
been provided through Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited.  
6.15. The Outcome Budget 2010-11 denotes that while considerable 
progress has been made in the implem entation of the first phase of the 
scheme, the implementation is behind th e targeted completion dates because 
of certain factors.  First Site prepara tion work could not be completed at all 
Court complexes identified and reported by the Courts. Secondly, increase in 
the number of reported Court Complexe s from 2066 to 3061. Thirdly, strict 
component-wise allocations 
6.16. The Committee was told that init ially a financial outlay of Rs 441.8 
Crores was approved by the CCEA fo r Phase-1 of the Computerization of 
Judiciary Project under the various H eads. However, in  the view of 
abovementioned factors, the Ministry has worked out a revised cost estimate 
of Rs.918.41 crore for the implementatio n of Phase I of the project.  Also, 
the timelines for completion of Phase-I of the project needed extension from 
earlier scheduled date of February 2009 to 31st March, 2012. 

 64
6.17. The Committee acknowledges the progress made so far by the 
NIC as an implementing agency fo r the Computerization of Judiciar y                 
(E-Court) Project. The Committee also takes into account the 
complexities being faced by the NIC and the Department in the 
implementation of the E-Courts projects.  
6.18. The Committee hopes that the Government would respond 
positively to the demands of the  Department of Justice for the 
additional allocation for the project . The Committee would also like to 
draw the attention of the Government over its inability to properly 
utilize the budgetary provisions for the purpose. As the actual 
expenditure over the above-mentioned  head has been very low in 
comparison of the grant allocated at the BE stage for the last 2 financial 
years i.e. 2008-09 and 2009-10. For the year 2008-09 only Rs.25.90 crore 
was actually realized against the estimated grants of Rs. 125.00 crores at 
the BE  stage. Likewise, only Rs.65 crores was released upto 26th March, 
2010 in comparison of the Rs.120 cro res estimated at the BE for the 
year 2009-10.  The Committee observes a poor utilization ratio of 20.72 
% and 54.16% respectively for the years 2008-09 and 2009-10 against 
the utilization ratio for total pla nned expenditures of the Department 
which were 98.10% and 61.12% respect ively for the same period. The 
Committee expresses its concern over su ch low percentage of utilization 
in comparison of the estimated allocations and recommends the 
Department should ensure the release of adequate amount for the 
purpose.   
6.19. The Committee takes note of the proposed revised cost estimate of 
Rs.918.41 crore for the implementation  of Phase I of the project. While 

 65
justifying the need of enhanced allo cations the Committee would like to 
point out that the ongoing procedural  delay in the execution of the 
Phase-1 of the scheme could not be  overcome only by enhancing the 
allocation. The Monitoring aspects of the project are also needed to be 
strengthened. The Committee, there fore, recommends that to reduce 
delay in the implementation of the Ph ase-1 the Ministry should devise a 
mechanism to monitor the site prep aration work, completion of sites 
and LAN Surveys and also the timely de livery and installation of the  of 
hardware at court complexes. 
GRAM NYAYALAYAS  
6.20. The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 has been enacted by the Parliament 
to provide for the establishment of th e Gram Nyayalayas at the grass root 
level for the purpose of providing spee dy and inexpensive access to justice 
to the citizens at their door steps. The Act came in to  force w.e.f.                 
2nd October, 2009, the birth anniversar y of the Father of the Nation, 
Mahatma Gandhi.  
6.21. The Committee has been apprised  that the Central Government is 
committed to provide assistance to th e State Governments for meeting the 
non-recurring cost of establishment of  the Gram Nyayal ayas. The Central 
Government would also meet 50% of the recurring expenses to be incurred 
on these courts in the first three year s subject to a ceiling of Rs.3.20 lakhs 
per court per annum. The State Governme nts have been requested to set up 
these courts early and inform the Central Government  regarding the 
implementation scheduled. Hitherto, the Government of Madhya Pradesh 
has notified forty Gram Nyayalayas , Government of Maharashtra has 

 66
notified nine Gram Nyayalayas, Gove rnment of Orissa has notified one 
Gram Nyayalaya and Government of Raj asthan has notified forty-five Gram 
Nyayalayas. In these 95 Gram Nyay alayas notified by the said State 
Governments, 47 have started functioning.   
6.22. For the year 2010-11, an amount of  Rs.40 crore has been provided for 
the establishment of Gram Nyayalayas. In addition, Rs. 1 crore have been 
allocated for the North Eastern Region. An amount of Rs.11.00 crore has 
been provided by the Central Govern ment in the Revised Estimates 2009-10 
for setting up these Gram Nyayalay as. The Performance Budget 2010-11 
indicates that an amount of Rs. 6.63 cr ores has been relaesed the various 
states till the date 28.02.2010 under this scheme.  
6.23. In its reply to the questionn aire of Committee the Department 
apprised that in n 2010-11, Rs.2.34 cr ore shall be required for releasing 
Central share towards recurring expenditu re at the rate of Rs.3.20 lakhs per 
Gram Nyayalaya in respect of these 95 Gram Nyayalayas.  Out of remaining 
36.96 crore, appro. 234 Gram Nyayalayas are likely to be set up in 2010-11.  
6.24. The Department has also furnishe d the feed back of  the Sttaes/UTs 
regarding the Gram Nyay alaya Act stating that States have different 
perspective over the establishment of the Gram Nyayalayas varying. Though 
some states have responded enthusiast ically and are in the process of 
implementing the Gram Nyayalayas Act, some states feel that establishment 
of gram Nyayalays would not produ ce any additional substantive gains. 
Besides, there are some states which despite being agreeing in principle 
seems reluctant in this regard given th e financial limitations thereby seeking 

 67
enhanced central assistance from the Ce ntre. The following table indicates 
the progress of setting up of Gram Nyayalayas.

6.25. The Committee welcomes the launching of such a significant 
initiative as the establishment of Gram Nyaylayas. The Committee 
hopes that it would further enlarge the  reach of the Indian judicial 
system and address the grievances of the people from the very 
grassroots level by delivering jus tice at their doorsteps.  The 
Committee takes note that some State s aspire for enhanced allocation. 
The present scheme provides for Rs 18 Lakhs per Gram Nayaylaya 
towards non-recurring expenditure and Rs. 3.20 lakhs per anum per 
court for the first three years towards recurring expenditure.  In view 
of the demands of the States, the scheme allocations may be reviewed 
after first three years and the allocations may be enhanced accordingly. 
NON PLAN SCHEMES 
NATIONAL JUDICIAL ACADEMY 
6.26. For the year 2010-11 Rs. 13 crore has been allocated for the National 
Judicial Academy. During the year 2009-10 the provision of Rs. 13.40 crore 
was made which was reduced to Rs . 11.16 crore at RE stage as per 

 68
requirement of NJA. However, the Co mmittee has been apprised that Rs 
6.70 crore has been actually released  to NJA. The Director, NJC while 
deposing before the Committee requested  for enhancement of its budgetary 
allocation. He put forth his points as follows  
………..We are operating at a very economic level.  According 
to a rough back-of-the-envelope calculation, we are spending 
Rs.20,000 per participant per year,  all included, including cost 
of establishment, electricity, s ecurity, travel, etc.  So, we 
operate at a very economic level . We are asking for a bit of 
quantum increase in the next year  because we want to scale up 
our activities, especially, on th e research and analysis side, to 
understand more deeply what th e problems facing the judiciary 
are.  There is, of course, the impact of the Sixth Pay 
Commission Report.  We operate with a very small number of 
staff.  Effectively there are five or six academic staff and twenty 
administrative staff.  We are all terribly stretched and 
overworked, and we need to expand our capacity.   But that has 
not restricted us from carryi ng on our own activities.  So, we 
are asking for a bit of quantum in crease in the coming year.  I 
think, we have been able to show with our results that we have 
been able to achieve a lot….   
6.27. The Committee was also apprised that the Annual Reports of the NJA 
for the years 2007-08 and 2008-09 were not  laid before the Parliament and 
pending Audits of Accounts. 

 69
6.28. The Committee is in agreeme nt with the Director, NJA's demand 
of enhancing the allocation for the Academy and endorses that the 
enhancement in allocations is justifi ed in view of the administrative 
expenses/ academic programmes/activi ties proposed to be undertaken 
by the Academy.   
6.29. The Committee, however, exp resses its anguish that the previous 
Annual Reports of the NJA are yet to  be laid in the Parliament and 
thus, pending audit of accounts an d recommends that NJA should 
expeditiously furnish its comments to the statutory auditors if the same 
are not done.  
6.30. In the reply to the questionnair e of the Committee,  it was informed 
that owing to the lack of adequate infrastructural facilities there was no 
possibility of expanding its activities to provide training to other officials 
involved in the administration of Justice in the lines of recommendations 
made by the Committee in its earlier Reports. The Committee was also 
apprised that the infrastructure in th e NJA, the only national institution for 
judicial education, at its present cap acity was barely adequate to provide 
each judge in the country on average one opportunity once in three years or 
so to come to NJA for a 3-4 day programme. 
6.31. The Committee takes note of the reply of the NJA and 
understands that in its present capacity , it is not possible for the NJA to 
provide training to other officials involved in the administration of 
Justice. However, the Committee is constrained to note that in a country 
of population of more than 1.2 billion, there is only one small national 
institution for judicial education. Th e Committee is also disappointed to 
note that the infrastructural facilit ies in the academy are not even 
sufficient to provide the training to the judicial officers. The Committee, 

 70
therefore, recommends that the Mini stry of Law and Justice should 
take necessary steps so that NJA coul d function effectively and cater to 
the need of the judicial educat ion for the Judicial and other 
administrative officers involved in the administration of Justice   
FAST TRACK COURTS  
6.32. The Fast Track Courts r ecommended by the Eleventh Finance 
Commission were initially to operate  up to 31.03.2005.  The Government, 
however, had decided to continue the 1562 FTCs that were reported 
operational on 31.03.2005 for a furthe r period of five years (up to 
31.03.2010). A provision of Rs.509 cr ore was approved by Government for 
this purpose. The Committee was apprised  that the out of 35.02 lakh cases 
transferred to Fast track Courts since inception 28.29 lakhs cases were 
disposed off.   
6.33. An allocation of Rs 75 crore ha s been made for the year 2010-11 for 
the Fast Rack Courts (FTCs). There has been an increase of Rs.10 crores in 
the allocations at BE stage 2010-11 agai nst the RE of 65 crores for the year 
2009-10. However, only Rs 56.13 crores was actually utilized last year.  
Even an appraisal of the details pr ovided by the Government regarding the 
grants allocated to the FTCs for the la st three financial years denotes that  
the actual flow of the funds has b een quite low in comparison of the 
allocations made at the RE stage fo r the three consecutive years; 2007-08, 
2008-09, 2009-2010

 71
6.34. The Committee is constrained to  note that the actual inflow of the 
funds for the Fast Track Courts has been lower in comparison to the 
allocations made at the RE stage . The Committee appreciates the 
Government's proposal to extend the  present scheme of Fast Track 
Courts and has accordingly made allo cations of Rs.75 crores for FTC at 
BE stage 2010-11. The Committee feels that the Fast Track Court which 
was introduced as a major reforms initiative still has relevance given the 
mounting level of pende ncy of cases. However, the Committee would 
also like to draw the attention of the Department towards the need of 
improvement in the functioning of FTCs  as there have been complaints 
in this regard.  The Committee in it s previous Reports had pointed out 
the matter and recommended that the Department should take follow 
up action to improve the functioning of FTCs.  
6.35. The Committee was apprised that  the Department had communicated 
with the Chief Justice of all the High Cour ts with the request to look into the 
observation of the Committee regard ing improving the performance of 
FTCs. The Department informed th e Committee about th e views of the 
Hon'ble Chief Justice of Allahabad in th is regards. He pointed out the need 
of following improvements:  
• A separate Monitoring Cell in each judgeship to sort out the 
difficulties with regard to service of summons and warrant. 
• Revising quota in respect of the num ber of sessions trials to be 
disposed every month by a  judge  
• Need of providing adequate staff to Fast Track Court. 
• Mandatory Training for the All the ju dicial officers and staff of Fast 
Track Courts 

 72
6.36. The Committee feels that the views of the Chief Justice of 
Allahabad High Court are an indicati ve of the fact that the FTCs need 
improvement at various functional aspects because the number of 
disposals of pending cases is not the sole yardstick to judge the 
performance of FTCs.  The quality of the functioning of FTCs is also 
equally important. Therefore, the  Committee recommen ds that having 
collected the views of all High Cour ts, the Department should consider 
their suggestions to make the functioning of FTCs more effectively. 
RETIREMENT AGE OF JUDGES 
 6.37. The Committee was apprised th at in pursuance of the Committee’s 
earlier recommendations to raise the retirement Judges of High Courts at par 
with the retirement age of the Judges of  the Supreme Court, the Department 
had considered the matter with the other concerned Departments. The 
Committee was also apprised the comments of all the concerned 
Departments in this regard and they  had in principle concurred in the 
proposal of raising the age of judges of the Courts from 62 to 65 years. The 
Secretary, Department of Justice also replied in affirmative in this regard 
while deposing before the Committee during deliberations upon the Demand 
for Grants 2010-11. She expressed her views as "We also do subscribe to the 
same view that there should an enhancement of age of retirement".   
 6.38. The Committee, therefore,  recommends that the Government 
should immediately bring forward a proposal to raise the retirement 
age of Judges of High Courts fr om 62 to 65 to be at par with the 
retirement age of a Judges of the  Supreme Court without any further 
delay.  

 73

7.0. Demand No. 63 in the detailed Dema nds of Grants of the Ministry of 
Law and Justice pertains to the Suprem e Court of India. The expenditure to 
be incurred on the Supreme Court of India is ‘Charged’. The total Budget 
Estimates of the Supreme Court of India for the year 2010-11 is Rs. 85 crore 
as against Rs. 100.69 crore in Revised Estimates for the year 2009-10. 
7.1. The Committee had r ecommended in its earlier Reports to establish 
the Constitutional Bench and other Bench es of the Supreme Court given the 
manifold benefits of this exer cise. The Law Commission in its 229 th Report 
had also expressed the same opinion regarding the establishment of other 
Benches of the Supreme Court. However,  in its reply to the questionnaire of 

 74
the Committee, Ministry acquainted the Committee that implement the 
Committee's recommendations, wide ranging  amendments are needed in the 
Constitution.  Moreover, the Ministry al so informed that having considered 
the matter in the meeting of the Full Co urt, the Chief Justice of India finds 
no justification for establishing the other Benches of the Supreme Court. 
Therefore, the Ministry did not intend to pursue the matter further. 
7.2. The Committee is not in ag reement with the Ministry and the 
opinion of the Chief Justice of Indi a as well. The Committee feels that 
unwillingness regarding establishment of the other Benches of the 
Supreme Court cannot be justified on the grounds that it would attract 
a cumbersome process of constituti onal amendment. The Committee 
also feels that such an amendment is  the need of the hour and would 
pose a step in the right direction to make the Hon’ble Court accessible 
to all the regions of the countr y. The Committee feels that the 
Constitution of India is a living  document and has enough scope to 
accommodate the demands arising out in a changed milieu in view of 
the provisions for it under Article 130 that reads - 
“The Supreme Court sits in Delhi.   It can, however, meet in any 
other place or places as the Chief Justice may, with the approval of 
the President.”  
7.3. The Committee, therefore, reitera tes the need for establishment of 
benches of the Supreme Court as it would be of immense help to the 
poor who cannot afford to travel from their native places to Delhi.  
7.4. The Committee in its earlier Re ports recommended that the Supreme 
Court journals containing all importa nt judgements and cases should be 

 75
publicized and commercialized to get wider publicity and even unreported 
cases should also get reference in the journals. The Committee had also 
recommended different High Courts of  the country to also publicize and 
commercialized their judgments and cases  through their jo urnals and make 
reference of unreported cases. The Committee was apprised that the 
abovementioned recommendations had been forwarded to the Supreme 
Court Registry for necessary action. The Committee was further apprised 
that in pursuance of the Committ ee's recommendations the reported 
judgements of the High Courts and Su preme Court are av ailable on their 
respective websites.  
7.5. The Committee appreciates that the Ministry has replied in 
affirmative and forwarded the abovementioned Committee's 
recommendations to the Supreme Court Registry for necessary action. 
The Committee hopes that the Supreme Court Registry would positively 
take decisions in this regard.  
7.6. The Committee in its earlier Repor ts had also recommended measures 
to strengthen the financial resources of the Supreme Court and High Courts 
and to enable the Supreme Court a nd High Courts to generate Revenue 
themselves which can also be utilized  by the Subordinate Judiciary. The 
Committee was apprised that the Department is in agreement with the views 
of the Committee. However, the Department apprised that the Department of 
Expenditure, Ministry of Finance was the controlling author ity for financial 
and budgetary matters in respect of the Supreme Court and for the High 
Courts the State Governments are the co ntrolling authority for financial and 
budgetary matters. Thus final decision in this regard lies at their end. 

 76
7.7. The Committee is pleased to  note that the Department is in 
agreement with the Committee's reco mmendation regarding enabling 
the Supreme Court and High Courts to generate Revenue themselves 
which can also be utilized by the Subordinate Judiciary. The Committee 
would, however, appreciate if the Department pursues the matter with 
the Department of Expenditure, Mini stry of Finance and the State 
Governments to consider the matter expeditiously. The Committee may 
be apprised their feedback accordingly. 
PENDENCY OF CASES 
7.8. In response to the queries raised  by the Ho'ble members, the Registrar 
Supreme Court while deposing before the Committee during the 
deliberations on the Demand for Grants  2010-11 put light on the matter of 
pendency of cases as follows.   
"……..Definitely, the Supreme Court is taking various steps to 
see that the pendency of cases is brought down and the cases 
are decided within a time fram e. There are various reasons 
which prevent us from doing so. Mainly, it is because of the 
deficiencies in the infrastructu re; funding is al so a problem; 
number of Judges is also a problem; and, various complex 
matters come before the various courts in India. We do feel that 
increase in the number of cases shows the increased faith in the 
judicial system. Sir, till about  4-5 years back, the number of 
disposals in the Supreme Cour t was higher than the number of 
institutions. But for the past few years, the cases have increased 
and with the number of Judges remaining the same, the 

 77
disposal ratio of each Judge  has gone up. So, we attribute 
increase in the pendency of cases mainly to the increase in the 
number of cases. That can be the only reason. It is true that it 
has increased."  
7.9. The Committee express it serious concerns over the huge 
pendency of cases in judiciary.  Ta king into account the reasons cited 
by the Registrar, Supreme Court in this regard, the Committee feels 
that the problem is not being add ressed seriously and wholehearted 
efforts are yet to be made to deal  with the problem. The Committee is 
of the view that both Executive and Judiciary should work in tandem 
to deal with the adversities arising out of mounting pendency. As far as 
the need of more judges is conc erned, the Committee reiterates its 
earlier recommendation that the vacanci es of judges in the High Court 
should be expeditiously filled up. The government should vigorously 
pursue the matter with the Chief Ju stice of the High Courts for 
necessary actions.

Law and Justice having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this
Fourth Report on the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council Bill, 2004.

3.         The Committee considered the Bill in two sittings held on the 16th February and 10th March, 2005.
 
4.         The Committee heard the oral evidence of the Secretary, Ministry of Law and Justice (Legislative Department) in
its sitting held on 16th February, 2005.
 
5.         To elicit views of the political parties, interested organisations and individuals on the provisions of the Bill, a Press
Communique was issued which was published in the national and regional dailies with predominant circulation in Andhra
Pradesh. 
 
6.         Twenty Memoranda containing suggestions on the Bill were received from representatives of the Political Parties,
Teachers’ Associations/Federations of Andhra Pradesh and NGOs.  
 
7.         In its sitting held on 22
nd March, 2005 the Committee considered the draft report on the Bill and adopted the same.
 
8.         The Committee in its meeting held on 10
th March, 2005 heard views of representatives of the Chief Minister of
Andhra Pradesh, Teachers’ Associations/Federations/NGOs and other persons interested in the subject matter. 
 
9.         The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in its meeting held on the 16th March, 2005.
 
10.       In the course of its deliberations, the Committee has made use of the background note on the Bill received from the
Ministry of Law and Justice (Legislative Department), suggestions received from organizations/experts; comments of the
Ministry on the views received from organizations/individuals/political parties and queries raised by the Members on the
Bill in the meetings.
 
11.       For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee have been printed
in bold letters in the body of the Report.
 
12.       On behalf of the Committee, I would like to acknowledge with thanks the contributions made by senior
representatives of Political Parties/eminent individuals/organizations who deposed before the Committee and submitted
their valuable suggestions on the Bill.

March 22, 2005
E.M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN
Chairman
Committee on Personnel, Public

REPORT
 
Need of Second Chambers in States
 
1.         Evolution of modern system of bicameral legislature in States can be traced in the observations of Dr. B.R.
Ambedkar, Chairman of the Constitution Drafting Committee during the course of deliberations of the Constituent
Assembly on 6 th January, 1949.  The Constituent Assembly envisaged the composition of Legislative Councils as a
transitional provision in the Constitution.  Opinion of the Assembly on whether provinces should have their second
chamber was divided and concern was expressed by Members about effectiveness of bicameral legislature.  Dr.
Ambedkar,   allaying the fears of the Members, replied that:-
“The question of whether to have a second Chamber in the provinces or not had been discussed by the Provincial
Constitution Committee, which was appointed by this House.  The decision of that Committee was that this was a
matter, which should be left to the decision of each province concerned.  If any particular province decided to have
a second chamber, it should be allowed to have a second chamber; and if any particular province did not want a
second chamber, a second chamber should not be imposed upon it.  In order to carry out this recommendation of

4threport of Committee on personnel, public grievances, law and justice
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Personnel,%20PublicGrievances,%20Law%20and%20Justice/4threport.htm[05-07-2016 11:00:32]
the Provincial Constitution Committee, it was decided that the Members in the Constituent Assembly representing
the different provinces, should meet and come to a decision on this issue.  The Members of the different provinces
represented in this Assembly, therefore, met in groups of their own to decide this question and as a result of the
deliberations carried on by the Members, it was reported to the office that the provinces had agreed to have a
second chamber for their provinces.  Ever since the French Constituent Assembly met, there had been consistently
a view which was opposed to second chambers.  The view of those who are opposed to second chamber could
better be put in the words of Abbe Seiyes.  His criticism was two-fold.  He said that if the Upper House agreed with
the lower one, then it was superfluous.  If it did not agree with the lower House, it was a mischievous body and we
ought not to entertain it.  The first part of the criticism of Abbe Seiyes was undoubtedly valid, because it was so
obvious.  But nobody had agreed with the second part of the criticism of Abbe Seiyes.  Even the French nation had
not accepted that view they too had consistently maintained the principle of having a second chamber.  The
Constitution was to introduce the second chamber, purely as an experimental measure.  We had not, by the Draft
Constitution, given the second chamber a permanent place; we had not made it a permanent part of our
Constitution.  It was a purely experimental measure, as I said” (C.A Deb. Vol.  7; 6.1.49;C. 1317).
 
Constitutional provisions regarding creation/abolition and composition of Legislative Councils
 
2.         As a corollary to the debate of the Constituent Assembly on the need of bicameral legislature in States and in
keeping with the views expressed by Dr. Ambedkar, the Constitution of India has embodied the provisions for
creation/abolition and composition of Legislative Councils.  The relevant articles of the Constitution are reproduced
below:-
“169. (1) Notwithstanding anything in article 168, Parliament may by law provide for the abolition of the
Legislative Council of a State having such a Council or for the creation of such a Council in a State having no such
Council, if the Legislative Assembly of the State passes a resolution to that effect by a majority of the total
membership of the Assembly and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the Members of the Assembly present
and voting”.
           
“171. Composition of the Legislative Councils – (I) The total number of Members in the Legislative
Council of a State having such a Council shall not exceed one-third of the total number of Members in the
Legislative Assembly of that State:
 
Provided that the total number of Members in the Legislative Council of a State shall in no case be less than
forty.
 
(2) Until Parliament by law otherwise provides, the composition of the Legislative Council of a State shall
be as provided in clause (3).
 
(3) Of the total number of Members of the Legislative Council of a State-
 
(a)
                as nearly as may be, one-third shall be elected by electorates consisting of Members of
municipalities, district Boards and such other local authorities in the State as Parliament may be law
specify;
 
(b)
               as nearly as may be, one-twelfth shall be elected by electorates consisting of persons residing in the
State who have been for at least three years graduates of any university in the territory of India or have been
for at least three years in possession of qualifications prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament as
equivalent to that of a graduate of any such university;
 
(c)
                as nearly as may be, one-twelfth shall be elected by electorates consisting of persons who have
been for at least three years engaged in teaching in such educational institutions within the State, not lower
in standard than that of a secondary school, as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament;
 
(d) as nearly as may be, one-third shall be elected by the Members of the Legislative Assembly of the State
from amongst persons who are not Members of the Assembly;
 
(e) the remainder shall be nominated by the Governor in accordance with the provisions of clause (5).

4threport of Committee on personnel, public grievances, law and justice
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Personnel,%20PublicGrievances,%20Law%20and%20Justice/4threport.htm[05-07-2016 11:00:32]
 
(4)        The Members to be elected under sub-clauses (a), (b) and
(c) of clause (3) shall be chosen in such territorial constituencies as may be prescribed by or under any law
made by Parliament, and the elections under the said sub-clauses and under sub-clause (d) of the said clause
shall be held in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single
transferable vote.
 
(5) The Members to be nominated by the Governor under sub-clause (e) of clause (3) shall consist of
persons having special knowledge or practical experience in respect of such matters as the following, namely:-
 
Literature, science, art, co-operative movement and social service.”
           
Present scenario
3.         At present there are Legislative Councils in five States, namely, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh and
Jammu and Kashmir.  The Legislative  Councils which were in existence in the States of West Bengal, Punjab and Tamil
Nadu were abolished by separate Parliamentary enactments with effect from 1
st August, 1969 and 1 st January, 1986
respectively.  Similarly, the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council (Abolition) Act, 1985 (No.34 of 1985) abolished the
Legislative Council of the State, which was created in 1957 by the Legislative Councils Act, 1957 (37 of 1957).
           
 
Efforts for revival of Legislative Council in Andhra Pradesh
4.         Between then and now, efforts have been made to revive the Legislative Council in Andhra Pradesh.  On persistent
demand of political groups/individuals, the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly passed a resolution for revival of the
Legislative Council on 22
nd January, 1990.  A Bill to revive the Legislative Council in the State (alongwith the State of
Tamil Nadu) was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 10 th May, 1990 and passed by that House on 28 th May, 1990.  This
Bill, however, lapsed on the dissolution of the Ninth Lok Sabha.  It could not, be processed further till the year 2004, when
the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly passed a resolution on 8 th July, 2004 by a majority of the total Membership of
the Assembly and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the Members present and voting for creation of the
Legislative Council in the State, and forwarded it to the Central Government for taking follow up action thereon as per the
provisions of article 169(1) of the Constitution. 
5.         Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council Bill, 2004 (Annexure......) was introduced in Lok Sabha on 16
th December,
2004.  The Bill seeks to provide for creation of a Legislative Council in the State of Andhra Pradesh, with a total strength
of 90 Members, 31 of which are to be elected by the local authorities, 8 each are to be elected by the Graduates and
Teachers constituencies, 31 by the Legislative Assembly and the remaining 12 are to be nominated by the Governor.  The
local authorities being represented in the Legislative Council are Municipal Corporations, Municipalities, Nagar
Panchayats, Cantonment Boards, Zila Praja Parishads and Mandal Praja Parishads.  The constitution of the Legislative
Council is, therefore, the same as it had existed prior to its abolition, except for the local bodies constituting the local
authorities’ constituency.
Views of the Government
 
6.         Explaining the circumstances and the developments necessitating the introduction of the Andhra Pradesh
Legislative Council Bill, 2004, the Secretary, Ministry of Law and Justice (Legislative Department) stated that creation of
Legislative Councils in States had always been a debatable subject and there had been arguments for and against creation
of the Legislative Councils.  First it was felt that a second chamber was necessary for adequate representation of certain
sections of the society, not sufficiently represented in the lower House.  The other argument was that the second chamber
would act as a revising chamber.  Thirdly, consideration by a second chamber would involve some delay in the passing of
a Bill and such delay was needed to enable the opinion of the people to be expressed on the measure, particularly in
matters of a controversial nature on which the views of the public were not clear.  It was essential to allow the necessary
time so that public opinion on the matter crystallized itself.  A second chamber would help in eliminating the errors of the
other House.   It was also thought that a second chamber would help in easing the pressure of time on the lower House, in
as much as important but comparatively non-controversial matters could be initiated in the Upper House and after full
discussion in the Upper House, the matters could be taken to the Lower House.  After such a full discussion in the Upper
House, the Lower House would not require much time to dispose of the matter.  Further, when the Lower House was fully
pre-occupied otherwise, the time of the Upper House could be utilized for discussion on urgent matters for which the
Lower House was not able to find time. 

4threport of Committee on personnel, public grievances, law and justice
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Personnel,%20PublicGrievances,%20Law%20and%20Justice/4threport.htm[05-07-2016 11:00:32]
7.         The Secretary further stated that there were arguments against having a second chamber in the State Legislatures. 
One such argument was that the Councils comprised of indirectly elected representatives, and as such impeded progressive
legislations.  It was also considered to be drain on the public exchequer.  Moreover, it was felt that the second chamber
was used to delay the Bills. 
8.         Referring to the debate in the Constituent Assembly and the views expressed by Dr. Ambedkar on the need of
bicameral legislature, the Secretary stated that earlier the concept of second chamber was considered a wasteful exercise.  
But in modern times the common man had to go to Court to get his concern heard.  So one needed more and more public
fora like the Legislative Council, where one could voice one’s grievance through the public representatives who could
bring matters of public importance/interest to the notice of the Government. 
9.         Further, the second chamber could address the inadequacy of addressing the concerns of the common man.  The
secretary also stated that as far as the legislative role was concerned, the contribution of the second chamber could not be
minimized.   There was no bar on introduction of Government as well as Private Members Bills in the second chamber.  It
had been experienced that debates on Private Members Bills could lead to some important decisions on the part of
Government, sooner or later.  
10.       The Committee considered suggestions received on the Bill from the representatives of NGOs, the various State
Teachers’ Associations/ Federations and Political Organisations and heard views of Dr. Jayaprakash Narayan, Convenor
Lok Satta, Dr. Ravi Mallu, Ex-M.P and nominee of the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, Shri Kantheti Satyanarayana
Raju, Chief Minister’s nominee, Shri J.D. Seelam, M.P., Rajya Sabha, Shri B. Kamalaker Rao and Shri B. Mohan Reddy,
President, Progressive Recognized Teachers’ Union, Andhra Pradesh, Dr. A. Chakrapani, Senior Advocate, Andhra
Pradesh Court,  among other representatives of Teachers’ Federations of the State. 
11.       Suggestions received on the Bill were forwarded to the Government for comments thereon.  Statement showing
comments received from the Government alongwith suggestions are appended to the Bill (Annexure......)
12.       The Committee observed that while there was unanimity on the provisions of the Bill still the demand of the
various Teachers’ Associations for voting rights to primary school teachers has, by and large, remained unfulfilled.  The
Government’s response to this effect is that the issue of the voting rights to primary school teachers has been under
consideration of the Government since 1957 but no firm decision, however, has been possible because of absence of
unanimity in views of various bodies connected with the issue.  The Committee is, however, of the view that in the
changed circumstances primary teachers’ demand can not be said to be totally unjustified.  There has been a sea change in
socio-economic fabric as a result of which now a days all the teachers in primary schools are highly educated and as such
their demand for enrolment in the list of teachers’ constituency may be re-looked   by the Government.
13.       Having considered suggestions/views of the representatives of Government of Andhra Pradesh, NGOs, Jurists,
various Associations of Teachers of Andhra Pradesh, Parliamentarians, and others, the Committee arrives at the conclusion
that there is an overwhelming support in favour of creation of the Legislative council in the State.  The Committee notes
that even the Constituent Assembly, while debating on the question of necessity of second chambers in States, had
advocated a transitional provision in the constitution for creation of bicameral legislature.  Since then, Legislative Councils
have been constituted in States to fulfill the aspirations of the people and address concern of common man.  Not only this,
many advanced countries of the modern world too have a system of bicameral legislature.  It also note that the Andhra
Pradesh Legislative Council was abolished in 1985 and since then till now, there have been untiring efforts for its revival
in the State.  This, in a way, reflects the zeal and urge of the people of the State, both to represent interests of the people
and get heard adequately in the changed socio-political and socio-economic scenario.
14.  Viewed in the light of the above, the Committee feels that bringing this legislation to revive the Legislative Council in
Andhra Pradesh after twenty years of its abolitions is a right step in the right direction, which will ensure not only
proportional representations of the Local Body Institutions, Assembly Constituency, Teachers’ Constituency and Graduate
Constituency, but also have benefit of experience and views of the distinguished persons nominated to the Council.  
15.       The Committee, favouring creation of the Legislative Council in Andhra Pradesh, extends its all out support to the
Bill and recommends adoption of the clauses 2-5 of the Bill.
Clause 1, Enacting Formula and Title
16.       Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted with some changes which were of consequential or
drafting nature, namely, the figure “2004” and the words and “Fifty-fifth” to be substituted by the figure “2005” and the
words “Fifty-sixth”, respectively.

INTRODUCTION 
 I, the Chairperson of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, 
Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorised by the Committee on its behalf, do hereby 
present the Fortieth Report on The Personal Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2010. The Bill seeks to amend 
the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 so as to include the mother along with the father as a fit person to 
be appointed as guardian; and to amend the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 so as to 
remove the incapacity of a married woman to take in  adoption and so as to provide that the mother, 
with the consent of father and vice versa, shall have equal right to give in adoption of their children. 
2.   In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee, 
the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred
@ the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 22nd 
April, 2010 and pending therein, to this Committee on the 23rd April, 2010 for examination and 
report. 
3.  Keeping in view the importance of the Bill, the Committee decided to issue a press communique 
to solicit views/suggestions from desirous individuals/organisations on the provisions of the Bill. 
Accordingly, a press communique was issued in national and local newspapers and dailies, in 
response to which memoranda containing suggestions were received, from various organizations / 
individuals / experts, by the Committee. 
4.  The Committee heard the oral evidence of the Secretary, Legislative Department, Ministry of 
Law and Justice on the provisions of the Bill in its meeting held on 6th May, 2010. 
5.   The Committee, during its study visits to Mumbai, Bengaluru and Chennai from 13th to 19th 
June, 2010, heard the views of the State Governments of Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu and 
other stakeholders such as Bar Associations, Employees’ Associations, individuals and institutions on 
the Bill.

placed before it : –
