OPINION OF JUSTICE J.S. VERMA
As desired on behalf of the Standing Committee of the Parliament, I reiterate my views expressed
personally before it on 13 October 2011, and answer the specific issues addressed to me for my
response.
Preface
I am of the firm view that the unanimous demand of the people as well as the avowed commitment
of all political parties for a strong Lokpal can be best met by conferring constitutional status to
the proposed Lokpal for the Union and the Lokayuktas for the States, akin to the Election
Commission and the Union Public Service Commission/State Public Service Commissions. To avoid
any delay in making the needed constitutional amendment for the purpose, the Constitution
Amendment Bill must eschew any contentious issue (all of which can be addressed in the
consequent legislation with all details) containing only the bare minimum required for the purpose.
I have already circulated a rough draft of the suggested Constitution Amendment Bill for
consideration of the Standing Committee before our above meeting, which does not contain any
contentious issue while mandating the Union to constitute the Lokpal and the States to constitute
the Lokayukta. It provides for all the details to be incorporated in the contemplated accompanying
legislation to complete the task.
Such a constitutional amendment would not attract the Proviso to Sub-Article (2) of Article 368
of the Constitution, and, therefore, it would not require ratification by the States. For ease of
reference, Article 368(2) is extracted below:
“An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for
the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when the Bill is passed in each House by
a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-
thirds of the members of that House present and voting, it shall be presented to the
President who shall give his assent to the Bill and thereupon the Constitution shall stand
amended in accordance with the terms of the Bill:
Provided that if such amendment seeks to make any change in–
(a) article 54, article 55, article 73, article 162 or article 241, or
(b) Chapter IV of Part V , Chapter V of Part VI, or Chapter I of Part XI, or
(c) any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule, or
(d) the representation of States in Parliament, or
(e) the provisions of this article,
584

585
the amendment shall also require to be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half
of the States by resolutions to that effect passed by those Legislatures before the Bill
making provision for such amendment is presented to the President for assent.”
As would be evident on a plain reading of Article 368(2), the only requirement is for it to be passed
by the majority of total membership of each House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds
of members present and voting.
With the unanimous demand in the people supported by unanimity of all political parties in the
Parliament to constitute a strong Lokpal/Lokayuktas, there can be no doubt of unanimous support
for a constitutional body, which would obviously be the strongest visualized in the constitutional
scheme. Once the constitutional amendment is made. It would become a part of the indestructible
‘basic structure’, immune from any future attempt to erode its status. The exercise for the
accompanying consequent legislation providing the details dealing with the contentious issues can
continue simultaneously since it must follow to complete the process.
There is no occasion to doubt the sincerity of the commitment and resolve or the people and the
political will in this behalf. Therefore, there can be no risk of any delay in this method.
With the above preface, my answers to the specific Issues referred for my opinion are as under:
Issues
(i) Whether the proposed Lokpal legislation to be enacted by Parliament can include in it
the structure for and content of State Lokayuktas by invocation of Articles 253/254
and/or entries 1, 2 and llA of List III of the Constitution and/or any other legal or
constitutional basis?;
(ii) W ould such a national legislation be constitutionally valid (with reasons there for) and,
if not, the reasons thereof ?;
(iii) W ould it be constitutionally and legally feasible to follow the model of the NHRC and/
or the RTI Act, 2005 and/or the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 etc. and/or any other
appropriate central legislation to provide for Lokpal and Lokayuktas in one central
enactment and the basis on which the validity and constitutionality of such a legislation
can be sustained?
Answer
These three issues being connected are combined for their answer.
Consequent upon the aforesaid constitutional amendment the proposed Lokpal legislation to be
enacted by the Parliament by invocation of Article 253 does not require any additional legislative
support. For ease of reference, Artic1c 253 is quoted below:
“Legislation for giving effect to international agreements – Notwithstanding anything in the
foregoing provisions of this Chapter, Parliament has power to make any law for the whole
or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention
with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference,
association or other body.”

586
This confers the legislative competence needed to implement the UN  Convention Against
Corruption, which has been signed and ratified by India. It is relevant to highlight that Article 6
of the Convention enshrines a specific obligation for member–States to establish bodies that prevent
corruption. Article 6 of the Convention is quoted in full below:
“Article 6. Preventive anti-corruption body or bodies
1. Each State Party shall, in accordance with the fundamental principles of its legal system,
ensure the existence of a body or bodies, as appropriate, that prevent corruption by such
means as:
(a) Implementing the policies referred to in article 5 of this Convention and, where
appropriate, overseeing and coordinating the implementation of those policies;
(b) Increasing and disseminating knowledge about the prevention of corruption.
2. Each State Party shall grant the body or bodies referred to in paragraph 1 of this article
the necessary independence, in accordance with the fundamental principles of its legal
system, to enable the body or bodies to carry out its or their functions effectively and free
from any undue influence. The necessary material resources and specialized staff, as well
as the training that such staff may require to carry out their functions, should be provided.
3. Each State Party shall inform the Secretary-General of the United Nations of  the name
and address of the authority or authorities that may assist other States Parties in developing
and implementing specific measures for the prevention of corruption.”
The directive principle of State policy in Article 51(c), as a principle fundamental in governance
is available as an aid. (Article 51 states: “The State shall endeavour to…(c) foster respect for
international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another...”.)
There is, therefore, no need to look for any  additional support for the legislative competence of
the Parliament to legislate on the subject for the whole territory of India. In addition, it would not
be out of place to  mention that the failure to take effective steps with respect to tbe establishment
of such institutions could lead to India being considered to be in breach of its obligations  under
international law, which must obviously be avoided at all costs.
The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 providing for the constitution of the NHRC and the
SHRCs was enacted by the Union Parliament for the whole territory of India to implement the Paris
Principles, 1991 for the ‘better protection of human rights’, in addition to the existing constitutional
guarantees and statutory rights with the machinery to enforce them. This was done by invoking
Article 153 for the whole territory of India. Similarly, for ‘combating corruption’ in a more
effective manner a uniform legislation enacted by the Union Parliament by invoking Article 253 can
provide for the Lokpal and the Lokayuktas.
The Parliamentary central enactment made by invoking Article 153 would be constitutionally valid,
such legislative competence in the Union Parliament being expressly provided as a part of the
constitutional scheme, consistent with the nature of federalism created by the Constitution.
Issue No. (iv):
If the answer to the aforesaid is in the affirmative, whether by virtue of Article 254 of the
Constitution of India and/or any other available power, the aforesaid proposed Lokpal Act to be
enacted by Parliament would also be entitled to repeal the existing State Lokayukta enactments?

587
Answer
Once the Union Parliament enacts the central legislation by invoking Article 253 for the whole
territory of India, the existing State legislations relating to the Lokayuktas being repugnant to it shall
be void, by virtue of Article 154(l), which states as under:
“If any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision
of a law made by Parliament which Parliament is competent to enact, or to any provision
of an existing law with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List,
then, subject to the provisions of clause (2), the law made by Parliament, whether passed
before or after the law made by the Legislature of such State, or, as the case may be, the
existing law, shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the
extent of the repugnancy, be void.”
In the light of the above provision, it would be advisable, in order to avoid needless litigation, for
the central law to indicate - with reference to the above Article – that the existing State laws shall
be treated as void and inoperative. It may however be added that this question would become
purely academic in the event that the route or a constitutional amendment (along the broad lines
I have suggested) is adopted, since the proposed amendment envisages parallel laws being enacted
by Parliament and by the State legislatures.

REPORT
The Administrators-General (Amendment) Bill, 2011 (Annexure-A) introduced in the Rajya
Sabha on the 18 th August, 2011 seeks to increase the jurisdiction of the Administrator-General in
relation to the administration of assets left by the deceased person (except the assets of certain
specified nature) from the monetary limit of the present rupees two lakhs to rupees ten lakhs.
2. To attain this objective, the Bill seeks to amend the Administrators-General Act, 1963 by
substituting the words “two lakhs” with the word “ten lakhs” in Sections 9, 10, 29 and 36 of the
said Act. The Bill was referred by the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha to the Department Related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice on the
19th August, 2011, for examination and report.
3. The Administrators-General Act, 1963 (45 of 1963) is an Act to consolidate and amend the law
relating to the office and duties of Administrator-General. Section 3 of the said Act provides for the
State Government to appoint an Administrator-General for the State or for two or more States, vested
with the right to apply for administration of estates of any deceased person exceeding Rs.  2,00,000
in value. The Administrator-General undertakes the proceeding for the letter of administration of estates
only if he is satisfied that there is an apprehension of misappropriation, deterioration or waste of such
assets and such proceedings are necessary for the protection of the assets.
3.1 Section 29 of the aforesaid Act empowers the Administrator-General to grant certificate to any
person who is interested in the assets of a deceased person and who claims otherwise than as a
creditor. Such certificate can be granted only in cases where the assets left by the deceased person
(excluding any sum of money deposited in a Government Savings Bank or any Provident Fund to
which the Provident Fund Act 1925 applies) does not exceed in value in the whole, the monetary limit
specified in that section.
3.2 The monetary limit specified in Section 29 was originally only Rs.  5,000 in 1963. On account
of decrease in money value and escalation in the value of assets and also for protection of the
interests of poor persons and legal heirs of the deceased persons, especially widows, minor children
and other dependents from protracted and expensive litigation in Civil Courts, the monetary limit in
the said Section was enhanced to Rs.  15,000 in 1972 to Rs.  50,000 in 1983 and to Rs.  2,00,000
in 1999.
4. The Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Bill elucidate the reasons and need for
bringing forth the present amendment. It states as under:–
“...The Administrators-General Act, 1963 is an Act to consolidate and amend the law relating
to the office and duties of Administrator-General. Section 29 of the said Act empowers the
Administrator-General to grant certificate to any person, interested in the assets of a deceased
person, claiming otherwise than as a creditor and such certificate can be granted only in cases
where the assets left by the deceased person (except the assets of certain specified nature) do
not exceed in value in the whole the monetary limit specified in that section. Originally, the
monetary limit specified in the said section 29 was only Rs.  5,000. On account of considerable
decrease in money value and to protect the interests of the poor persons and legal heirs
especially widows, minor children and other dependents of the deceased persons from protracted
and expensive litigation in civil courts, the monetary limit in the said section was enhanced
to Rs.  15,000 in 1972, to Rs.  50,000 in 1983 and to Rs.  2,00,000 in 1999.”

2
4.1. It further states:–
“Certain representations have been received by the Central Government requesting for
enhancement of the monetary limit specified in section 29 of the Administrators-General Act,
1963 from Rs. 2,00,000 due to the escalation in the value of assets and on account of
considerable decrease in money value. The Maharashtra State Legislature has amended the
aforesaid Act in its application to that State by enhancing the monetary limit from Rs. 2,00,000
to Rs.
 10,00,000. Similarly, the Uttar Pradesh State Legislature has also taken steps to
amend the Act in its application to that State for enhancing the monetary limit from
Rs. 2,00,000 to Rs. 10,00,000.
5. The background note dated 26
th August, 2011  submitted by the Legislative Department further
states as under:–
“...As the proposed legislation is relatable to a subject in the concurrent field namely, entry
11 of List III - Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, the State
Government and the Union territory Administrations have been consulted on the proposal. The
Legislative Department vide their letter dated 28
th April, 2010 requested all the State
Governments and the Union territory Administrations to furnish their views and comments on
the proposed amendment. So far 24 out of 28 State Governments and all Union territory
Administrations have furnished their views. 20 State Governments namely, Assam, Chhattisgarh,
Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra,
Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Orissa, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tripura, Uttarakhand
and West Bengal and 5 Union territory Administrations namely, Andaman and Nicobar,
Chandigarh Administartion, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu and Delhi have
supported the proposal. The Government of Arunachal Pradesh, Union territories of Lakshadweep
and Puducherry have informed that they have no comments to offer. Government of Jammu
and Kashmir and Sikkim have informed that they have no comments to offer. Governments of
Jammu and Kashmir and Sikkim have informed that the Administrators-General Act, 1963 is
not in force in those States. State of Karnataka have informed that the escalation shall be
between two lakhs and six lakhs so that estate of deceased person could be prevented from
imminent danger of misappropriation, deterioration or waste. Nothing has been heard from the
rest of State Governments. A statement howing views of the State Governments and Union
territory Administrations is annexed to this note as Annexure-II.
In view of the position stated above and having regard to the decrease in money value
and escalation of prices of properties, it is considered necessary to increase the monetary limit
of jurisdiction of the Administrator-General from the existing limit of Rs. 2,00,000 to
Rs. 10,00,000 by suitably amending the references to the monetary limit specified in sections
9, 10, 29 and 36  of the said Act… ”
6. The Committee, in its meeting held on 10
th January, 2012, considered the proposed amendment.
All Members present in the meeting were in agreement with the Government’s proposal. The Secretary,
Legislative Department was also present in the meeting to assist the Committee and provide clarifications,
if required. No dissents have been received.
7. While considering the Bill, the Committee took note of the following facts submitted by the
Secretary, Legislative Department in his written presentation:
(a) Section 3 of the Administrators-General Act provides that the State Government shall
appoint an Administrator-General for the State but the same person can be appointed
as Administrator-General for two or more States; Section 6 provides that, in so far as

3
the Administrator-General of any State, the High Court to be deemed a court of
competent jurisdiction for the purpose of granting probate for letters of Administration;
Section 7 provides for the High Court to grant letters of Administration to the
Administrator-General unless they are granted to the next-of-kin of the deceased;
Section 8 provides that the Administrator-General is entitled to letters of Administration
in preference to creditors, certain legatees and friends of the deceased; and Section 29
empowers the Administrator-General to grant certificate to any person, claiming assets
of a deceased person otherwise than as a creditor and that such certificate can be
granted only in cases where the assets left by the deceased person does not exceed
in value in the whole the monetary limit specified in that Section.
(b) Valuation of assets under Section 29 does not include any sum of money in a
Government Savings Bank or any Provident Fund Account to which the Provident
Fund Act, 1925 applies. It also covers all savings schemes of the Post Offices like
NSS, KVP, NSC, etc. floated through subordinate legislations or through notifications.
(c) Originally the Act enacted in 1963 specified only Rs.
 5,000/-monetary limit under
Section 29. In 1972, as a result of representations made by the war widows association,
Chandigarh on behalf of the widows in general and war widows in particular, the Act
was amended to increase the monetary limit to Rs.
 15,000/-. The monetary limit to the
said Section was further enhanced to Rs. 50,000/-. In 1983, it was further enhanced
to Rs. 2,00,000 in 1999 on account of considerable decrease in money value and
escalation in the value of assets and also for protection of the interests of poor persons
and legal heirs of the deceased persons especially widows, minor children and other
dependents from protracted and expensive litigation in Civil Courts.
(d) The Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh State Legislatures have amended the Administrators-
General Act in its application to those States by enhancing the monetary limit from
Rs. 2,00,000 to Rs. l0,00,000. Since the subject matter of the proposal is relatable to
a subject in the concurrent field namely, entry 11 of List III-Concurrent List of the
Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, the State Governments and Union Territory
Administrations have been consulted on the proposal. 20 State Governments and 5
Union Territory Administrations have conveyed their support to the proposal.
(e) The representations received by the Central Government also requested for enhancement
of the monetary limit specified in Section 29 of the Administrators-General Act, 1963
on account of escalation in the value of assets and considerable decrease in money
value and to increase the monetary limit of jurisdiction of the Administrator-General
from the existing limit of Rs.
 2,00,000 to Rs.  10,00,000 by suitably amending the
references of limit specified in Sections 9, 10, 29 and 36 of the said Act.
(f) In view of the above, the proposal to amend Section 29 of the Administrators-General
Act, 1963 with a view to raise the monetary limit from Rs.  2,00,000 to Rs.  10,00,000
with consequential amendments in Sections 9, 10 and 36 of the said Act has been
mooted.
8. Having considered the justifications given in the Statement of Objects and Reasons of
the Bill, the written submission made by the Legislative Department, and the Secretary of that
Department, the Committee agrees with the proposal of the Ministry to enhance the monetary
limit from Rs. 2,00,000/- at present to Rs. 10,00,000/- by suitably amending the reference to
monetary limit in Sections 9, 10, 29 and 36 of the Administrators-General Act, 1963. Principally,
this conclusion has been reached on the basis that the value of money has decreased over the

4
years. Rs. two lacs was prescribed in the year 1999. Over the past twelve years, the figure of
Rs. two lacs specified in Sections 9, 10, 29 and 36 of the said Act would have declined
considerably. Passage of time has thus rendered the figure of two lacs unrealistic, ineffective
and virtually infructous. Continuance of this unrealistic figure would render the remit or
jurisdiction of the AGs office too burdensome and unrealistic. Hence the enhancement to
Rs. ten lacs.
The Committee unanimously so recommends.

REPORT  
CHAPTER-I 
OVERALL  ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS OF THE MINISTRY 
1.0 The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the coordinating agency of the 
Central Government in personnel matters specially issues concerning recruitment, training, career 
development, staff welfare as well as the process of responsive, people-oriented, modern 
administration. The Ministry comprises three Departments, namely:- 
  (i) Department of Personnel and Training; 
  (ii) Department of Pensions  and Pensioners’ Welfare; and 
  (iii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances 
1.1 All the three Departments of the Ministry have  been functioning under the charge of Secretary 
(Personnel) who is presently assist ed by four Additional Secretaries,  three Joint Secretaries and other 
supporting officers and staff. The Ministry is divided into seven Divisions, each of which is headed by 
an officer of the level of Joint Secretary or above. The Divisions are: 
  (i) Establishment Officer; 
  (ii) Services and Vigilance; 
  (iii) Establishment; 
  (iv) Administrative tribunal and Administration; 
  (v) Training; 
  (vi) Pension and Central Services; and 
  (vii) Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances. 
1.2 The Ministry has under its administrative control four attached offices, namely: 
  (i) Staff Selection Commission (SSC); 
  (ii) Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM); 
  (iii) Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA); and 
  (iv) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). 
1.3 The other offices under the administrative control of the Ministry are: 
  (i) Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), a constitutional body; 
  (ii) Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), a statutory body; 
  (iii) Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), a statutory quasi-judicial body; and 
  (iv) Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB), a body set up by a resolution of the 
Government.

Budgetary provision 
1.12. The Budgetary provisions make it clear that the major share of funds has been allocated for Non 
Plan provisions. Whereas funds to the tune of Rs. 75 crore has been provided for Plan provisions, 
Non-Plan has got a share of Rs. 229 crore, i.e., more than three times. When the Ministry was asked 
the reasons for this difference between  Plan and Non-Plan provisions, the Ministry stated that it is the 
coordinating agency of the Central Government in personnel matters, especially on the issues 
concerning recruitment, training, career development,  staff welfare and also to act as a watchdog of 
Government ensuring that certain accepted standards and norms as laid down by it are followed by all 
the Ministries/Departments in these areas. Towards this end, its role is essentially regulatory and 
policy making rather than that of an actual implementing agency. Even then the Ministry had 
formulated several Plan Schemes which are being implemented. In fact, the Ministry had sought a 
total Plan allocation of Rs. 120.33 crore for 2005-06, but the Planning Commission had allocated only 
Rs. 75 crore. Besides, out of the Non-Plan allocation, nearly 55.12 per cent is meant for payment of 
salaries to officers and staff of the Ministry and its attached offices and another 15.15 per cent goes to 
office and travel expenses. 10.42 per cent of the budget is earmarked for payment of professional 
services and another 3.93 per cent is for giving loan to State Governments for payment of House 
Building Advance to All India Service Officers. Balance 15.38 per cent is on account of other heads.

1.23 The Union Public Service Commission is a constitutional body, created under Article 315 of the 
Constitution. The Commission’s charter of duties is given in Articles 320 and 321 of the Constitution. 
In brief, it is the duty of the Commission to conduct examinations for appointment to services of the 

Union and to advise Government on all matter relating to framing of recruitment rules, method of 
recruitment and the principle to be followed in making promotions and transfers from one service to 
another. The Commission is also required to be consulted in respect of disciplinary matters affecting a 
civil servant including appeals and memoranda filed by individual Government servants.

CHAPTER-II  
FUNCTIONING OF CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION (CBI) 
2.0 During the discussion on Demands for Grants (2005-06) of the Ministry of Personnel, Public 
Grievances and Pensions, the Director, CBI made a brief presentation before the Committee 
explaining the various issues that have arisen in the context of the functioning of the organisation and 
the need to resolve those issues expeditiously. 
2.1 The CBI came into being in the year 1941 with rather limited role and responsibility to 
investigate offences of bribery and corruption connected with transactions relating to War and Supply 
Department, Government of India. Over the last 64 years, the organisation has evolved from an anti-
corruption agency to a multi-faceted, multi-disciplinary central police - law enforcement agency with 
capability, credibility and legal mandate to investigate and prosecute offences anywhere in India. At 
present, CBI has the following Divisions: 
  (1) Anti Corruption Division; 
  (2) Economic Offences Division; 
  (3) Special Crimes Division; 
  (4) Directorate of Prosecution; 
  (5) Administration Division; 
  (6) Policy and Coordination Division; and 
  (7) Central Forensic Science Laboratory 
2.2 The CBI derives the power of investigation from the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 
1946, (DSPE) with jurisdiction covering all the Departments of the Government of India and Union 
Territories. As per section 2 of the Act, DPSE has jurisdiction to investigate offences in the Union 
Territories only. However, the jurisdiction can be extended by the Central Government to other areas 
including Railways and States under section 5(1) of the Act, provided the State Governments have 
accorded consent under section 6 of the Act. Duri ng the oral evidence on Demands for Grants (2005-
06), it was pointed out that this causes problem many a time and results in inordinate delays in the 
process of investigation. For example, in case of non-consent of the concerned State Government, 
there is very little that the Union Government can do. 
2.3 In the Seventh Report (1993-94) of the Committee on Home Affairs on Central Bureau of 
Investigation and Central Vigilance Commission, the following observation was made by the 
Committee: 
“The Committee notes that though most of the States give their consent for investigation by 
the CBI, sometimes with the change of Government or for some other reasons certain States 
at times withdraw their consent before or during the investigation, thus frustrating all the 
efforts of the CBI to bring the culprits to book.” (see para 31, page 6 of the 7th Report of the 
Committee on Home Affairs). 
2.4 During the meeting of the Committee, the Memb ers observed that despite these constraints, 
there was always demand for CBI enquiry from various States, organisations and other quarters. The 
following are excerpts from some of the observations made: 

“.....new cases are being passed on to the CBI at  regular intervals. Cases are coming to CBI 
because everyone says that the case should go to the CBI. Whatever is the nature of the case, 
it should be referred to the CBI”. 
Financial and administrative powers 
2.5 During discussion on Demands for Grants (2005-06), Members pointed out that lack of financial 
power acts as a major hindrance in the working of the organisation. Lack of delegation of powers is 
one of the major bottlenecks in the Department. Even for the smallest of things, CBI has to get 
clearance from the Ministry. Delegation of powers  to the subordinate and attached offices is a 
welcome step, but instead a situation has been created whereby for their trivial financial requirement, 
it has to get clearance from the Ministry. 
2.6 Discussing this aspect, the Chairman of th e Committee made certain important observations, 
whereby it was proposed that a separate Act could be brought in for the CBI. He stated as below: 
“..... Why don’t you enact a law so as to make a separate budgetary provision for them (CBI) 
and allow them to work well? The administrative control makes them kneel down before 
officials and they are not getting their work  done in time. We need an independent 
investigating authority  ........ CBI is the only agency on which we can depend ........ You have 
to come out with some proposition, so as to allow it to function as an independent agency.” 
2.7 The Committee observes that all these years, CB I has been able to maintain its reputation 
of a premier investigating agenc y of the country functioning wi th credibility and impartiality. 
However, dependence on the executive wing of th e State for both financ ial and administrative 
matters impinges upon its role  as an independent investig ating agency. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the po ssibility of promulgating a separa te Act for CBI in tune with 
the requirement of the time, rather than derivi ng its powers from the Delhi Special Police 
Establishment Act, 1946, may be examined by the Government. 
2.8 The Committee also takes note of the fact th at under the present DSPE Act, procedural 
nuances involved in obtaining th e consent of the State Governme nt for investigation of cases 
within its jurisdiction cause inordinate delays and in case of withdrawal of consent by the 
concerned State Government due to some reason or the other, investigation takes a back seat. In 
view of the aforesaid situation, the Commi ttee reiterates its earlier recommendation (para 31, 
page 6 of the 7
th Report of the Committ ee on Home Affairs) that CBI should be empowered by a 
suitable legislation to investigate all offen ces under the Central laws like Prevention of 
Corruption Act, Income Tax Act, Central Customs & Excise Act, etc. in any part of the country 
after obtaining the concurrence of the Central Government. 
2.9 Keeping in view the need for functional independence of the CBI, it is imperative that 
financial powers are commensurate with the requi rement of efficient and smooth functioning of 
the organisation. Whereas similar delegation by th e Ministry of Home Affairs to the Heads of 
Central Para Military Forces (CPMFs) has kept pace with the changing requirement, difference 
in terms of delegation of these powers to CBI ha s resulted in glaring disparities in the financial 
powers of the CBI vis-a—vis those of the Heads of CPMFs. Thus, while recommending for 
enhancement of financial powers of the CBI, th e Committee would also like to suggest that an 
Internal Financial Advisor for CBI may be appo inted to render expert advice on financial 
matters since similar system is already functioning in Central Police Organisations.

2.13 The Committee is unhappy over the status of budg etary allocation to CBI, especially under 
the Plan Heads. For example, under Plan section of Major Head 2055, i.e., Modernisation of

Actuals are less than Budget Allocation each ye ar. The Committee finds that the reply of the 
Ministry for explaining the gap between BE and Actuals is not satisfactory and is indicative of 
their casual approach  in the matter. The Committee feels that  more funds should be provided

CHAPTER-III 
POLICIES, PROGRAMMES AND SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY  
I. CITIZENS’ CHARTER  
3.0 As per the Annual Report of the Ministry, for the year 2004-05 the Citizens’ Charter initiative in 
the Union Government started in 1996-97 and received endorsement of the State Governments/UT 
Administrations in the Conference of Chief Ministers held in May, 1997. As per the Action Plan for 
effective and responsive administration, it was decided that both Central and State Governments 
would formulate Citizens’ Charters starting with those Ministries/Departments/Organisations which 
have a large public interface. A Core Group under the Chairmanship of Secretary, Ministry of 
Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is functi oning to examine the draft Citizens’ Charters of 
Central Government Ministries/Departments/Organisations. 
3.1 The Ministry has stated that as on 31st March, 2005, 29 Ministries/Departments of Government 
of India have brought out 107 Citizens’ Charter and 24 State Governments/UT Administrations have 
brought out 629 Citizens’ Charter.  
3.2 When asked as to whether any proactive steps are being taken by the Union Government to 
motivate/encourage the State Governments/UT Admi nistration to come up with their Citizens’ 
Charters, the Ministry has given the following reply: 
“(i)  The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances has been 
promoting and coordinating the formulation and implementation of the Citizens’ Charter 
among various State Governments/ UTs besides Central Government 
Ministries/Departments. The Department has been issuing guidelines along with ‘Do’s and 
Don’ts’ from time to time for formulation of Citizens’ Charters. 
(ii) Regional Seminars on Citizens’ Charters are organised by the Department with a view 
to bring National and State level organisations along with other stakeholders including 
NGOs, intelligensia, media, etc. on the same platform to share experiences in the formulation 
and implementation of Citizens’ Charters. 
(iii)  It has been further informed that with a view to address the problem relating to lack of 
awareness about Citizens’ Charter amongst employees  and citizens as well as to initiate the 
process of consultation with stakeholders, th e Department took up a project of organizing 
Department specific awareness workshop on Citizens’ Charter for State Governments. 
(iv)  The Department brings out an annual advertisement in Hindi and in English in major 
newspapers across the country containing the details of Nodal Officers of Citizens’ Charters 
of Central Government Ministries/Departments/Organisations. 
(v)  The Department has got evaluated 20 selected Citizens’ Charters of Central 
Departments/Organisations and of State Governments, through a professional agency which 
provided the feedback on the implementation of the Charter initiatives in the concerned 
Departments and the evaluation proforma devised by them has been circulated to all Central 
Government Ministries/Departments and State Governments/UT Administrations. 
(vi) A professional agency is developing an appropriate ‘Charter Mark’ Scheme to 
encourage and reward improvement in public service delivery with reference to the 
commitments and standards notified in the Charter. 
 The implementation of Citizens’ Charter is an  ongoing exercise, as it has to reflect the 
extensive and continual changes taking place in the domain of public services. Indian 
Government continuously strives to serve the ci tizens in an effective and efficient way so as 
not only to meet but to exceed their expectations.” 
3.3 The Committee notes the initiati ve taken by the Ministry in promoting Citizens’ Charters. 
The Scheme took off in 1996-97 and so far all th e State Governments have not yet come up with 
their Citizens’ Charters. Further, at the Cent ral level about 29 Ministries/Departments of 

Government of India have brough t out such Charters. The Committ ee is of the opinion that all 
Central Government Ministries/Departments/O rganisations should be impressed upon to 
come out with their Citizens’ Charters. Besides, as the nodal Ministry in the Union Government, 
proactive steps should be continued to enco urage/motivate the State Governments in this 
direction. 
3.4 The Committee feels that the programme of Ch arter Mark is indeed laudable and should 
be used extensively to encourage/motivate the various Ministries/Departments to take the 
initiative. Further, the Committee feels that apart from organising Department specific 
awareness programmes and giving advertisements in the print media for spreading awareness, 
electronic media should  also be involved in popularizing the Citizens’ Charters as these have a 
wider mass appeal. 
3.5 The Committee would like to recommend that a proper reviewing mechanism should be in 
place to evaluate the various Charters and furn ish feedback on the im plementation of these 
Charters. They should be utilised to improve the lapses in the existing system.

3.13 The Committee observes that the Repo rt of the Standing Committee under the

III. TRAINING AND CAPACITY BUILDING INITIATIVES  
3.16 Training and capacity building of personnel has emerged as important prerequisites for an 
effective administration. In the era of globalization, with the advent of latest information technology 
methods, enriching of human resources has become an imperative need. During the discussion on 
Demands for Grants (2005-06) of the Ministry, the Secretary focused on this aspect at length. He 
informed the Committee that the Ministry has been thinking on the lines of evolving a composite 
training programme with attempts to evolve modern and advanced training modules and capacity 
building initiatives. The Secretary stated as below: 
“We have also initiated capacity building exerci ses. There are a large number of institutes in 
States and some of them are extremely good in stitutes and their efficiency is extremely 
laudable. We are trying to build up capacity through training, by purchase of equipment, 
exposing officers to foreign courses and such other things. For that we have got a budget, 
and we are also receiving assistance from bilateral funding agencies and multi-lateral 
funding agencies, which we are passing on to the State Governments.” 
3.17 However, when it was pointed out that allocation made under major Plan Schemes such as 
capacity building, provision of infrastructure, etc. has been meagre, the Ministry furnished the 
following reply: 
“.... training is a decentralized  activity and is carried out by different cadre controlling 
authorities and State Governments in respect of the employees who are directly under them. 
The primary responsibility of the Department of  Personnel and Training is only in respect of 
the Indian Administrative Service and the Central Secretariat Service. Apart from this, being 
a nodal agency for training, the Department helps in coordinating training programmes and 
also in the development of trainers in the St ates. Due to expansion of these activities, the 
allocation has gone up substantially during th e 10th Plan as compared to the 9th
 Plan 
period.” 
3.18 Replying to the query regarding the difference between BE and RE figures for the year 2004-05, 
the Ministry has furnished the following reply: 
“BE and RE for the year 2004-05 in respect of the training activities has been Rs. 29.49 crore 
and Rs. 25.41 crore respectively. The differen ce on account of training comes to only Rs. 
4.08 crore. The reduced allocation is primarily on account of the reduction in availability of 
funds from the Planning Commission.” 
3.19 When asked to furnish the reasons for the lack adaisical attitude of the Ministry regarding the 
setting up of State Training Institutes, the Ministry has stated as below: 
“Consequent upon the bifurcation of three States, new State Training Institutes were to be 
established by the respective State Governments and not by the Ministry. This Ministry had 
only allocated some funds for providing equipment to these State Training Institutes in the 
expectation that the respective State Governme nts would set up such institutes. Since the 
respective State Governments did not set up the institutes, the requisite support could not be 
provided. As such, there was no laxity on the part of the Ministry.” 
3.20 When it was asked about the reasons for variation between BE & RE (2003-04), the Ministry 
stated that in so far as training areas are concerned, the developmental activities as projected at the BE 
stage are being carried out. However, in view of the reduced availability of funds from the Planning 

Commission, at the RE stage, there had to be some rescheduling/rephasing of project activities. This 
means that certain activities, which were part of specific projects, were taken up at a slightly later 
stage. The major variations were in respect of the following projects/schemes. 
(Rs. in lakh) 
Scheme/project BE RE Actuals
 2003-04 2003-04 2003-04
Domestic funding of foreign training 900 725 724.85
Strengthening of State Training Institutions 550 160 140
Setting up of a Center for Public Policy at  400 275.00 221.2
IIM-Bangalore (UNDP grant component)  
3.21 Under the project on Strengthening of State Training Institutions, over 45 training modules had 
to be developed. Since the actual development of these training modules took longer than anticipated, 
activities which were planned subsequent to the development of these training modules had to be 
rescheduled. 
3.22 Under the project for setting up of Centre fo r Public Policy, UNDP grants were available for 
activities such as faculty development, payment of fees, up-gradation of the library and engagement of 
consultants, etc. Since this was an early stage in  the project, identification of faculty members for 
development and identification of the appropriate consultants took time. As a result these activities 
also had to be rephased. 
3.23 When the Ministry was asked about its comments as to whether any proposal to initiate training 
of middle and lower rung officials of the bureaucracy has been thought of, the following reply was 
furnished: 
“The Ministry is of the view that training of personnel who belong to the lower rungs of the 
bureaucracy is extremely important for facilitating good governance. However, as stated 
earlier, such training is carried out by the concerned cadre controlling authorities and the 
State Governments to whom such personnel belong. In order to draw attention to the value of 
training personnel at such levels, this Ministry has taken up a pilot project for training all the 
district level officers in one district in each of the seven States as follows: 
State District
Maharashtra Satara
Tamil Nadu Theni
West Bengal Burdhwan
Uttar Pradesh Sitapur
Bihar Vaishali
Rajasthan Kota
Madhya Pradesh Sehore
This initiative has been taken recently out of  some balance funds under the UNDP assisted 
project on Strengthening of State ATIs. The in itial feedback clearly highlights the critical 
importance of training Government functionaries at the lower rungs of the bureaucracy since 
they are the critical interface of the Government with the citizens. 
In view of the feedback received through this initiative, a proposal has been submitted to the 
Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region to provide funds for similar training in all 
the districts of the North East. A proposal is also being formulated for supporting similar 
training in other districts of the country. It is expected that the concerned cadre controlling 

authorities of the Central Government would take an initiative to train the lower rung 
employees of their own departments”. 
3.24 Dwelling on the issue of training, the Committee had earlier recommended that the Lal Bahadur 
Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA) should be adequately equipped to conduct 
programme for officers joining in Secretariat positions  as well as other services. When asked as to 
whether any such proposal has been considered by the Academy, the Ministry stated that the Academy 
has been conducting courses in which officers drawn from secretariat positions have been exposed to 
ethical frameworks that policy makers can use for resolving complicated public policy issues. During 
the last five years, the LBSNAA conducted 9 courses on ethical issues and 268 officers attended these 
programmes. The courses are open to all IAS officer s as well as officers from other services working 
in Central Secretariat. Such courses are proposed to be conducted during the coming years as well. 
3.25 Further the Ministry has informed that a module on “Evaluation of Training” has been 
developed. A total of seven Training of Trainers co urses on Evaluation of Training have so far been 
conducted, in which, 146 trainers from various training institutes have been trained. These trainers can 
now conduct further programmes in their respective institutes. During the training year 2005-06, it is 
proposed to conduct an additional seven Training of Trainers courses on “Evaluation of Training”. 
3.26 The Committee is of the opinion that traini ng is the most important component in the 
efficient functioning of any administrative set up. Though the Ministry has furnished lengthy 
notes on the various aspects of training, the activities run far short of expectation. The funds 
allocated for the functioning of various State Tr aining Institutes have remained unutilised as 
these have not yet been established. Though the Ministry states that this falls under the realm of 
State Governments, the Committee is  of the opinion that the Centra l Ministry has to take a far 
more proactive step in impressing upon the States to initiate measures in this direction. 
3.27 The Committee further recommends that tr aining of middle and lower rung officials 
should be taken up with utmost priority to improve the administ rative set up. For this purpose, 
adequate funds should be alloca ted in the Union budget and the in stitutes of excellence such as 
the LBSNAA, the Centre for Public Policy, I ndian Institute of Management, Bangalore etc 
should be involved. 
IV.  ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS  
3.28 As per the Annual Report of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, it has 
been operating two Plan Schemes namely, ‘Scheme on Modernisation of Government Offices’ and 
‘Scheme on Administrative Reforms’, the former from 1986 and the latter from 2000-01. These two 
Schemes have been merged from the year 2002- 03 and a composite Plan Scheme under the 
nomenclature ‘Plan Scheme on Administrative Reforms’ has been formulated. The World Bank 
Project on ‘Capacity 
Building for Good Governance’ is also part of this Plan Scheme. The Scheme, inter alia, provides for 
empanelment of professional/research agencies to pilot projects on Administrative Reforms in the 
following areas: 
  (1) Evolution of Benchmarking; 
  (2) Application of Information Technology; 
  (3) Research Projects on Administrative Reforms; 
  (4) Development of Knowledge Management Systems; and 
  (5) Assessment of Quality in Government. 
 A Steering Committee has been set up to oper ationalise the various proposals under this 
Scheme. Some of the Schemes which are under implementation include: 

  (1) Setting up of Wide Area Network (WAN); 
  (2) Evaluation of Efficiency and Productivity in Government; 
  (3) Less Paper Office Initiativ e in the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public 
   Grievances; and 
  (4) Change Management Project. 
3.29 On being asked as to how does the Government propose to bring about administrative reforms 
in the context of advent of information technology on a large scale, the Ministry has stated that 
information technology would be used for effective and quick delivery of public services which will 
be the focus of administrative reforms. Already 22 mission mode projects have been identified under 
the National  e-Governance Plan for implementa tion by the concerned Ministry/Department on 
priority basis. These are as follows: 
Central Government State Governments Integrated Services 
Income Tax Land Reco rds Electronic Data 
Interchange  
  (EDI/E-commerce) 
Passport, Visa, Immigration Road Transport E-Biz 
DCA21 Property Registration Common Service Centres 
Insurance Agricult ure India Portal 
National Citizen Database Treasuries E-Government Gateway 
Central Excise Municipalities  
Pensions Gram Panchayats  
Banking Commercial Taxes  
 Police  
3.30 During the year 2004-05, an amount of Rs. 190 lakh had been allocated at RE stage, out of 
which an amount of Rs. 154.15 lakh has already been utilized. In view of the greater number of 
projects to be taken up through empanelled agencies, an amount of Rs. 250 lakh is proposed to be kept 
for the year 2005-06. 
3.31 The Ministry has furnished an overall financial status of the Scheme. During the 10th Plan 
period, a total allocation of Rs. 11.47 crore was earmarked for Pilo t Projects. During the first three 
years till 30th March 2005, an amount of Rs. 6.067 crore has been utilized for Pilot Projects, which 
comes to 53 per cent of the total budgetary allocation of Rs. 11.47 crore. 
3.32 The Government in its National Common Minimum Programme has, inter alia envisaged 
setting up of an Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) to prepare a detailed blueprint for 
revamping the public administration system. A Task Force has been set up to finalise the Terms of 
Reference for the ARC. The Ministry has informed that the proposal is awaiting approval of the 
Cabinet. After Government’s approval becomes ava ilable, constitution of ARC will be notified along 
with detailed Terms of Reference. 
3.33 The Committee is pleased to note that a number of initiatives have been taken for 
reforming the administrative system of the count ry and making it modern in tune with the 
requirement of time. However, the Committee is  constrained to observe that despite the 
initiatives in new programmes and schemes a nd claims being made by the Government 
regarding the use of information technology as a benchmark of administrative reforms, results 

in terms of concrete outcomes are yet to em erge. The Plan Scheme of Modernisation of 
Government Offices, which was earlier a distinct  scheme was launched in the year 1987-88 to 
help the Ministries/Departments modernize thei r offices. Since then an amount of Rs. 24.30 
crore has been sanctioned for implementation of only 330 proposals, which averages to about 18 
proposals in a year. The Committee feels that a fa r greater pace is needed to bring about any 
palpable change in the administrative set up of  the nation. The Committee is not satisfied with 
the reply of the Ministry that since inception of the Scheme, an amount of Rs. 27.20 crore has 
actually been disbursed by the Department fo r 341 proposals including  those of the current 
financial year. Moreover, the funding pattern of 75:25 between the Union Government and the 
concerned Ministry raises doubt that in case th e concerned Ministry fails to invest the amount 
required of it, the projects will not be forthcomin g. The Committee feels that instead of the fund 
sharing pattern, a central pool should be co nstituted with allocation to the various 
Ministries/Departments as per their needs. Further it should be made mandatory for the 
Ministries/Departments to initiate project proposals pertaining to modernization and 
administrative reforms. 
3.34 The Committee recommends that similar to the initiative of Charter Mark, whereby 
agencies that are implementing their Citizens ’ Charters exemplarily and are providing an 
excellent standard of service, receive certifica tion/recognition in the fo rm of a ‘Charter Mark’ 
after an independent assessment, rewards /incentives should be given to the 
Ministry/Department excelling in implementing the projects on administrative reforms. 
3.35 The Committee while noting the fact that init iatives in Administrative Reforms are being 
taken at the Centre/Union Government level, fe els concerned about the progress made by the 
State Governments in this direction. True  reform can only take place when the 
benefits/advantages percolate to the masses at the grassroot level. The Committee observes that 
very little has been done in this regard by th e nodal Union Ministry of Personnel, Public 
Grievances and Pensions. The Committee recommends  that concrete steps should be taken to 
motivate/encourage the State Governments to come  up with such initiatives. If needed, Central 
allocation should be made for the State Gov ernments for taking up ad ministrative reforms 
scheme. 
3.36 The Committee notes the recent decision of the Union Cabinet, as reported in the media, to 
set up the Second Administrative  Reforms Commission to prepa re a blueprint for revamping 
the public administration system. The Commission would reportedly go into the whole gamut of 
issues relating to public administration. The Committee urges upon the Government to finalise 
the terms of reference for the Comm ission at the earliest, so th at it starts functioning and 
completes its work within the stipulated period. 
V. CIVIL SERVICES REFORMS  
3.37 The Annual Report of the Ministry states that the Government has constituted a Committee 
under the Chairmanship of Shri P.C. Hota, former  Chairman, UPSC and Secretary (P) to examine the 
whole gamut of Civil Service Reforms and make suitable recommendations to the Government. The 
Hota Committee submitted its Report to the Cabinet Secretary on 30.07.2004. 
3.38 When asked about the Government’s plan of action regarding consideration of the Report, it has 
been stated that the Hota Committee’s recommendations relating to (i) reduction of age limit for 
recruitment to civil services; (ii) weeding out of corrupt officers; (iii) changes in service rules so as not 
to use suspension as an instrument to intimidate; (iv) protection to honest civil servants; (v) code of 
ethics for civil servants; (vi) drawing up a model code of governance benchmarking the standards of 
governance; 
(vii) improving accountability in service delivery are under consideration of the Government. 

3.39 Further, it has been informed that the Government had appointed the following Committees on 
Civil Service Reforms and reforms in governan ce apart from the Hota Committee as mentioned 
before: 
  (a) Surinder Nath Committee on Performan ce Appraisal, Promotion, Empanelment and 
Placement for the All India Services and other Group A Services (2003); 
  (b) Yugandhar Committee on In-service Training (2003); and 
  (c) Alagh Committee on Recruitment and Selection Procedure (2001). 
Recommendations made by these Committees are bei ng considered and future reform measures will 
be initiated based on the decisions taken thereon. Further, it has been informed that the ARC will be 
requested to look into the suggestions made by various Committees in the area of recruitment into 
Civil Services while finalizing recommendations. 
3.40 On the issue of establishing a Civil Service College, the Ministry has informed that it is at a 
preliminary stage and Educational Consultants India Limited has been asked to prepare a preliminary 
report which is yet to be received. They have been reminded to expedite the same. The matter would 
be discussed in greater detail after the preliminary re port is received so that the future course of action 
can be finalized. 
3.41 The Committee notes the fact that a number of  expert Committees have been constituted 
and all of them have subm itted their Reports. However, any conc rete step is yet to be taken by 
the Government in this regard. The Committee understands that in a large democracy like India 
with an intricate and complex bur eaucratic set up in place, subs tantial groundwork is needed 
before initiating any overhaul of the system. But in this age of gl obalisation, fast decisions and 
their implementation are the call of the d ay. Therefore, the Committee desires that the 
recommendations of all these Commi ttees should be expeditiousl y examined and a framework 
should be prepared for carrying out civil serv ice reforms without any fu rther delay. In this 
context, the Committee strongly feels that th e appointment of the Second Administrative 
Reforms Commission should not co me in the way of implementation of recommendations made 
by the various Committees on Civil Services Reforms. 
3.42 The Committee also recommends that the form alities relating to establishment of Civil 
Service College should be completed as soon as po ssible and the institute be set up at the earliest 
with all modern infrastructure. 
VI. GOOD GOVERNANCE  
3.43 The issue of good governance came to the fore during the meeting of the Committee on 
Demands for Grants (2005-06) of the Ministry. It was stressed that in this age of globalisation, 
governance should be tuned to the need of the pe ople and has to amalgamate changes to keep pace 
with the administrative requirements in a fast changing global environment. 
3.44 The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances has taken up for 
implementation the Sub-Project on Capacity Building for Good Governance with technical assistance 
from World Bank under the broad Project for Technical Assistance for Economic Reforms. The Sub-
Project comprises the following three major components: 
  (1) Conceptualizing and implementing a Charter Mark Scheme for recognizing excellence 
in the implementation of Citizens’ Charters; Public Grievance Redress mechanism 
rating model; 
   A scheme of Awards to institutions for excellence in Public Service Delivery; 
  (2) Training and Capacity Building of Government Employees for management of records; 
and 

  (3) Documentation and dissemination of best practices and setting up of a facility with 
digital repository of best practices and resources to support good governance initiative. 
3.45 During the meeting of the Committee, the Secretary informed the Committee about the 
Conference of Chief Secretaries on “Good Governance, Administrative Reforms and Related Issues” 
which was held recently under the Chairmanship of  Cabinet Secretary. As the Secretary stated, the 
idea was to take the States on board about the future  reforms initiative and to understand the problems 
that they are facing. At the end of the conference , it was decided that a Model Code of Governance 
would be drawn up which would enshrine the fundamental principles and benchmarks of good 
governance. This will be a comprehensive document covering all areas of governance including 
ethics, service delivery, efficiency, accountability etc. 
3.46 Further, the Secretary informed that a series of  meetings of the District Collectors were being 
held. At these Conferences , young officers share their experiences regarding the happenings at the 
grass root levels. As the Secretary stated: 
“These regional conferences are throwing valuable information and pointing out what 
exactly is going on there and wh at are the expectations of thes e officers. We held a larger 
Conference in May in order to crystallize th e way forward about service delivery at the 
district level.” 
3.47 The Committee appreciates the initiatives ta ken by the Government in the direction of 
establishing good gove rnance in the country. The Committee is  of the view that more funds 
should be allocated in the Un ion Budget for carrying out schemes under the Good Governance 
project. However, only allocation of funds will  not serve the purpose. Proper review mechanism 
should be in place to see that available f unds are optimally utilised and concrete physical 
progress takes place.  
3.47.1 Moreover the Committee feels that governance can be termed as good only when the 
benefits/advantages percolate to the bottom. Rather than keeping these initiatives restricted to 
the Central level, serious effort is needed to initiate such measures amongst the State 
Governments, which in turn can encourage/motiva te the grassroot level organisations to follow 
such practices. More such Conferences of distri ct level officials should be held so that 
experiences from the grassroots can be shared  at a wider forum and future initiatives are 
decided based on consent. 
VII.  NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF SMART GOVERNMENT (NISG)  
3.48 Setting up of NISG was one of the 108 recommendations of the National Task Force on 
Information Technology and Software Development. However, the Ministry has stated that no funds 
were released and no projects were entrusted to  NISG as the proposal for approval of NISG was 
pending approval of the Cabinet. 
3.49 When asked about the reasons for delay in setting up of NISG and making it functional despite 
an allocation of Rs. 9 crore under the Tenth Five Y ear Plan, the Ministry has informed that NISG has 
started its operation from its headquarters located in the campus of International Institute of 
Information Technology (IIT), Hyderabad. Chief Executive Officer of NISG has taken charge with 
effect from 6th November, 2003. Presently the ins titute is involved in projects such as UNDP 
sponsored project ICT for Development, DC A 21, e-Biz, Bangalore One, e-Governance Gateway etc. 
3.50 However, explaining the causes for delay in establishing the institute, the Ministry has informed 
that funds allocated under the 10
th plan could not be utilized as Cabinet’s approval/endorsement for 
setting up of NISG and equity contribution of the Government was awaited. For obtaining Cabinet’s 
approval, a Cabinet note seeking inter alia endorsement/approval for the setting up of NISG was 
prepared in February 2004 and was approved by the then Minister in-charge for consideration in the 
Cabinet. However, with the change of Government at the Centre, the Cabinet Note was returned and 
the Cabinet Secretariat directed the Department to obtain fresh approval of the Minister in-charge in 

the new Government after fresh inter-Ministerial consultations and to submit a revised Cabinet Note. 
Accordingly, consultations were made with the Ministry of Finance, Department of Information 
Technology and the Planning Commission and based on their comments, a fresh Cabinet Note was 
prepared and approved by the present Prime Minister, being Minister in-charge. 
3.51 The Cabinet has now approved/endorsed the proposal for setting up of NISG and the proposal 
for equity contribution to NISG on 24.03.05. Action to release the equity share is being taken. 
3.52 The Committee is unhappy to no te that even after proper allo cation of funds in the 10th 
Plan period for establishment of NISG, del ay has taken place in its establishment and 
functioning. The Committee is not convinced wi th the reason which the Ministry has adduced 
for the delay in the establishment of the institute. The Committee is  of the opinion that in order 
to fast track development initia tives, all such Governmental and bureaucratic hassles should be 
streamlined. 
3.53 The Committee is also not satisfied with the mere reply that NISG has started functioning 
from its present location in Hyderabad. Rather, it would like to know the details of activities 
taken up by the NISG so far alon g with expenditure incurred for such activities. Further, the 
Committee recommends that all formalities relating to the operationalisation of NISG should be 
completed without any further delay and all steps should be taken to ensure its smooth 
functioning. 
VIII. e-GOVERNANCE 
3.54 E-Governance has emerged as a focus area in the modern system of administration. During the 
discussion in the Committee on Demands for Grants (2005-06) of the Ministry, the Secretary(P) stated 
that capacity building exercises are being taken up in the realm of e-Governance. To quote from his 
submissions:- 
“In cooperation with other Ministries like the Ministry of Information Technology and 
Cabinet Secretariat, there is a Group of Secretaries which gives guidance in this regard. We 
have tried to work out an arrangement whereby the e-governance initiatives are all focused 
and they are all planned as per a time bound programme. These initiatives, which are 21 in 
number are currently monitored by the Cabinet Secretary and it is our hope that once they 
have run their full course, there shall be a significant impact on e-governance.” 
3.55 It has been further in formed that as a part of this initia tive, the Institute of e-Governance has 
been established which is an attempt to create an effective model for public-private partnership in 
matters of capacity building. The objective would be to make this institute to be able to leverage the 
capacities which are available all over the country, especially in the private sector for achieving fast 
results. The matter has been approved by the Cabine t. As the Secretary has stated, Rs. 1 crore has 
already been released for this institute and more money would be subsequently disbursed. The 
magnitude and scope of this institute would be quite vast. 
3.56 The Committee feels that the progress made in the direction of e- governance is laudable 
and appreciates the initiatives taken by the Un ion Government in this direction. The Committee 
is of the opinion that the benefits of informat ion technology should be utilised to the optimum 
and lack of resources should not hamper the development process on this count. 
Ministry/Department specific projects should be undertaken with an efficient monitoring system 
and regular feedback. Efforts should be ma de to involve foreign agencies and more 
bilateral/multilateral projects should be undert aken whereby foreign investments and technical 
know-how may be utilised. Best practices in this field from across the world may be thoroughly 
examined and followed suitable to the Indian context. 

3.57 The Committee feels that a holistic approach  is needed to sprea d the e-governance 
initiatives in every nook and corner of the country. State Governments should be impressed 
upon to undertake such measures  and necessary funds should be made available at their 
disposal to carry out such activities. A coordi nated approach between the Centre and the States 
will go a long way in utilizing the benefits of  information technology in the process of 
governance. 
IX. ANNUAL REPORTS  
3.58 The Committee in its earlier Report had taken up the issue of inordinate delay in submission of 
Annual Reports of various organisations and offices such as Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), 
Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), CBI etc.  It was recommended by the Committee that a 
time frame should be prescribed for each stage of processing and laying of Annual Reports, so that the 
Committee could examine the Annual Report of th e preceding year while examining Demands for 
Grants of the succeeding year. In its reply, the Mi nistry has stated that prescribing a suitable time 
frame for laying the Annual Reports of the CVC and UPSC in Parliament is under examination of the 
Government. During the discussion on Demands for Grants (2005-06), the issue regarding late 
submission of Annual Reports came to the fore. The Ministry in its reply has furnished the status of 
Annual Reports of the various bodies/offices under its purview, which is as follows:  
Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) 
The latest Annual Report of UPSC for the year 2003-2004 has since been received and will be laid 
before the Parliament as soon as the explanatory memorandum is finalized.  
Staff Selection Commission (SSC) 
So far as SSC’s Annual Report is concerned, it is prepared and published after the close of the 
financial year covering its recruitment activities from 1st April to 31st March. SSC’s Annual Report is 
for official use and is circulated in the Ministries and Departments and not tabled in the Parliament. 
Their Annual Report for the period 2004-05 is under preparation and is likely to be published and 
circulated by the end of the first quarter of the current financial year.  
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) 
As per Section 14(1) of the CVC Act, the Annual Report of the CVC should be submitted within 6 
months of the close of the year. The CVC, theref ore, has time up to June, 2005 to submit its Annual 
Report for the year 2004. The CVC has been informed of the observation of the Committee. 
Kendriya Bhandar 
Kendriya Bhandar is governed by the provision of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002. 
As per the provisions of this Act, the audited statements of accounts, audit report and Annual Report 
are required to be considered in the General Body meeting within 6 months after the close of the 
corresponding year. The Annual Report and the Audite d Statement of Accounts for the year 2004-05 
is, therefore, required to be considered by the General Body before 30.09.2005. Only after the General 
Body has approved the same, the Report can be sent by the Kendriya Bhandar to the Government. 
These are required to be laid in the Parliament before 31.12.2005.  
Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA)  
It has been noted by the Comm ittee that the Annual Report of  LBSNAA (2004) gives information 
about the various courses, curriculum and research units of the Institution. However, it falls short of 
giving any progress report of the Academy, data regarding various programmes taken up during the 
year, utilisation of budget allocation and an overall critical evaluation of th e activities during the past 
one year. 

3.59 The Ministry has replied that these suggestio ns of the Committee are extremely valuable and 
will be communicated to th e LBSNAA so that these are kept in  mind while preparing Annual Report 
in future. 
3.60 The Committee notes the procedure regarding s ubmission and status of Annual Reports of 
the various offices and organisations under the ad ministrative charge of the Ministry. In this 
context, the Committee would lik e to recommend that Annual Repo rts should be presented to 
Parliament on time and made available to the Committee so that it can carry out a proper study 
thereof. Further, it is felt that Annual Report s reflect the total functi oning of the concerned 
Ministry or offices under it. It will  be fruitful if instead of giving  only the positive side of the 
scheme of things, a critical evaluation and assessment of the functioning of the organisations will 
go a long way in its improvement. Rather than be ing repetitive year after year, while furnishing 
details about projects and schemes, an objectiv e approach should be adopted in framing the 
Annual Report.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel,
Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorised by the Committee on its behalf, do hereby
present the Fiftieth Report on The Prevention of Bribery of Foreign Public Officials and Officials of
Public International Organisations Bill, 2011. The Bill seeks to prevent corruption relating to bribery
of foreign public officials and officials of public international organisations and for matters connected
therewith or incidental thereto.
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee,
the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred
♣ the Bill, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on the
25th March, 2011 and pending therein, to this Committee on the 1 st April, 2011 for examination and
report.
3. Keeping in view the importance of the Bill, the Committee decided to issue a press communique
to solicit views/suggestions from desirous individuals/organisations on the provisions of the Bill.
Accordingly, a press communique was issued in national and local newspapers and dailies, in response
to which memoranda containing suggestions were received, from various organizations/ individuals/
experts, by the Committee.
4. The Committee heard the presentation of the Secretary, Department of Personnel and Training,
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions on the provisions of the Bill in its meeting held
on 15
th June, 2011. The representatives of DoPT made one more presentation before the Committee
on the 12 th March, 2012 to clarify certain provisions of the Bill. The Committee also heard the views
of stakeholders/NGOs in its meetings held on 10 th and 24 th January, 2012.
5. While considering the Bill, the Committee took note of the following documents/information
placed before it :–
(i) Background note on the Bill submitted by the Department of Personnel and Training,
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions;
(ii) V iews/suggestions contained in the memoranda received from various organisations/
institutions/individuals/experts on the provisions of the Bill and the comments of the
Department of Personnel and Training thereon;
(iii) V iews expressed during the oral evidence tendered before the Committee by the stakeholders
such as office bearers of CII, PHD Chamber of Commerce, FICCI and ASSOCHAM; and
Central Vigilance Commissioner, Director, CBI; Director of Enforcement; and other non-
official witnesses viz. Shri Ravinder Kumar and Shri Radhey Shyam Agarwal in its
meetings held on the 10
th and 24 th January, 2012; and
(iv) Other research material/documents related to the Bill.

1
REPORT
The Prevention of Bribery of Foreign Public Officials and Officials of Public International
Organisations Bill, 2011 was introduced* in the Lok Sabha on the 25 th March, 2011. It was referred ♣
by the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha to the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice on the 1
st April, 2011 for examination and report.
2. The Bill (Annexure-A) seeks to prevent corruption relating to bribery of foreign public officials
and officials of public international organisations and for matters connected therewith or incidental
thereto.
3. The Statement of Objects and Reasons, appended to the Bill reads as under:–
“Bribery of public officials to obtain advantages in international business raises serious moral
and political concerns, undermines good governance and sustainable economic development,
and distorts competition. Corruption in awarding business contracts has social, political,
environmental and economic costs which no country can afford. Serious consequences result
when public officials take bribes in awarding contracts to foreign businesses for public services
such as roads, water, electricity etc. resulting in inappropriate decisions and undermining plans
for development.
2. The United Nations Convention against Corruption  annexed to the Resolution 58/4  of
31st October, 2003 was adopted by the General Assembly of the United Nations and opened
it for signature at the High-level Political Signing  Conference held in Merida, Mexico, from
9th to 11th December, 2003. India has signed the Convention on 9
th December, 2005. The
ratification of Convention would require criminalising the act of foreign bribery and it would
strengthen India’ s existing anti-corruption laws that demonstrate India’ s commitment to good
governance and  give more credibility in its fight against bribery and corruption.
3. India already has in place a framework for combating  corruption under certain laws,
namely, the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 and the Prevention of Money  laundering Act,
2002 which covers a number of areas that need international standards for the criminalisation
of bribery. Article 16  of the Convention requires that each State Party shall adopt such
legislative and other measures as may be necessary to establish as a criminal offence, the
giving or taking of undue advantage to or by a foreign public official or an official of a
public international  organisation, directly or indirectly, for the official himself or herself or
another person or entity when committed  intentionally. However, the bribery of foreign public
officials in international business transactions is not covered under the above said Acts.
Therefore, a need has been felt to bring a legislation to give effect to the aforesaid Convention.
4. The Prevention of Bribery of Foreign Public Officials and Officials of Public International
Organisations Bill, 2011 seeks to prevent corruption relating to bribery of foreign public
officials and officials of public international organisations and for matters connected therewith
or incidental thereto. The proposed legislation, inter alia,—
(a) prohibits accepting gratification by foreign public official or official of public international
organization and making such act punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall
not be less than six months but which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable
to fine;
